p: Welcome to the first lesson. Today we look at the tool you will use throughout the course and on exam day: the Level 3 Systematic Approach to Tasting Wine, the SAT. It is a way of describing a wine completely and in a fixed order, and then drawing two conclusions from that description: how good the wine is, and whether it will improve with time. It is not how you would drink a glass with friends; it is rigorous, almost clinical. But that is exactly why it stops you from missing anything.

The aim is to build two skills. First, describing a wine accurately. Second, reasoning from that description to logical conclusions. In the exam, that is precisely what the examiners look for: have you correctly identified the aromas, flavours and structural components, and have you drawn sensible conclusions about quality and readiness?

How is the grid laid out? The first part has three sections: appearance, nose and palate. Each section lists headings on the left and, on the right, the terms you may use. For the appearance of a white, for example, you might choose clear for clarity, pale for intensity and lemon for colour. The second part is the conclusions section, with two headings: quality level and readiness for drinking. Here you must always use the terms on the grid. On the back of the SAT you will find the Wine-Lexicon, a list of aroma and flavour descriptors.

One essential rule: where the terms are separated by dashes, you choose just one. If a red seems to sit between ruby and garnet, do not write ruby-garnet or ruby to garnet; you would lose the mark for being imprecise. Pick one; if the examiner accepts both as valid, you still get the mark. And use exactly those words: for intensity, pale, medium or deep, nothing else. Headings introduced by "for example", such as aroma characteristics, are different: there you are not restricted, although the lexicon is strongly recommended.

The scales. At Level 2 they had three points, such as acidity low, medium, high. At Level 3 the middle band is split into three: medium minus, medium and medium plus. That gives a five-point scale, but the points are not evenly spaced: medium plus means medium, but towards the top of that band. The medium band was split because that is where most wines fall. Do not be afraid of the extremes: if an acidity feels high, but you have tasted something even sharper, remember that high also has its own shades.

Before tasting, prepare the room and yourself. You need good natural light, no competing smells, space for glasses and notes, and spittoons close by. Your palate should be clean: no toothpaste just before, no strongly flavoured food. Drink water, because a dry mouth picks up aromas less well, and spitting many wines also means losing saliva. Glasses must be clear, odour-free and without detergent residue. The ISO tasting glass is ideal: its rounded bowl lets you swirl, and its narrower rim concentrates the aromas. Pour the same amount each time: around fifty millilitres is enough to assess everything and swirl without spilling.

On to appearance. Clarity has only two options: clear or hazy. Almost all wines are clear; a hazy wine may be faulty, but only the nose and palate will tell you. Some wines are deliberately hazy, but they will not appear in the exam.

Colour intensity is judged by tilting the glass to forty-five degrees and seeing how far the colour reaches from the core, the deepest part, out to the rim, where the wine is thinnest. For reds you can also look down into an upright glass and try to see the stem: if you can see it clearly through the wine, the intensity is pale; if you cannot see it at all, it is deep. All whites look colourless at the rim: one with a wide, watery rim is pale; one whose colour reaches almost to the edge is deep.

Colour is separate from intensity: it is the mix of red, blue, yellow, green or brown. For whites and rosés, look at the core, where colour shows best; for reds, look at the rim, because the core is often nearly opaque. For whites the range runs from lemon-green through lemon, the most common, to gold, amber and brown; the last two usually mean very old or deliberately oxidised wines. For reds, from purple, with blue or violet tints, to ruby, the most common, then garnet, with orange or brown hints but still more red than brown, then tawny, more brown than red, and finally brown. For rosés: pink, salmon when there are orange hints, and orange when the colour itself is orange, which is rare.

Other observations. All wines form legs, or tears, on the glass: more sugar or alcohol makes them slower. A deposit usually means the wine was not fined or filtered. Some still wines have a slight spritz: sometimes a fault, such as refermentation in bottle, but some light whites are deliberately bottled with a little carbon dioxide for freshness. With sparkling wines, the look of the bubbles also depends on how clean the glass is, so it is not a reliable sign of quality.
Now the nose. Swirl, bring your nose to the rim and take a short sniff. You assess four things: condition, intensity, aroma characteristics and development.

Condition asks: is the wine sound or faulty? Faults are not assessed in the exam, but you should know them. Cork taint, or TCA, smells of damp cardboard and mutes the fruit. Reduction recalls rotten eggs, boiled cabbage or drains; at low levels it can even add complexity, and it often blows off with air. Too much sulfur dioxide stings like a freshly struck match; the highest levels are found in sweet whites. Oxidation is the opposite of reduction: a deeper colour heading towards brown, notes of caramel, honey or coffee, and less fruit; but some wines are made in an oxidative style on purpose. Out-of-condition wines have lost their freshness because they are too old or were stored badly. Volatile acidity, at high levels, smells of vinegar or nail varnish remover; at low levels it can lift complexity. Brettanomyces gives animal, sticking-plaster, leather or horse-sweat notes: some drinkers enjoy a little of it.

Intensity on the nose: if you can smell the aromas without deliberately sniffing, they are pronounced; if you struggle even when sniffing, they are light; everything else sits in the medium band, with its three shades.

Characteristics: aromas are primary, secondary or tertiary. Primary aromas come from the grape and from alcoholic fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbaceous notes, spice, wet stones. A simple wine has a few aromas from one group; a complex one has many, and varied. Secondary aromas come from winemaking after fermentation: vanilla and toast from oak, butter from malolactic conversion, bread and biscuit from lees and autolysis. Tertiary aromas come from ageing: if oxidative, such as long ageing in wood, think coffee, caramel and nuts; if protected from oxygen, as in long bottle ageing, think petrol, honey and mushroom. Either way, fresh fruit turns cooked or dried. But be careful: dried or cooked fruit can also show in young wines made from dried grapes or grown in very hot climates.

Development. If primary and secondary aromas dominate, the wine is youthful. If some tertiary notes are starting to appear, it is developing. If tertiary aromas lead, it is fully developed. And when the attractive aromas fade and unpleasant ones arrive, it is tired, past its best. Some wines are released already developing, like a Rioja Reserva, or already fully developed, like age-indicated tawny Ports and all Sherries. And not every wine improves: almost all rosés, many inexpensive whites and many cheap reds go from youthful to tired within months.
On the palate there are many components, and they affect each other: alcohol and fruit, for example, can give an impression of sweetness. Take several sips.

Sweetness runs from dry through off-dry, medium-dry, medium-sweet and sweet to luscious. Many inexpensive wines keep a little noticeable sugar: they are off-dry. Classic sweet wines such as Sauternes or most Ports are sweet; wines whose sugar almost sticks to your lips, like Rutherglen Muscat or Pedro Ximénez Sherry, are luscious.

Acidity makes your mouth water, and that is the best clue. The main acids are tartaric and malic from the grape, plus lactic from malolactic conversion. Cool-climate wines have high acidity. Remember that sugar and acid mask each other, and that alcohol can give a similar burning sensation, so always check for that mouth-watering effect.

Tannins are felt on the gums above the front teeth: they dry the mouth and can add bitterness. They are assessed for reds only. Look at both the amount and the nature. A cheap Pinot Noir from barely ripe grapes may have medium tannins that are hard and astringent; a premium Shiraz from a warm region may have high tannins that are ripe and velvety. If the astringency is high but the wine feels light, the tannin level is actually low; if astringency is low but the mouth feels full, the tannins are high.

Alcohol gives warmth and body. The bands: low is below eleven per cent, medium from eleven to thirteen point nine, high from fourteen upwards. For fortified wines: low from fifteen to sixteen point four, medium from sixteen point five to eighteen point four, high from eighteen point five upwards.

Body is the overall sense of weight in the mouth. It comes mostly from alcohol, then from sugar; high acidity makes a wine feel lighter, ripe tannins add weight, while hard, astringent tannins can make it feel lean.

For sparkling wines you assess the mousse: delicate, creamy or aggressive. A creamy mousse is generally expected; an aggressive one explodes on the palate and then vanishes; a delicate one, fine and soft, is often found in wines with long ageing or bottled at lower pressure.

Flavour intensity and characteristics follow the same logic as the nose. As the wine warms in your mouth, earthy, spicy and toasty notes become more obvious, while fruit and floral notes can recede a little.

The finish is how long the pleasant sensations last after you swallow or spit. A lingering bitterness is a bitter aftertaste, not a long finish. Simple wines fade within seconds; great wines can last a minute or more.

Finally, conclusions. For quality, use four criteria, remembered as BLIC: balance, length, intensity and complexity. Balance is like a pair of scales: fruit and sugar on one side, acidity and tannin on the other, and every element, including alcohol and oak, must be well integrated. Intensity matters, but beyond a certain point it adds no more quality. Length of finish usually goes hand in hand with intensity. Complexity can come from primary aromas alone. An outstanding wine meets all four criteria; very good, three; good, two; acceptable, one; poor, none. There are also faulty wines, which are not assessed.

For readiness, ask yourself: is this a wine made to develop? A wine with only primary aromas, low acidity and little tannin is not: drink now, not suitable for ageing or further ageing. A wine with firm structure, good acidity and concentrated flavours will improve: primary fruit gives way to tertiary notes and tannins soften, while alcohol, sugar and acidity stay the same, even if sweet wines seem a little drier with age. If it is enjoyable now but can still grow: can drink now, but has potential for ageing. If drinking it now would be a waste: too young. If it has already given its best: drink now, not suitable for further ageing. And if only decline is left: too old.

To sum up: three descriptive sections, appearance, nose and palate, and two conclusions, quality and readiness. One term where there are dashes, five-point scales, and BLIC for quality. Practise often, because the real secret of this method is calibrating your palate against other tasters.

In this lesson we look at how food and wine affect each other. The aim of pairing is simple: together they should give more pleasure than either would alone, and above all we want to avoid unpleasant combinations. One key starting point: we do not all have the same sensitivity. The same level of bitterness can bother one person a great deal and another hardly at all. Then there is preference: some people love strong sensations, others do not. That is why a perfect pairing for one person can seem ordinary, or even unsuccessful, to another. Always think about the person as well as the principles.

Let's start with what happens in the mouth. When you eat, your taste buds adapt and change how you perceive whatever you taste next. Think of orange juice right after brushing your teeth: it tastes painfully sour. Some foods, such as chocolate or thick creamy sauces, coat the mouth and dull the sense of taste. And generally, food changes wine more than wine changes food, and usually for the worse.

Remember this golden rule. Two components in food make wine taste harder: more astringent, bitter and acidic, and less sweet and fruity. They are sweetness and umami. Two make wine taste softer: less bitter, astringent and acidic, sweeter and fruitier. They are salt and acid.

Umami in food increases the perception of bitterness, astringency, acidity and the warming effect of alcohol, and decreases body, sweetness and fruitiness. Umami is a taste in its own right, but you rarely meet it alone: it comes with saltiness in monosodium glutamate, or with other flavours in cooked or dried mushrooms. A simple experiment: taste a raw button mushroom, then one microwaved for thirty seconds; cooking greatly boosts the umami. Many foods thought of as difficult with wine, such as asparagus, eggs, mushrooms and ripe soft cheeses, are high in umami but low in salt. Cured or smoked seafood and meats, and hard cheeses like Parmesan, have both umami and salt, so they are much less troublesome. Be especially careful with low-tannin reds and with whites made with oak or skin contact: with umami they can turn surprisingly bitter.
Sweetness in food has the same effects: a sweet dish makes a dry wine seem less fruity and unpleasantly sour. The rule is to choose a wine at least as sweet as the dish, ideally sweeter.

Acidity in food is a friend: it increases the body, sweetness and fruitiness of the wine and decreases its perceived acidity. A very high-acid wine comes into balance and seems fruitier. But if the wine is low in acid, a very acidic dish can make it taste flat and flabby.
Salt increases body and decreases astringency, bitterness and acidity: another great ally, bringing out fruit and softening tannins.
Bitterness in food increases bitterness in the wine. Sensitivity varies hugely, and bitter tastes add up: a pleasantly bitter dish and a balanced wine can together cross the line into unpleasant.

Chilli heat increases bitterness, astringency, acidity and the burn of alcohol, and decreases body, richness, sweetness and fruit. Sensitivity varies from person to person here too. The higher the alcohol, the stronger the effect, and alcohol in turn makes the chilli burn more: some people love that.

Other considerations. It is usually best for the flavour intensity of food and wine to be similar, so that one does not overpower the other, although an intensely flavoured dish like a curry can sometimes work with a light, simple, unoaked white. Acidic wine with fatty or oily food pleases most people: the acidity cuts through the richness and cleanses the palate. Sweet and salty is another contrast many enjoy: the classic is sweet wine with blue cheese.

How do we apply all this? Split foods and wines into high-risk and low-risk. High-risk foods: sweet dishes, which need a wine with at least as much sugar. Umami-rich dishes, which emphasise tannin and bitterness, so they need wines with concentrated fruit; or you can adjust the dish with a little salt or acid, if that suits it. Bitter dishes, where white wines or low-tannin reds are safer. Hot, spicy dishes, which call for whites or low-tannin reds that are not high in alcohol, ideally with more fruit and a touch of sweetness. Low-risk foods: salty and acidic dishes, as long as an acidic dish meets an equally acidic wine.

High-risk wines are those with lots of structure at once: tannin from grapes and oak, high acidity and alcohol, and complex flavours. The more components, the more possible interactions, so more risk but also more interesting results. Low-risk wines are simple, unoaked wines with a little residual sugar. A dish will rarely spoil them, but because they change so little, the pairing is also less exciting.

A good method is to study classic pairings and understand why they work. Oysters with Muscadet or Champagne: unoaked wines, so there is no bitterness for the oyster's umami to exaggerate; light in flavour, so they do not swamp a delicate taste; and high in acidity, so they stay vibrant even with a squeeze of lemon. Other wines with the same features should work too, such as Rías Baixas Albariño or Hunter Valley Semillon.

What about the traditional rules? Matching or contrasting flavours, say a smoky dish with a smoky wine, can work, but success depends first on structure: sugar, salt, acid and fat in the food against sugar, alcohol, acid and tannin in the wine. If the structure works, flavours can add something; if it fails, the pairing fails anyway.

Local wine with local food: the idea that a region's dishes and wines grew up together. Often true, but most regions make many styles, so you still need to think. And many great cuisines developed where little or no wine is made.

Red wine with red meat, white with fish: it was thought that tannins bind to meat proteins and soften. In fact the salt in meat dishes seems to matter more. Some fish are high in umami, which makes a red seem more bitter, but salt and acid, common in fish dishes, can counteract this. Harder to avoid is oily fish, which reacts with compounds in red wine to give a metallic taste: there, white is the safer choice. If the structure of the dish, sauces included, is compatible, there is no reason not to serve white with meat or red with fish.

Finally, the perfect match. Classic pairings do exist: goat's cheese and Sancerre, oysters with Muscadet or Champagne, Stilton with Port, olives with Manzanilla. Most people enjoy them. But there is no objectively perfect pairing, because sensitivities and preferences differ. The most we can say is: most people will find that this dish goes well with wines in this style.
To sum up: sweetness and umami harden wine, salt and acid soften it, bitterness and chilli need care, and structure matters more than flavour.
To enjoy a wine at its best, it must be stored correctly and served at the right temperature. You do not need expensive equipment: common sense and widely available tools are usually enough.

Let's start with storage. A badly stored wine changes in flavour and, in severe cases, becomes faulty. There are four rules. First: for long-term storage, keep the temperature cool and constant, ideally between ten and fifteen degrees; extremes of heat and cold do damage. A kitchen is one of the worst places, because the temperature swings constantly. Long spells in a fridge are not good either: the cork hardens, loses its elasticity, lets air in and the wine goes stale; sparkling wines lose their fizz. Second: bottles sealed with cork should lie on their side, so the cork stays in contact with the wine and does not dry out; a dry cork lets air in and the wine oxidises. Screw-capped bottles can stand upright without risk. Third: keep wine away from strong light. Sunshine or artificial light warms the wine, ageing it prematurely, and artificial light can even create unpleasant flavours in some wines. Fourth: keep it away from vibration, so it can rest undisturbed.

Now service, and first temperatures. Sparkling wines such as Champagne, Cava and Asti are served well chilled, at six to ten degrees. Sweet wines such as Sauternes and Eiswein, well chilled at six to eight. Light to medium-bodied whites such as Muscadet, Pinot Grigio, New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, and Fino Sherry, chilled at seven to ten. Medium to full-bodied oaked whites such as white Burgundy or Fumé Blanc, lightly chilled at ten to thirteen. Light-bodied reds such as Beaujolais and Valpolicella, lightly chilled at around thirteen degrees. Medium to full-bodied reds such as red Bordeaux, Rioja, Australian Shiraz, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Barolo, Amarone and Vintage Port, at room temperature, fifteen to eighteen degrees.

Be careful with room temperature: with air conditioning and central heating, rooms are often too hot or too cold. A red that is too cold tastes thin and harsh: let it warm up slowly, or cup the bowl of the glass in your hands, but never put it on a radiator, as the sudden heat can ruin it. A red that creeps above eighteen degrees loses freshness and its flavours become muddled; once cooled down, it regains its balance.

To keep whites, rosés and sparkling wines cold, use an ice bucket. Fill it three-quarters full with equal amounts of ice and water, so the bottle is completely surrounded by iced water. The water carries heat from the bottle to the ice; air insulates, so a bottle sitting in ice alone chills very slowly. And do not over-chill, which masks the flavours.

Glassware. Each shape brings out particular characteristics. Reds suit larger glasses, because a wide surface in contact with air develops aromas and flavours. Whites and rosés suit medium glasses, which gather the fresh fruit and direct it upwards. Sparkling wines suit flutes: the bubbles travel through more wine before bursting, which also lifts the aroma; the old saucer-shaped coupe is a poor choice, because the bubbles disappear very quickly. Fortified wines are served in small glasses because of their high alcohol, but large enough to swirl and nose. Cleanliness is vital: even a glass straight from the dishwasher can hold detergent or salt residue, which gives odd flavours and kills the sparkle faster. The best approach is to polish each glass before use with a linen cloth, which leaves no fluff.

Opening a bottle of still wine: cut the capsule below the lip of the bottle, wipe the neck with a clean cloth, draw the cork as gently as possible, wipe the neck again inside and out, and pour a sample to check the wine is sound.

Decanting is mainly for wines with a heavy deposit, which is natural and forms as many good reds age. Some young wines benefit from aeration, but swirling in the glass does the same job. And opening the bottle hours in advance achieves nothing: too little wine is in contact with the air. The method: take the bottle out of its rack keeping it horizontal, in a decanting basket if you have one, without disturbing the deposit; gently remove the capsule and cork; then, in front of a light, pour slowly into the decanter and stop as soon as the deposit reaches the neck.

Opening sparkling wine needs care, because the pressure is high and the cork can fly out and injure someone. A well-chilled wine has less pressure. Remove the foil, loosen the wire cage while always holding the cork in place, tilt the bottle at about thirty degrees, grip the cork with one hand and the base with the other, and turn the bottle, not the cork. Ease the cork out, resisting its push: it should leave with a quiet sigh, not a bang.

Ordering wine: it helps to know how many servings a standard seventy-five centilitre bottle gives. Six glasses of one hundred and twenty-five millilitres, four of one hundred and seventy-five, or three of two hundred and fifty.

Finally, keeping an opened bottle. Within days the wine loses aromatic intensity, then it oxidises and develops vinegary notes. The simplest fix is to reseal it and put it in the fridge, but that only buys a few days. There are better systems. Vacuum systems remove the oxygen from the bottle and seal it, but they do not suit sparkling wines, which would lose their bubbles. Blanket systems cover the wine with a gas heavier than oxygen, such as nitrogen or argon, forming a protective layer between wine and air. Inexpensive devices of both kinds are easy to find.
To sum up: cool, constant, dark and still for storage; the right temperature for each style; a suitable, spotless glass; and a few precise moves for opening, decanting and keeping wine.

Thousands of grape varieties are grown around the world, but all vines have a great deal in common. In this lesson we look at how a vine is built, where grape varieties come from, and why almost every vine in the world is grafted.

Let's begin with species. There are many species of vine, but grape growers care about only a handful. The most important is Vitis vinifera, the Eurasian species: it produces almost all wine grapes and has been used for winemaking for thousands of years. Then there are three important North American species. They are rarely used for wine because their flavours are widely considered unattractive, but unlike vinifera they resist phylloxera, an insect that attacks the roots. That is why they are used all over the world as rootstocks.

What is a grape variety? Vinifera has thousands of them, and for the drinker the main differences are colour and flavour. For the grower, other things matter too: when the variety buds and ripens, and how well it resists disease. The key point is that a variety is never propagated from seed, because a seed would produce a new and different plant. To keep its character, growers use one of two techniques. A cutting: a section of shoot is planted, takes root and becomes a new vine; this is how commercial nurseries work. Layering: in the vineyard, a cane is bent down and part of it buried with the tip poking out; once the buried section has rooted, it is cut free from the parent. Because of phylloxera, cuttings are now used almost everywhere. Either way, the new plant is identical to the original. So a grape variety is a group of plants that all trace their lineage, cutting by cutting, back to a single vine. Vine variety, grape variety and cultivar mean the same thing.

Clones. Although every vine of a variety is genetically identical, small mutations can appear as the plants grow. Some are positive: better fruit or better disease resistance. Growers select those vines and multiply them; this is clonal selection. A clone is a vine or group of vines with its own particular set of characteristics, but it remains the same variety. When ordering from a nursery, growers often specify the clone as well as the variety. Some mutations are so significant that the result is treated as a variety in its own right: Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, for example, are all mutations of an old variety simply called Pinot.

Creating new varieties. Researchers want varieties better suited to particular climates and soils, more disease resistant, more productive or of higher quality. Instead of waiting for a lucky mutation, they use controlled cross-fertilisation: pollen from the flower of one vine is placed on the flower of another; the fertilised flower becomes a berry with seeds, and a seed, once planted, grows into a completely new variety, even if both parents were the same variety. Nobody knows in advance what it will be like: hundreds of seeds are needed, many seedlings fail, it takes two or three years to see the first grapes, and much longer to know whether the variety is worth growing commercially. That is why very few varieties bred in the last hundred and fifty years have found a lasting place.

Crossings and hybrids. When both parents belong to the same species, the result is a crossing. Technically every variety is a crossing: DNA shows that Cabernet Sauvignon comes from Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc. But the word is mostly used for varieties bred by researchers, such as Müller-Thurgau, from Riesling and Madeleine Royale, or Pinotage, from Pinot Noir and Cinsault. A hybrid has parents from two different species, usually at least one American. Like American vines, hybrids are rarely used for wine, with some exceptions such as Vidal, grown in Canada. But hybrids and American crossings play a crucial role: they are the world's rootstocks.

Now the anatomy of the vine, in four parts. First, the green parts, which grow fresh each year. The main structure is the shoot, carrying leaves, buds, tendrils and flowers, later berries. Tendrils are for gripping: a vine cannot hold itself up, so when a tendril touches a wire it coils tightly round it. Buds form where the leaf joins the shoot: they are embryonic shoots that mature during the season and by the end of the year contain, in miniature, everything that will become next year's shoot, leaves, flowers and tendrils. Flowers have both male and female parts and are grouped in inflorescences; each fertilised flower becomes a berry, and the inflorescence becomes the bunch. Leaves are the plant's engine: through photosynthesis they use sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen. Glucose feeds the vine and makes ripe grapes sweet.

Second, one-year-old wood. Shoots turn woody in winter and the next spring the buds formed the previous year burst into new shoots. This wood is vital, because vines normally fruit only on shoots growing from buds formed the previous year. At winter pruning, one-year-old wood becomes either a cane, long, with eight to twenty buds, or a spur, short, with two or three buds. We will come back to this in the lesson on vineyard management.
Third, permanent wood, meaning wood more than a year old: the trunk and, where present, the arms or cordons. Pruning limits how much there is, and its shape depends on the training system.

Fourth, the roots. They absorb water and nutrients, anchor the vine and store carbohydrates so it can survive the winter. In most modern vineyards, vinifera is grafted onto the roots of other species, because on its own it cannot resist phylloxera.

Phylloxera is a small insect native to North America. Vinifera has no defence against it, and when it was accidentally introduced to Europe in the nineteenth century it destroyed almost all the vineyards. Its life cycle is complex; in one phase it lives underground and feeds on the roots. Infections enter through the feeding wounds and over a few years the vine weakens and dies. American vines, which evolved alongside the pest, clog its mouthparts with sticky sap and seal off the wounds with protective layers. Today phylloxera is found almost everywhere; the exceptions include Chile, parts of Argentina and South Australia, protected only by strict quarantine.

Phylloxera cannot be controlled with chemicals. At first, growers planted American vines or hybrids, but by the end of the nineteenth century a better, if more expensive, answer was found: grafting vinifera onto an American or hybrid rootstock, combining American roots with European flavour. Since then, rootstocks have been bred for other benefits too, such as protection against nematodes or better drought resistance. So they are used even where phylloxera is not a problem, despite the extra cost.

There are two grafting techniques. Bench grafting is the most common: an automated process in specialist nurseries, where short pieces of vinifera cane and rootstock cane are joined by machine and kept warm until they fuse; then the vine is planted. Head grafting is used to switch variety in an established vineyard: the vine is cut back to its trunk and a bud or cutting of the new variety is grafted on. If it takes, the next vintage already gives the new grape. A newly planted vine needs at least three years to produce a commercial crop, so head grafting lets growers respond quickly to the market, costs far less than replanting, and the new variety starts with an established root system.

To sum up: vinifera makes the wine and American species supply the rootstocks; varieties are propagated by cuttings or layering; clones come from mutations; crossings join parents of the same species and hybrids of different species; the vine has green parts, one-year-old wood, permanent wood and roots; and grafting is the defence against phylloxera.

To survive, a vine must take everything it needs from its surroundings. It needs five things: heat, sunlight, water, nutrients and carbon dioxide. Each one affects how well the vine grows and the quantity and quality of its grapes. In this lesson we take them one by one, then see how they combine into climate, weather and soil.

First, the annual cycle. In winter the vine is dormant, with no green parts. In spring comes budburst, the start of the growing season. In late spring and early summer the vine flowers and tiny berries form: that is fruit set. Through summer the berries grow but stay hard, green, very acidic and sugar-free. In late summer or early autumn, ripening begins: the berries swell with water, sugar rises, acidity falls and flavours develop. The first sign is a change of colour, from green to blue-black, pink or golden depending on the variety: veraison. After harvest the vine drops its leaves and goes dormant again.

Photosynthesis is at the heart of it all: using sunlight, the vine combines carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Glucose, together with nutrients from the soil, fuels growth and above all ripens the grapes. Carbon dioxide is always plentiful; but heat, light, water and nutrients keep changing, and those changes decide the size and quality of the crop.

Heat. Below ten degrees the vine does not grow: that is why it is dormant in winter and bursts into bud in spring. It needs enough warmth to flower, set fruit and ripen, and the amount of heat in the growing season is what decides which varieties can be grown where. Riesling thrives in cool places where Grenache could never ripen.

What affects heat? Latitude: most vineyards lie between thirty and fifty degrees north and south; closer to the Equator it is too hot, closer to the Poles too cold. Altitude: temperature drops as you climb, so high regions such as Cafayate in northern Argentina can make wine close to the Equator. Ocean currents: the Humboldt Current off Chile and the Benguela Current off South Africa cool regions that would otherwise be too hot, while the Gulf Stream warms north-west Europe. Fog: it cools many of California's top areas and the Casablanca Valley in Chile. Soil: dark or stony soils absorb the sun's heat and give it back, which is precious in cool climates; wet soils warm slowly and can delay budburst. Aspect: slopes facing the Equator receive the most heat, so south-facing in the Northern Hemisphere and north-facing in the Southern; the steeper the slope, the stronger the effect. You can see it in the Mosel in Germany, where the best vineyards are well exposed and extremely steep.

Continentality and diurnal range. Continentality is the temperature difference between the hottest and coldest months. Seas and lakes warm up and cool down slowly, so they warm the air in winter and cool it in summer: near water, continentality is low; far inland, it is high. It sets the length of the growing season and so the total heat available. Diurnal range is the difference between day and night. Cool nights slow the loss of aroma and acidity; warm nights speed up ripening. In a warm climate, a vineyard with a wide diurnal range makes fresher, more aromatic wines. Being near water, even a river, narrows the diurnal range, and so does cloud cover: on clear nights the temperature plunges, on cloudy days it rises slowly.

Temperature hazards. In winter, below minus twenty degrees, the vine can be badly damaged or killed; the weakest point is the graft, which can be protected by covering it with soil, known as earthing up. But a winter that is too mild is also a problem: without dormancy, as in subtropical climates, the vine may crop more than once a year, lives shorter and gives poorer grapes; and more insect pests survive. Spring frosts happen when air below zero settles at ground level and freezes the moisture on new buds and shoots, killing them: the damage can be enormous. There are four main defences. Heaters, lit when frost is forecast: their heat keeps the air moving so cold air cannot settle. Wind machines, large fans that pull warmer air down from above. Sprinklers: as the water freezes it releases heat that protects buds and shoots. And vineyard design: cold air sinks, so plant mid-slope, avoid hollows, and train vines higher. A cold spring can also delay budburst, shortening the season, and disrupt flowering and fruit set, reducing the crop. At the other extreme, prolonged severe heat slows and then shuts the vine down, even with enough water, and the grapes do not ripen properly.

Sunlight. Without light there is no photosynthesis. More light means more glucose for growth and ripening, and flowering benefits greatly too. Latitude matters: the further from the Equator, the longer the summer days, one reason Riesling ripens in Germany. Near seas and lakes there is more cloud; in the middle of continents, more sun; vineyards above rivers or lakes can also get light reflected off the water. And aspect again: facing the Equator gives the most light, which matters most far from the Equator, where the sun is weaker. The hazards: cloud during flowering reduces the crop and, if it persists, prevents full ripening; intense sun can sunburn the berries, giving bitter flavours in the skins. Growers manage the vine's canopy to catch more light or provide shade.

Water. The vine needs it for photosynthesis and to swell its berries. Water travels from the roots to the leaves through transpiration, and the hotter it is, the more is needed. Once the canopy is big enough, limiting water is useful: the vine keeps photosynthesising but stops growing shoots and focuses on its grapes, and a smaller canopy means less shade. Rain is the main source; where it falls short and local law allows, growers irrigate. Three methods: drip irrigation, the most advanced and expensive, with a dripper for each vine that can be computer controlled; sprinklers, cheaper but wasteful and, like rain, they create damp conditions and so disease, although they can double as frost protection; and flood irrigation, very cheap, but only for flat or gently sloping sites with plenty of water. The hazards: drought, which causes water stress, halts photosynthesis, wilts the leaves and stops ripening, and can eventually kill the vine; and too much water, which keeps shoots and leaves growing during ripening, steals sugar from the grapes and adds shade; in extreme cases waterlogged soil drowns the roots. Slopes or drainage pipes prevent this.

Rain at the right time. Heavy rain during flowering greatly reduces the number of berries. Damp conditions encourage fungal disease. Heavy rain just before harvest swells the berries and dilutes flavour, and if they split they attract rot. Hail damages grapes and vines and can wipe out a whole crop; Mendoza in Argentina is particularly prone, and expensive netting is used there. Hail storms are very localised, so sometimes the best protection is owning vineyards in several places.

Climate and weather. Climate is the average pattern of temperature, sunlight and rainfall over many years: it does not change from one year to the next, though it can shift over decades. Weather is each year's variation from that average, in other words the vintage. Some regions vary a lot: in Bordeaux, for instance, 2013 was cool and wet, while 2015 was hot and dry. Others are very predictable, like California's Central Valley, hot and dry year after year.

To classify climate, we use the average temperature of the growing season, April to October in the Northern Hemisphere and October to April in the Southern. Cool: sixteen point five degrees or below. Moderate: sixteen point five to eighteen point five. Warm: eighteen point five to twenty-one. Hot: above twenty-one. Then, taking continentality, sunlight and rainfall into account, there are three types. Continental: a big gap between summer and winter, short summers and a rapid drop in temperature in autumn; in cool continental climates such as Chablis and Champagne, spring frost is a risk, so late-budding, early-ripening varieties suit best; summers are often dry, and if it is warm, irrigation may be needed. Maritime: cool to moderate temperatures, little difference between seasons and rain spread through the year; ripening can continue well into autumn, which is how maritime Bordeaux ripens thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon; but spring and summer rain can harm flowering, fruit set and grape health. Mediterranean: little seasonal difference, but warm, dry summers; found around the Mediterranean, along much of coastal California, in Chile, South Africa and south-eastern Australia. Compared with maritime, it gives fuller-bodied wines with riper tannins, more alcohol and less acidity; low rainfall helps grape health but can bring drought.

Finally, soil, which supplies water and nutrients. It sits on top of the bedrock, from a few centimetres to several metres deep, and is made of particles of different sizes, stones and humus, which is decomposing organic matter. Stones, where present, warm the vineyard. Among the fine particles the most important are sand, the largest, and clay, the smallest. Humus is rich in nutrients and holds water very well. Ideally the vine wants plenty of water early in the season for growth, then mild water stress after veraison, which promotes ripening. Water binds to clay and humus: too much clay and the soil gets waterlogged, which can kill the roots; too much sand or stone and water drains away, so irrigation may be needed even where rainfall is high. Many of the best soils are a mix of sand and clay called loam, which drains well but keeps enough water. Still, there is no single ideal soil: it depends on the climate. The main nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Vines do not need much: too much makes them vigorous, with a dense canopy shading the fruit. But over time nutrients run down and growers replace them with natural or chemical fertilisers. A typical sign of deficiency is chlorosis: the leaves turn yellow, photosynthesis slows and the grapes struggle to ripen. The right fertiliser fixes it.

To sum up: heat, sunlight, water, nutrients and carbon dioxide; latitude, altitude, currents, fog, soil and aspect shape heat and light; continentality and diurnal range complete the picture; three climate types, continental, maritime and Mediterranean; and a soil that provides water at the right moment, without excess.

The grape grower has a simple goal: a healthy crop of ripe grapes suited to the style of wine the winemaker wants. To get there, everything we know about the environment has to become practical choices: where to plant, how to train and prune, at what density, how to deal with pests and diseases, and when and how to harvest.

Site selection. For a new vineyard, first assess the natural conditions: average temperature, rainfall, sunshine hours, soil fertility and drainage. These guide the choice of variety, planting density and training system. Then the business side: access to power and water, available labour, access for tractors and harvesters, and land cost. And the variety must suit the climate, have a market and, in the EU, be permitted by the appellation rules.

Planting. The land is cleared, the soil tested and deficiencies corrected with fertiliser. Young vines, usually pre-grafted at a nursery, are planted by hand or machine and often protected from animals with plastic sleeves. Sometimes irrigation is allowed to help them establish, even where it is otherwise forbidden. The first crop usually comes in the third year. Vines can live a very long time, but most are replaced between thirty and fifty years old. Some estates mention old vines on the label: they are thought to give exceptional fruit with more concentration, but yields fall and disease susceptibility rises with age, so quality has to be balanced against profitability. After the vines are dug up, the land is usually left fallow for three years or more, and growers plan a replanting cycle so that as little land as possible is out of production at any time.

Now managing the vine: training, pruning, trellising and density. Training refers to the shape of the permanent wood, in two broad families. Head training has little permanent wood: sometimes just a trunk, sometimes a few short arms at the top. It can be spur-pruned or replacement cane-pruned. Cordon training has a trunk with one or more permanent horizontal arms, the cordons, and is usually spur-pruned: it takes longer to establish, but the sturdy cordon with shoots spaced along it makes mechanisation, including machine harvesting, easier. Either can be trained low, to benefit from heat held by the soil, or high, to avoid frost.

Pruning removes unwanted leaves, canes and permanent wood, shapes the vine and limits its size. It happens every winter and summer. Winter pruning sets the number and position of the buds that will grow shoots next season; buds should not be too close together, which helps canopy management. Two styles. Spur pruning: short pieces of one-year-old wood cut back to two or three buds, spaced along a cordon or around the top of the trunk. Replacement cane pruning: long canes with eight to twenty buds; usually one or two are kept and tied horizontally along the wire. It is more complex and needs a large, skilled workforce. It is also called Guyot: single Guyot with one cane, double Guyot with two. Summer pruning trims the canopy to curb growth and send sugar to the grapes rather than to shoots and leaves, and can include leaf stripping to expose the bunches to sunlight.

Trellising and canopy management. The canopy is all the green parts of the vine. The key choice is whether to use a trellis, a permanent structure of posts and wires supporting the canes and the year's growth. Untrellised vines are bush vines, head-trained and spur-pruned, with shoots hanging down, sometimes to the ground: they suit warm or hot, dry, sunny regions like the Southern Rhône or the Barossa Valley, where the shade protects the grapes. In cool or wet regions, the shade hinders ripening and poor airflow encourages disease; in Beaujolais this is avoided by tying the shoot tips together, sometimes called gobelet. Untrellised vines cannot be machine harvested.

In trellised vineyards, each row has posts joined by horizontal wires, and canes and shoots are tied to them. There are three reasons. First, positioning the shoots controls how much light enters the canopy: where sun is limited, they are spread apart for an open canopy that exposes the fruit; where sun is intense, leaves can shade the grapes against sunburn. Second, an open canopy lets air flow, which matters in wet climates where stagnant damp air breeds fungal disease. Third, it helps mechanisation: grapes in one zone, leaves in another, so harvesting and spraying work better. The most widely used system is Vertical Shoot Positioning, VSP: shoots are trained upwards and tied to the wires, forming a single narrow, open, well-aired canopy. In hot, sunny regions the shoot tips can be left untied to flop over and shade the fruit. Compared with an untrellised bush vine, the advantage is machine harvesting.

Planting density is the number of vines per hectare, a square with hundred-metre sides. It ranges from about one thousand to ten thousand vines per hectare. One acre is roughly zero point four hectares. Among many factors, water and nutrient availability matter most. Where water is very limited, plant at low density so each vine's roots can draw on a large volume of soil without competing. Where soils are poor but rainfall is enough, a vine tends to grow too vigorously, so plant at high density: root competition restrains vegetative growth; leaving the right number of buds matters too: too few, and each gets too much energy and grows rampantly; too many, and the vine struggles to ripen its crop. High density with strict bud control is typical of many European vineyards. Where soils are very fertile, as in parts of the New World, high density is not enough to tame the vine, so growers plant at low density with large vines carrying several cordons or canes, which can give good quality at high yields.

Two examples. First: an inland region, hot and very sunny, with very little rain and almost no irrigation water, but soil that holds water well. Water is the main challenge, so plant at low density. To protect the fruit from sunburn, use bush vines or a trellis with flopping shoots; disease pressure is low because it hardly rains. Second: a coastal region with a moderate climate, high rainfall all year and low soil fertility. Resources are plentiful, so plant at high density to create competition. With damp air and frequent cloud, choose VSP for an open, bright, well-aired canopy.

Yields. They are measured by weight, tonnes of grapes per hectare, or by volume, hectolitres of wine per hectare. Predicting them matters for legal limits, as in the EU, for contracts, or simply to know how much tank space is needed. An estimate comes from the number of buds left after winter pruning, but frost, poor fruit set, pests and diseases can change it dramatically. If yields look too high, growers can green harvest: removing unripe bunches shortly after veraison. It is risky: done at the wrong time, the vine compensates by swelling the remaining berries, the yield returns to its original level and the flavours are diluted. It was long thought that high quality always demands low yields, but in fact a firm link between yield and quality is very hard to establish: too many site-specific factors are involved.

The vineyard calendar. Budburst: March to April in the Northern Hemisphere, September to October in the Southern; it starts when the mean daily temperature passes ten degrees, but the threshold depends on the variety: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are early budding, Cabernet Sauvignon late, and early budders are more exposed to spring frost. Early shoot and leaf growth: March to May in the north, September to November in the south; fuelled first by winter reserves, then by photosynthesis; vines need water and nutrients, shoots are tied in and spraying continues. Flowering and fruit set: May to June in the north, November to December in the south; warmth, sunshine and little or no rain are needed. Not every flower becomes a grape: if more flowers than usual fail to set, it is called coulure; if berries form small and seedless, it is millerandage. Both cut yields and usually come from cold, cloudy or rainy weather at flowering. Then six to eight weeks when the berries grow, green and hard. Veraison and ripening: July to September in the north, January to March in the south; black grapes turn red then purple, white grapes become translucent and golden; sugar rises, acidity falls, colour, flavour and tannin build up. Warm sunny weather and mild water stress are ideal. Summer pruning and green harvesting may happen now. Harvest: September to October in the north, March to April in the south, ideally in dry weather; spraying must stop early enough to leave no residues. Dormancy: December to March in the north, July to September in the south: shoots turn woody, leaves fall, the vine stores reserves in its roots, and winter pruning takes place.

Pests and diseases. They reduce yield and quality: grapes are lost or damaged, and damaged leaves photosynthesise less. We have met phylloxera. Nematodes are microscopic worms that attack roots, hamper water and nutrient uptake and sometimes spread viruses: prevention works best, by sanitising the soil before replanting and using resistant rootstocks. Birds and mammals eat large amounts of grapes, and half-eaten fruit invites rot: netting is the best answer for birds, fencing for rabbits, deer or wild boar. Insects feed on grapes and leaves: growers can spray insecticides or use integrated pest management.

Fungal diseases. Downy and powdery mildew thrive in warm, humid conditions and attack all green parts, leaves and grapes: the fruit loses its flavour and can give the wine a mouldy, bitter taint. Grey rot is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea: it loves damp, attacks the berries, taints flavours and strips colour from black grapes. Yet under certain conditions, on certain white varieties, the same infection becomes noble rot and gives some of the world's greatest sweet wines. Fungi are controlled with fungicides: traditionally sulfur against powdery mildew and Bordeaux mixture, a copper-based spray, against downy mildew, now joined by many newer products. Spraying is usually done by tractor, more often in wet maritime climates, and must stop well before harvest. An open canopy also helps: it keeps air moving, dries the leaves and lets sprays reach everywhere, so fewer are needed.

Other diseases. There are many viruses: most do not kill the vine but severely reduce yield and quality; they are contagious, spread through cuttings or nematodes, and there is no cure: vines must be dug up and the land sanitised. Bacterial diseases can kill the vine; they are spread by small insects called sharpshooters; there is no cure, only strict quarantine and breaking the insects' life cycle, and infected vines must be removed.

Viticultural practices. In the second half of the twentieth century, the use of man-made chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, grew sharply. Environmental damage has become a growing concern for growers, consumers and legislators, and many regions are trying to cut chemical use. Three approaches. Sustainable agriculture does not ban man-made chemicals but restricts them: by understanding pest life cycles and following the weather, growers spray at the right moment rather than by the calendar, so fewer applications are needed. Integrated pest management is central: natural predators of pests are encouraged, which makes biodiversity essential, with a mix of plants between the rows that, once mown and ploughed in, also feed the soil. Organic agriculture shares many of these ideas, but allows only a few traditional treatments in very small quantities, and to claim it on the label a producer needs certification; there are many certifying bodies with slightly different standards, but all require a conversion period. Biodynamic agriculture, based on the work of Rudolf Steiner and Maria Thun, follows organic practice and adds philosophy and cosmology: the soil is part of a system connected to the Earth, the air and the other planets, work follows the cycles of planets, moon and stars, and homeopathic preparations are used to fertilise, treat disease and deter pests. It too has certification bodies.

Harvest. As grapes ripen, sugar rises and acidity falls, and measuring sugar is a common way to track ripeness; meanwhile the grapes develop their signature flavours and skin tannins become less bitter and astringent. There is no universal perfect moment: the ideal balance of sugar, acid, flavour and tannin depends on the variety, the climate and above all the style and quality of the wine. Growers pick when the grapes have the qualities they want, though bad weather sometimes forces an early harvest: hail destroys, rain swells the berries and dilutes the juice. And the winery must schedule deliveries so it is never overwhelmed.

By hand or by machine? It depends on how the vineyard is planted, the cost and availability of labour, the slope, the weather and winemaking choices. And note: premium wine is made from both. Machine harvesters shake the trunk and catch the berries as they fall, leaving the stalks behind. They are not selective: they also collect unhealthy, unripe or damaged grapes, bits of leaf, insects and other material other than grapes, MOG, which is removed by sorting at the winery when possible. Their big advantage is speed, essential when bad weather threatens or for varieties like Sauvignon Blanc that can overripen quickly. They can also work at night, delivering cool grapes, which saves energy on chilling and slows oxidation. But they only work on flat or gently sloping land, with grapes that come off the stem easily without damage, and not for styles that need whole bunches, such as Beaujolais or Champagne. Hand picking, with secateurs, is slower and labour intensive, so it can cost more; but it allows selection in the vineyard, leaving rotten or unripe fruit behind, and it is essential for noble rot, which varies from bunch to bunch and even within a bunch. It damages the grapes less, especially in shallow stackable crates, and keeps whole bunches with their stems: a very clean, pure juice for whites, and the whole bunches needed for whole-bunch red fermentations. It is also the only option on very steep slopes, such as in the Douro, the Mosel and the Northern Rhône.

To sum up: site, planting, head or cordon training, spur or cane pruning, an open or shaded canopy, density matched to water and nutrients, yields that are hard to predict, a precise calendar, protection against pests, fungi, viruses and bacteria, three farming philosophies, and the choice between hand and machine.
Some factors and processes are common to every wine, white, red, rosé and sweet. Understanding them well is the key to understanding, in what follows, why each style is made the way it is.

Two approaches. Winemaking starts with grapes and ends with wine: the grapes are processed and prepared for alcoholic fermentation, in which yeast turns sugar into alcohol, and the wine is then stored until it is packaged. At every step people make choices, and science has multiplied the options. Some winemakers control every detail to reach a precise stylistic goal. Others intervene as little as possible, simply monitoring: their wines, sometimes called natural wines, often taste very different. These are the two ends of a spectrum, and most winemakers sit somewhere in between. Here we focus on the techniques used for the vast majority of wines.

The parts of the grape. The bloom is the waxy layer on the skin and carries yeasts that can ferment the wine. Seeds and stems contain tannins, and seeds also bitter oils; stems are only available with hand harvesting. The skin, and the layer just beneath it, is rich in flavour compounds that give each variety its signature character, and contains tannins and colour compounds, far more plentiful in black grapes. The pulp is mostly water, then sugar, vital because the yeast will turn it into alcohol, and acids: mainly tartaric, then malic, which carry through into the wine. Tannins are many different compounds: at veraison they taste very bitter and astringent, and less so as the grapes ripen. Oak can also add tannin, to both reds and whites.

Oxygen reacts with grape juice and with many wine components: this is oxidation, sometimes positive, sometimes negative. For a winemaker who wants a wine dominated by primary fruit, oxygen is a constant threat. Antioxidants such as sulfur dioxide are used; grapes are picked at night, when it is cooler and reactions are slower; they are kept chilled; and in the winery, equipment is filled with carbon dioxide or nitrogen before use. This is protective, or anaerobic, winemaking. Some argue it gives bland wines, and that more oxygen contact during winemaking builds complexity and character: it is a question of style.

In maturation, wines made protectively rarely benefit from oxygen: they are kept in inert, airtight, completely full vessels of stainless steel or epoxy-lined concrete. Wines matured with oxygen go into wooden vessels, usually oak, which is watertight but not airtight: small amounts of oxygen pass through. Red tannins soften, primary fruit fades and tertiary notes such as leather and earth appear; reds become paler with a hint of brown, whites deepen towards orange. The effect depends on vessel size and time: a two-hundred-and-twenty-five-litre barrique oxidises more than a large cask, because the wine touches more wood in proportion, so wines rarely stay in barrique for more than two years. If the vessel is not full, oxygen acts even more: this is done deliberately for oxidative fortified wines such as Oloroso Sherry, Tawny Port and Rutherglen Muscat, which develop caramel, toffee and nuts. But for most wines too much oxygen is damaging: the wine loses its fruit, smells stale and is oxidised and unfit for sale; in extreme cases, bacteria turn it into vinegar.

Sulfur dioxide is almost indispensable: it is both an antioxidant and an antiseptic. It is used on freshly picked grapes and adjusted throughout winemaking. Maximum levels are set by law, because it can be toxic, although levels in wine are far below toxic and lower than in some dried fruit, and it can trigger allergic reactions even at low levels. Some is produced naturally during fermentation. Most winemakers prefer to keep additions low, not least because too much makes a wine harsh and short of fruit; a few use none at all. As an antioxidant, once it has protected the wine it becomes bound and stops working, so levels must be constantly monitored and topped up. As an antiseptic, it is toxic to many unwanted yeasts and bacteria, while the main fermentation yeast tolerates it.

Oak. Almost all wooden vessels are oak. Besides gentle oxidation, the wine extracts tannins, which add structure and textural complexity, and flavours such as toast, vanilla, smoke and cloves. Hygiene is a challenge: wood harbours yeasts, bacteria and moulds, and tainted wood ruins wine. Four factors matter. Species and origin: mostly European oak, broadly similar whether from France, Hungary or Russia, with some French forests considered the finest, and American oak. Size: the two-hundred-and-twenty-five-litre barrique and the two-hundred-and-twenty-eight-litre pièce have far more effect than large vessels of over two thousand litres. Production, above all toasting: staves are heated so they can be bent, and the heat transforms tannins and flavour compounds, giving sweet spice and toast; the temperature and duration set the toast level and so the flavours. Age: each use reduces the effect, and by its fourth use a barrel gives very little. Not every wine wants new oak, and some producers avoid it for subtler oak character.

Oak alternatives: staves or smaller chips can be added during fermentation or maturation in inert vessels, giving oak flavour and tannin at a much lower cost; and barrel oxidation can be imitated by adding small, controlled amounts of oxygen, known as micro-oxygenation. Premium wines are not normally made this way yet.

Inert vessels add no flavour and allow no oxidation. Stainless steel is the most common: easy to clean, any shape and size, with temperature control through external jackets or internal coils carrying hot or cold liquid. Concrete, lined with epoxy resin, was common before stainless steel: harder to clean, but its thick walls steady the temperature without expensive equipment. Egg-shaped concrete vats have become fashionable, thought to encourage a natural flow of the wine. Glass bottles are inert vessels too.

Grape processing. On arrival the grapes usually receive their first dose of sulfur dioxide. For premium wines they are checked on a sorting table to remove unripe or rotten fruit, rarely possible at high volume. Destemming and crushing are optional: machine-harvested grapes arrive without stems, and even with hand picking most winemakers remove them, usually in a machine that can then crush. Crushing breaks the skins and releases free-run juice, without damaging the seeds, which would release bitter oils and harsh tannin. Pressing separates liquid from solids: for whites before fermentation, for reds usually after. Again, the seeds must stay intact, and modern presses are gentle. Traditional vertical basket presses, with a plate coming down from above, are still widely used, often automated, especially but not only in Champagne. Pneumatic presses are more recent: an inflatable tube inside a perforated horizontal cylinder applies pressure over a large area in a controllable way; some are enclosed to keep oxygen out. Juice from early in the pressing differs from juice at the end, so winemakers can separate the fractions, treat them separately and blend them for the style they want.

Adjustments, before, during or after fermentation, within local law. Grape juice is called must. Sugar and alcohol: in cool climates grapes may lack sugar. The must can be enriched by adding rectified concentrated grape must, a colourless, odourless syrup, before or during fermentation: more sugar means more alcohol. Enrichment is forbidden in many places and strictly controlled where allowed. Done carefully it can improve the wine; overdone, the wine tastes hard and thin, with too much alcohol for its flavours. When sugar comes from other sources, such as sugar beet, it is called chaptalisation. Water can also be removed from the must to concentrate sugar, but that concentrates everything, tannins, acids, flavours and even faults, and reduces volume. Removing sugar is very hard, but alcohol can now be removed from finished wine. Acidity: if grape acid has fallen too far, winemakers acidify, usually with powdered tartaric acid; in Europe only warmer regions may do so, and it is common in warm and hot regions worldwide. Deacidification, more common in cool climates, neutralises excess acid with an alkali.

Alcoholic fermentation turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide through the action of yeast, also giving off heat and flavour compounds. The main yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which tolerates high levels of alcohol and sulfur dioxide. It will not start below five degrees and normally runs until the sugar is used up. It can stop early, though: if the yeast runs out of nutrients, above thirty-five degrees, or when very high sugar and alcohol together inhibit the yeast; with extremely sweet musts it may even struggle to start. Winemakers sometimes stop it deliberately: by killing the yeast with sulfur dioxide or grape spirit, or by removing it through filtration, usually after halting fermentation by chilling below five degrees. Two levers control fermentation. Yeast: ambient yeasts from the bloom and the winery can give complex flavours but cannot be controlled and vary from batch to batch, unsuited to high volumes; cultured yeasts are selected strains of cerevisiae chosen for reliable performance and attractive flavours, though some argue they limit complexity. Temperature: too hot kills the yeast; cooler fermentation keeps the most volatile, often floral, aromas and encourages fruity flavours in whites; warmer temperatures are needed to extract colour and tannin from black skins. Many vats now have their own heating and cooling, and heat can also be released by pumping over. Precise temperature control has been one of the great advances in the quality and consistency of modern wine.

Malolactic conversion usually follows alcoholic fermentation and is carried out by lactic acid bacteria: they turn tart malic acid, as in apples, into softer lactic acid, as in milk. It lowers and softens acidity, creates buttery flavours and releases carbon dioxide. It is encouraged by warming the wine and not adding sulfur dioxide; avoided by keeping the wine cool, using sulfur dioxide or filtering out the bacteria.

Lees. Straight after fermentation, wine looks cloudy with dead yeast cells and grape fragments. Heavy particles drop within hours: these are the gross lees, which cause unpleasant aromas if left. Smaller ones settle slowly: the fine lees, removed gradually during maturation. Sometimes a white is kept on its fine lees to add flavour and a richer texture.

Pre-bottling maturation. Not every wine benefits: to keep primary fruit, wines are bottled after a few months in inert vessels, both cheap wines and some premium ones, like a top Australian Riesling, which never sees oak or oxygen. To survive medium or long ageing, a wine needs enough tannin, acidity and alcohol, and above all flavours that will develop in an interesting way. During maturation the vessel may add oak or oxygen, and components react with one another, sometimes forming particles that settle.

Blending matters for almost every wine, even single-variety ones. It mostly happens after fermentation or during maturation, for three reasons. Balance: for example adding press wine to free-run wine for more tannin. Consistency: differences between bottles of the same wine are seen as a fault, so barrels that developed slightly differently are combined, as are vats from different plots or picking dates. Style: many producers keep a house style despite vintage variation; to create blending options they separate press fractions, use different vessels, put only part of the wine through malolactic, or use different varieties, plots and vintages, always within local rules.

Clarification, because almost all customers want a clear wine. Three techniques. Sedimentation: the gross lees settle and the wine is gently pumped into another vessel, called racking; repeated rackings improve clarity, and for some fine wines this is the only clarification. Gravity is slow; a centrifuge can speed things up, but it is very expensive. Fining: some components clump together over time and can cause haze in bottle; a fining agent is added that binds to them and forms clumps, which are then removed. It is widely practised and important for stability, though some winemakers avoid it to protect flavour and texture. Filtration physically removes particles. Depth filters, made of a thick layer of material, trap solids inside and can cope with very cloudy wine, even gross lees. Surface filters, like very fine sieves, trap particles on the surface; expensive and quick to clog, they are used after depth filtration. When the pores are small enough to remove yeast and bacteria, it is sterile filtration, often the final step before bottling. Some wines are bottled unfiltered to preserve character and texture.

Stabilisation. Every wine changes: it is stable if it changes slowly and predictably over its intended life. An inexpensive red to drink within a year should not throw a deposit; a mature Vintage Port will throw a thick one over fifty or sixty years in bottle. Three areas. Tartrates: tartaric acid is less soluble in wine than in juice and forms crystals, clear in whites and purple in reds, harmless and tasteless but off-putting to many consumers. Cold speeds their formation: long maturation in a cool cellar removes some; otherwise the wine is chilled below zero for a short time and the crystals filtered out. Microbiological stability: yeasts and bacteria can make wine undrinkable, so winery hygiene is vital. Only fortified wines are safe, thanks to their alcohol. A dry, high-acid wine that has been through malolactic is fairly resistant, and some winemakers take that risk rather than sterile filter; but wines without malolactic, or with low to medium alcohol, low acidity and a little sugar, are at risk and need careful handling, sulfur dioxide and sterile filtration. Oxygen stability: too much dissolved oxygen, or oxygen entering through the packaging, oxidises the wine and turns it brown; this is avoided by limiting exposure, keeping sulfur dioxide topped up and, at bottling, flushing bottles with carbon dioxide or nitrogen before filling.

Packaging. Glass bottles are the most common: cheap, strong, airtight and taint-free, and consumers prefer them. Their drawbacks: they are heavy, which adds transport cost, and rigid. Hence lighter-weight bottles, or shipping in bulk to bottle near the market. And an opened bottle leaves space for air. Plastic bottles are much lighter but let a little air through: wine loses freshness within months. Bag-in-box collapses as wine is poured, so no air enters through the tap, but some passes through the bag wall: most need using within about eighteen months of filling. Plastic and bag-in-box are fine for wines meant for early drinking; for long-term ageing, glass is still best.

Closures must protect the wine until it is drunk. For many wines, drunk within a year, ease of use and the bottling line decide; for wines meant to age in bottle, the closure must also let them mature positively. Closures let in different amounts of oxygen: a slow trickle favours tertiary flavours; none at all keeps fresh fruit longer. So closure is a winemaking choice, although some markets have strong preferences. Cork is the original closure and still the most widely used, chosen for many age-worthy wines because it lets in a tiny amount of oxygen, giving what many consider the ideal balance of primary and tertiary character. But a small and declining percentage of corks cause cork taint, from the chemical TCA, with a mouldy, cardboard smell; and a further share, rising with the wine's age, lets in too much oxygen. Cork producers have invested heavily in preventing TCA. Synthetic corks, made of plastic, were once only suitable for wines drunk within a year, but premium versions now allow longer storage. Screw caps, championed by Australia and New Zealand, have grown rapidly: they do not taint the wine, seal it completely and keep fruit fresh longer than cork, so they are popular for whites and reds alike where primary fruit matters. There is still debate about how wines meant for long ageing develop without oxygen, and some screw caps now allow a little through. Acceptance varies a lot from market to market.

Post-bottling maturation. Most wines are best drunk within a year; ageing them loses fresh fruit. But some improve for years and are not at their best soon after bottling: Vintage Port, the finest German Rieslings, the classed growths of Bordeaux. The chemistry is still poorly understood, but the conditions are agreed: a cool, dark place, a constant temperature of around ten to fifteen degrees, constant humidity, and cork-sealed bottles lying on their side.

To sum up: oxygen as friend or foe, sulfur dioxide as a shield, oak and inert vessels, grape processing, adjustments, alcoholic and malolactic fermentation, lees, maturation, blending, clarification, stabilisation, packaging and closures.

Compared with red, white winemaking is relatively simple. In this lesson we look at the main choices, then at how high-volume inexpensive whites and premium whites are made, with four international varieties: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio. Finally, sweet wines, which are mostly, though not only, white.

The sequence is: sorting, destemming and crushing, optional skin contact, pressing, juice clarification, alcoholic fermentation, racking off the gross lees, optional malolactic conversion, maturation, clarification and stabilisation, packaging. The key decisions concern skin contact, juice clarity, fermentation temperature and vessel, the use of lees, malolactic conversion and maturation.

Skin contact. Usually it is kept to a minimum to limit oxidation: the grapes are crushed, the free-run juice is drained off and the rest goes to the press. Some winemakers load the press with whole, uncrushed bunches: it is gentle, reduces oxidation and can give purer, more delicate wines. For some aromatic varieties, however, the juice is left on the skins for a few hours, cool enough to stop fermentation starting, to boost flavour intensity and texture.

Juice clarity. Freshly pressed juice contains fragments of skin and pulp: fermented untreated, it can develop unpleasant aromas or even stick. So it is clarified before fermentation, using the same techniques as for wine: settling, centrifugation, fining, filtration. Some winemakers keep a few solids: they are thought to make the wine less prone to oxidation and add complexity and texture, but the risk of off-flavours means this is rare for wines meant to show pure varietal character.

Temperature and vessel. For whites, the ideal is twelve to twenty-two degrees. Too cold gives pear-drop aromas and fails to capture the variety's fruit; warmer encourages more complex, non-fruit aromas, but varietal character can be lost. In stainless steel, temperature is controlled mechanically. Whites can also be fermented in barrel: control is harder, but the small size and cool cellars dissipate heat well; even so, barrel fermentations usually run at the warmer end of the range.

After fermentation there are three choices: mature in oak or in inert vessels, possibly with staves or chips; use the fine lees for texture and flavour; allow or block malolactic conversion. For whites built on primary fruit, blending is mostly about consistency; for neutral varieties like Chardonnay, it can create complexity, combining batches with different lees contact, malolactic and oak. Finally, most whites are fined and filtered: their pale colour shows any haze, and whites with residual sugar are at risk of microbial spoilage, so they are often sterile filtered.

High-volume, inexpensive whites. Widely made and widely enjoyed: not complex and not made to age, but for many people excellent value, easy drinking, reliable and fairly priced. Some name the variety on the label; but it is easier to make large volumes by blending varieties, and then the label may just say dry white or fruity white. Fairly neutral varieties are used, like Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio, which appeal widely and ripen easily, especially in warm climates, where acidity can fall too low and is corrected in the winery. Chardonnay may be unoaked, with peach and melon, or oaked, with vanilla and toast, and often has some residual sugar. Pinot Grigio is usually unoaked, with light pear-drop aromas, light body and medium acidity. Sauvignon Blanc, currently popular, is used too, but rarely at the lowest prices: it is vigorous and high yielding, but herbaceous flavours dominate if the fruit is underripe.

How they are made: protective handling and constant sulfur dioxide monitoring; destemming, crushing and pressing; acidification, because the grapes come from warm regions, and low-acid Chardonnay tastes flat and flabby. The juice is highly clarified to keep fruity flavours; settling is slow and ties up tank space, so centrifuges or filters are used where possible. Fermentation is in stainless steel, kept cool to hold on to as much primary fruit as possible, which is vital when the grapes have little flavour, such as high-yielding Pinot Grigio. Cultured yeasts ensure a quick, reliable fermentation. To keep acidity and fruit, malolactic is blocked by chilling and adding sulfur dioxide, and the wine is racked off its lees straight away. Some Chardonnays do go through malolactic for a soft, buttery style. Barrel ageing is costly and slow, so chips or staves in steel give a toasty note if wanted. Many of these wines have residual sugar, more often Chardonnay than Pinot Grigio: usually they are fermented dry and then unfermented grape juice or rectified concentrated grape must is measured in, giving precise control of sweetness. Buyers expect a bright, clear wine with no sediment, so these wines are stabilised, fined and sterile filtered; and although they are drunk young, sulfur dioxide is topped up at bottling against oxidation.

Premium whites. A wide category with a huge range of prices, but the common aim is quality, often at the expense of volume. The best winemakers adapt their techniques to the vintage, the plot and the style. We will look at aromatic and less aromatic varieties separately.
Aromatic varieties, such as Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling, but also Muscat, Gewurztraminer and Torrontés, have pronounced aromas: the aim is to keep and enhance the primary fruit.
