Sauvignon Blanc is highly aromatic with high acidity; early ripening, it suits cool climates that keep its freshness. The most famous come from the Loire and from Marlborough. Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are elegant and restrained: green apple, asparagus, often a hint of wet pebbles. Marlborough is just as cool, but long hours of intense sunlight give vibrant flavours: gooseberry, elderflower, grapefruit, passion fruit, sometimes herbaceous notes. South Africa and Chile also make fresh, fruity Sauvignon, and Margaret River in Western Australia often blends it with Semillon for a slightly less aromatic but fuller wine. Most are best drunk young. But there is another approach, classic in Pessac-Léognan in Bordeaux: fermentation and maturation at least partly in oak, giving a rounder body and spicy, toasty notes, and blending with Semillon, which adds body and richness. California and New Zealand make some too, as a point of difference.

Riesling makes many styles. It tolerates cold winters and buds late, avoiding spring frost, so it suits cool climates, where it gives green fruit and often floral notes; in warmer places it becomes richer, with citrus and stone fruit, arguably losing some delicacy. It ripens mid to late season: left on the vine it gains sugar without losing its naturally high acidity, making it perfect for balanced wines at every sweetness level, including botrytised ones. It is one of the longest-lived whites: it can age for years, even decades, and still taste fresh, developing honey and toast while keeping its acidity; some develop the famous petrol note. Germany is its homeland, where it is made at every sweetness level, the sweetest from botrytised grapes, always balanced by high acidity, concentrated yet refreshing. In Europe, Alsace and Austria also make premium Riesling: in Austria mostly dry or very sweet; in Alsace mainly dry, with late-harvest and botrytised wines when the vintage allows. Australia is famous for Clare Valley and Eden Valley Riesling, often bone dry, with high acidity and lime aromas. Washington State makes dry Riesling too, while New Zealand and the Finger Lakes in New York State favour a fruity, off-dry style.

How aromatic varieties are handled: gently, to keep fruit and floral aromas, with sulfur dioxide monitored throughout. Crushed fruit or whole bunches go to the press, straight away or after a little skin contact. The juice must be fairly clean so nothing masks the fruit, and it is clarified gently, by settling. Fermentation is in inert vessels, since flavour from the vessel would interfere with pure fruit: stainless steel, easy to cool, is the New Zealand choice for both Sauvignon and Riesling; in Alsace, large old oak foudres are sometimes used for Riesling, allowing a little oxidation for texture and complexity without oak flavour. Cool fermentation is slow and steady and encourages primary aromas. Yeast choice depends on the winemaker. Sauvignon is usually fermented dry; Riesling ranges from dry to lusciously sweet: premium sweet Rieslings are usually made by stopping fermentation early with chilling or sulfur dioxide, leaving the desired sugar, while for the sweetest botrytised wines fermentation stops naturally. Little happens after fermentation: high acidity is prized, so malolactic is prevented with sulfur dioxide, also because buttery notes would clash with the fruit. Riesling may spend some time on its lees for texture. Bottling comes early, without new oak, although in Alsace and sometimes Germany, Riesling may rest up to a year in large old casks. Riesling is rarely blended; Sauvignon is usually varietal too, but, as we saw, it is blended with Semillon in some Bordeaux whites and in Western Australia. The creamy, spicy style of some Californian Fumé Blanc and of Pessac-Léognan comes from barrel fermentation, sometimes with ambient yeasts, a few months on the lees, usually with malolactic, and a proportion of new oak.

Less aromatic varieties, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris or Grigio, are more neutral: for the winemaker that is an advantage, because they can shape the style more. They can keep the grape flavours pure, or use a range of techniques to add complexity and texture.

Chardonnay ripens easily in many climates, but it buds early and suffers where spring frosts are common. In cool climates it shows green fruit and citrus; in moderate ones, fleshy fruit like white peach and melon; in warm and hot regions, tropical fruit like banana and pineapple, and there it loses acidity fast at the end of ripening, so harvest timing is critical. It is the perfect blank canvas. In Burgundy alone: in the north, Chablis, with high acidity, green apple and citrus, sometimes wet stones and slate; in the Côte d'Or, the best combine stone fruit with creamy oak; further south in the Mâconnais, riper, rounder wines with a hint of toasty oak. Most go through malolactic, and many have extended lees ageing; with age the best develop nutty and mushroom notes. Outside Burgundy the style depends more on the individual winemaker than on local tradition; many used to be heavily oaked, but premium producers are now moving firmly away from that. Regions with a name for premium Chardonnay include Russian River Valley and Los Carneros in California, Adelaide Hills, Geelong and Mornington Peninsula in Australia, Gisborne and Marlborough in New Zealand, and Casablanca Valley in Chile. But fine Chardonnay is made almost everywhere.

This grape is called Pinot Gris in France and Pinot Grigio in Italy, and the two countries' styles are very different; elsewhere the label name often signals which style the wine resembles. Premium examples can be almost unrecognisable from the vast volumes of inexpensive Pinot Grigio. It buds and ripens early, and in warm climates or when left on the vine it gains a lot of sugar but loses much acidity. In Alsace it is dry or off-dry, often with an oily texture, ripe tropical fruit, ginger and honey; its deeply coloured skins can give a golden hue. In New Zealand several producers call it Pinot Gris: the same viscous texture and medium acidity, but purer fruit and often a little more sugar. Tasmania and Oregon also make rich, often dry versions. In Italy, Alto Adige, Trentino and Friuli-Venezia Giulia make high-quality dry Pinot Grigio, with far more depth than the high-volume wines of the Veneto plain. Clone matters too: in the north, German and French clones with small berries and more concentration; in the Veneto, a pale-skinned clone with large fleshy pulp, fairly neutral, especially at high yields and with early picking.

How they are made: crushed grapes or whole bunches, the latter common for Chardonnay. For some neutral varieties, controlled exposure to oxygen at this stage is thought to improve ageing ability, whereas it would strip aromatic varieties of their delicate aromas. Gentle clarification by settling, sometimes leaving some solids for complexity. Fermentation in a range of vessels: stainless steel or concrete for fresh fruit, as in Chablis, north-east Italian Pinot Grigio and New Zealand Pinot Gris; large old oak for Alsace Pinot Gris; small new barrels for toast and roundness, as with Côte d'Or Chardonnay. Temperatures and yeasts vary. Some Pinot Gris styles keep residual sugar: in New Zealand fermentation is stopped by chilling or sulfur dioxide; in Alsace very ripe grapes may stop naturally. After fermentation the options multiply. The first: whether to mature in barrel, all or part of the wine. New barriques give the toast of Côte d'Or and New World Chardonnay; older, larger oak, typical of Chablis and Pinot Gris, gives less flavour but gentle oxidation; steel or concrete keeps fresh fruit. Malolactic is encouraged for a rounder, creamier palate: it is used in almost all premium white Burgundy, Chablis included, where it softens sharp acidity; but it lowers perceived acidity and dulls primary fruit, so it does not suit fruity styles. Extended fine-lees contact gives Chardonnay and Pinot Gris a richer mouthfeel, often enhanced by lees stirring, bâtonnage: breaking up the lees and mixing them back into the wine. Premium Chardonnay and Pinot Gris are not usually blended with other varieties.
Sweet wines. Most wines are fermented to dryness; sweet wines keep unfermented sugar, and there are three ways to get it.

First, stop the fermentation. The traditional way is fortification, adding grape spirit: it kills the yeast, but radically changes the wine's balance; we will meet it with fortified wines. Alternatively, a high dose of sulfur dioxide is added or the wine is chilled, and then filtered to remove the yeast; from then on no yeast must reach the wine, or fermentation would restart. This is used for many high-quality German Kabinett and Spätlese and for sweet sparkling wines such as Asti. The alcohol stays low.

Second, add a sweetening component. In Germany, medium-sweet wines can be made by adding unfermented grape juice, Süssreserve, kept by filtering or with sulfur dioxide, to dry wine just before bottling. Rectified concentrated grape must does the same job, often in inexpensive wines.

Third, concentrate the grape sugars, which also concentrates acids and flavours. Noble rot lies behind many of the greatest sweet wines: Sauternes, Tokaji, and the Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese of Germany and Austria. It is the same fungus as grey rot, Botrytis cinerea, under special conditions: the grapes must already be ripe, and the climate must give humid, misty mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. Morning damp lets the fungus develop, piercing the skin with microscopic filaments; the afternoon sun slows it and evaporates water, concentrating sugars, acids and flavours. The fungus adds its own flavours: honey, apricot, citrus zest and dried fruit. Noble rot never spreads evenly, so several passes of hand picking are needed: expensive, requiring skilled labour over a long period. And in famous regions like Sauternes the ideal conditions do not come every year: too damp, and grey rot takes over, splitting the berries and inviting infection. On labels, botrytised usually means noble rot.

Drying on the vine, known in French as passerillage: ripe grapes stay on the vine, dehydrate and shrivel towards raisins, concentrating sugar. Warm, dry autumns are needed, otherwise grey rot develops. The wines have over-ripe fruit, dried and tropical, and a rich texture: they are sometimes labelled Late Harvest.

Drying after picking: healthy grapes are picked and dried in warm, dry conditions, removing any rotten berries so rot cannot spread. This is the technique behind Italy's passito wines, such as Recioto della Valpolicella: wines with a raisiny quality.

Freezing on the vine: healthy grapes hang on into winter; when it freezes, the water in the pulp turns to ice, which stays behind in the press, and the juice that runs off is highly concentrated. This is how German Eiswein and Canadian Icewine are made, with very pure varietal character. The same effect can be imitated by freezing picked grapes in the winery.

With concentration techniques, fermentation stops naturally once the yeast have converted as much sugar as they can. That can happen at very low alcohol, sometimes as low as seven per cent, because yeast struggle to survive in such sugary juice: German Trockenbeerenauslese is the classic example.

To sum up: skin contact, juice clarity, temperature and vessel, lees, malolactic and oak are the levers of white winemaking; high-volume wines aim for clean fruit and consistency; aromatic varieties are protected, neutral ones are enriched; and sweet wines come from stopping fermentation, adding sweetness, or concentrating sugar through noble rot, drying or freezing.

Making red wine is more involved than making white, because the juice must ferment with the skins to extract colour and tannin. That has two consequences: there are many more choices before, during and after fermentation, and pressing happens after fermentation rather than before. Also, in red winemaking malolactic conversion is standard practice, not a stylistic choice. In this lesson we look at the ways colour and tannin are extracted, how inexpensive and premium reds are made with five international varieties, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Syrah or Shiraz, and Grenache or Garnacha, and finally rosé.
Crushed fruit fermentation, the most common case: the grapes are destemmed and crushed.

Pre-fermentation extraction. Some winemakers let crushed grapes macerate at low temperature before fermentation starts: cold maceration, or cold soaking. It extracts colour and flavour compounds; tannins dissolve better in alcohol, so little is extracted at this stage.

Temperature. Reds usually ferment between twenty and thirty-two degrees, depending on style: warmer than whites, to extract colour, flavour and tannin. But temperatures must not exceed thirty-five degrees, which can kill the yeast. Temperature control lets the winemaker fine-tune extraction: for example, although tannins become more soluble as alcohol rises, lowering the temperature towards the end of fermentation reduces their extraction.

Cap management. Left alone, fermenting red wine soon forms a thick mass of skins and pulp on its surface: the cap. If it simply floats, little is extracted from it. There are several techniques, which can be combined or used at different stages, and extraction is controlled by how long and how often each is done. Punching down: traditionally done by hand with paddles, which carried the risk of carbon dioxide poisoning; today mechanical paddles do the same job. It is very effective for colour and tannin, so winemakers must not overwork the cap, especially late in fermentation when tannins extract more easily: too much tannin makes a wine bitter and astringent. Pumping over: juice is drawn from the bottom of the vat and pumped over the cap; it is popular and also a good way to release heat and aerate the juice. Rack and return, known in French as délestage: all the juice is drained into another vessel, leaving the cap behind, then pumped back over it; it is usually done only once or twice, because it is very extractive, and it releases heat well. Rotary fermenters: rotating horizontal tanks that keep juice and skins in constant contact. Because of all this, reds ferment in large vessels, often open-topped, of oak, concrete or stainless steel; fermenting red wine in barrels is impractical, because it would be almost impossible to keep skins and juice in contact.

Post-fermentation maceration extracts more tannin, which may or may not be wanted: how long the wine stays on its skins depends on the style. Some winemakers find that very long macerations give a smoother tannin structure.

Press wine. When maceration ends, the free-run wine is drained off and the remaining mass is pressed. At first the press wine resembles the free run, but as pressing continues it becomes deeper in colour and higher in tannin. Press fractions can be kept separate and the later ones used to adjust colour and tannin in the final blend.

Whole bunch fermentation. Some winemakers include whole, uncrushed bunches, sometimes a whole vat, sometimes a small share for a subtler effect. The stems must be fully ripe, or they give a bitter taste. The aim is an oxygen-free environment for the intact fruit. Two things happen: the berries make some alcohol inside their cells without any yeast, intracellular fermentation; and, more importantly, distinctive fruity aromas form inside the berry. Three variations. Carbonic maceration: only whole bunches, in a vat filled with carbon dioxide; when the alcohol inside the berries reaches about two per cent, the skins split and release the juice; the grapes are usually pressed then, and yeast finishes the fermentation off the skins. Colour is extracted but little tannin: soft, fruity wines with notes of kirsch, banana, bubble gum and cinnamon-like spice. Semi-carbonic maceration: whole bunches without added carbon dioxide; those at the bottom are crushed by the weight above, ambient yeast ferments that juice, and the gas it produces fills the vat, so the intact berries undergo carbonic maceration; then the grapes are pressed and fermentation finishes off the skins. Some notable premium Pinot Noirs are made this way, but with fermentation continuing on the skins: the berries are progressively broken up by punching down over the first few days, then fermentation carries on on the skins, sometimes followed by post-fermentation maceration; the intracellular aromas integrate better with varietal aromas and the fruit is fresher. Finally, whole bunches mixed with crushed fruit: submerged among the crushed grapes, the bunches are kept away from oxygen and undergo intracellular fermentation, then are crushed by punching down. The more whole bunches, the more carbonic character: the technique is thought to give a silkier texture and brighter, fresher fruit.

Maturation. The biggest decision is whether to use oak. Almost all reds go through malolactic, and their more robust flavours and textures mean they gain less from long lees contact. Oak is widely used, as barrels or as staves and chips. But the trend for maturing premium reds entirely in small new barrels is declining: many producers now seek subtlety and integration, with oak of different ages and larger sizes. A producer's best wines still usually spend longer in oak with more new oak, because their more concentrated fruit can support it.

Blending varieties is common in reds, to balance colour, body, tannin, acidity or flavour. Press fractions are also used to boost the more delicate free-run wine, and wines from barrels of different ages, sizes and toast levels are combined, or oaked wine is blended with wine from steel or concrete for a subtler oak influence. Most reds are fined or filtered; some winemakers avoid it, believing it harms structure, and long maturation brings natural sedimentation anyway.

High-volume, inexpensive reds come from warm, sunny, dry regions, using varieties that thrive there: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah and Grenache. With skins rich in colour, tannin and flavour, they give fruity wines with adequate colour even at high yields, though with less colour, lighter tannins and less intense flavour than premium versions, and often a flattened varietal character. Pinot Noir is rarely used: it is hard to grow, prefers cool climates and struggles to give colour and tannin at high yields. As with whites, they may be single-variety or blends, sometimes sold simply as fruity red.

How they are made: a fruity, low-tannin style, so protective handling and monitored sulfur dioxide. Destemming and crushing, often acidification with tartaric acid. Pre-fermentation maceration is possible but ties up vats, so not always feasible. Fermentation with cultured yeast at twenty-two to twenty-five degrees to maximise fresh fruit, in static or rotary vessels, without working the cap hard. No post-fermentation maceration, for reasons of time and space, and because extra tannin is not wanted; if more structure is needed, a small portion is macerated longer and blended back. Carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration also gives fruity, low-tannin wines and is common for inexpensive Grenache and basic Beaujolais. For maturation: stainless steel until bottling for pure fruit, or a few months in oak to smooth tannins and add spice and toast, usually in second- or third-fill barrels, or chips and staves. As with whites, buyers expect a clear wine: stabilisation, fining and sterile filtration, with sulfur dioxide topped up at bottling.
Premium reds, variety by variety.

Cabernet Sauvignon is thick-skinned, so it has plenty of colour, flavour and tannin. It ripens late, and in cooler places, in poor years, it may not ripen fully, giving astringent tannins and herbaceous flavours. It is the classic grape of the Haut-Médoc in Bordeaux: long-lived wines with grippy tannins in youth and notes of cedar and blackcurrant leaf; with age the tannins soften and the flavours open up. It is usually blended with some Merlot, which ripens earlier and adds juicy plum and a smoother texture. In Europe it is also found in southern France, Italy and Spain, often blended with local varieties such as Sangiovese or Tempranillo. Outside Europe it is made both varietally and in blends, and warmth and long hours of sun give full-bodied wines with ripe blackcurrant and black cherry and smooth tannins: Napa Valley, Coonawarra, Margaret River, Hawke's Bay, Stellenbosch, Colchagua Valley. In the winery it is destemmed and crushed, as its stems give herbaceous, astringent notes. A pre-fermentation maceration may maximise colour. Fermentation runs at twenty-six to thirty degrees, warm enough to extract and cool enough for fresh fruit. Because it is so tannic, high temperatures and extractive cap management are avoided late in fermentation, especially if tannins are not fully ripe; post-fermentation maceration, by contrast, can extract gently and soften tannins. Its structure suits oak and bottle ageing: with intense flavour, medium to full body and high tannin, it can take a high proportion of new oak, usually two-hundred-and-twenty-five-litre French barriques, for anything from six months to three or four years, typically twelve to eighteen months. On its own it can be tannic and lacking in body, so it is often blended with Merlot, or in Australia with Shiraz.

Merlot is the other great grape of Bordeaux: it buds and ripens earlier than Cabernet and dominates in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Premium Merlot follows two styles. The international style: picked as late as possible, with intense purple colour, concentrated blackberry and plum, soft velvety tannins and often toasty new oak; made successfully across the New World, in southern France and at some Bordeaux estates. The other style: picked earlier, with medium body and alcohol, higher acidity, fresh red fruit and some vegetal, leafy notes; rare outside Bordeaux. It is made much like Cabernet, but its skins are a little more supple, so less vigorous extraction is needed. The toast, vanilla and clove of new oak suit its juicy plum fruit, and twelve to eighteen months in oak is common here too.

Pinot Noir, by contrast, buds and ripens early and has thin skins. It is very old, so there are many clones. It ranges from light and fruity with red cherry to complex and earthy with spice and forest floor. Colour and tannin are tricky to extract: the aim is maximum extraction without overworking the juice, or its elegant primary aromas are lost. It suits cool and moderate climates: it is the perfect black grape for Burgundy. Entry-level wines are light, with marked acidity and a touch of oak for structure; those from the better Côte d'Or sites have more intensity and complexity, from delicate and almost floral to more tannic and spicy. In very cool vintages, especially on lesser sites, it may not ripen fully, giving vegetal notes of cabbage and wet leaves. In Europe, Baden in Germany is also known for fine Pinot Noir. In the New World: Los Carneros and Sonoma, Martinborough, Marlborough and Central Otago, Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Tasmania, Walker Bay, and Casablanca Valley. Finding the right climate is vital: too hot and the fruit turns jammy. In the winery, some producers destem and crush, with a pre-fermentation maceration; others, increasingly, include some whole bunches, which enhance red fruit and floral notes, breaking them up by punching down. Temperatures often rise above thirty degrees: cooler for lighter, fresher styles, warmer for wines meant to age. Post-fermentation maceration is not widely used. Premium Pinot usually spends twelve to twenty-four months in oak, but too much new oak would overwhelm its delicate flavours, so many use second- or third-fill barrels with only a little new oak. It is not usually blended with other varieties, though different plots or differently treated batches may be combined. The best wines develop in bottle for many years, gaining forest floor and mushroom.

Syrah has small, thick, dark-skinned berries and will not ripen in very cool climates. It ranges from medium-bodied with pepper and fresh black fruit to smooth and full-bodied with very ripe black fruit and liquorice. Its intensity, colour and tannin make the best examples suitable for long ageing. In Europe it is most famous in the Northern Rhône, at the cool limit for Syrah, so style depends on site: lesser sites give light wines with simple black fruit, herbaceous notes and slightly grippy tannins; south-facing slopes such as Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage give fuller wines with berry fruit and pepper, then meat and leather with age. In Languedoc and Roussillon it is blended with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault, with riper fruit and tannins. In Australia it is called Shiraz: hot regions like the Hunter and Barossa Valleys make soft, earthy, spicy styles with concentrated black fruit; cooler ones like Great Southern, Geelong and Heathcote make leaner, more peppery wines. Other classic sources are Chile, South Africa, Hawke's Bay and Washington State. Winemaking shapes the style: in warm and hot climates, full-bodied, very ripe, high-alcohol wines come from vigorous cap management and plenty of new oak; more restrained styles start with earlier picking and lower alcohol, then gentler extraction, some whole bunches, long post-fermentation maceration for fine tannins, and larger, older barrels of three hundred to five hundred litres instead of barriques.

Grenache, or Garnacha, ripens late and needs warm or hot climates; conveniently, it is very drought tolerant. Its sweet, thin-skinned grapes give wines high in alcohol, low in acidity and full-bodied, with soft tannins and red fruit. In Spain it is an important blending partner in Priorat, where with Carignan it gives deeply coloured, tannic wines with fresh black fruit and toasty oak, and in Rioja, planted mainly in Rioja Baja, where with Tempranillo it adds perfume, body and alcohol; it is also widely grown in Calatayud, Cariñena and Navarra, and several regions make rosé from it. It is the most planted grape of the Southern Rhône and arguably at its finest in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, blended mainly with Syrah and Mourvèdre into full-bodied, richly textured wines with concentrated spicy red fruit. In Languedoc and Roussillon it often has a spicy, perfumed character recalling local herbs. Outside Europe the best is probably Australian, from the Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale: once intensely concentrated and alcoholic, now more restrained; old bush vines give small crops of concentrated grapes, with intense red berry fruit and peppery spice. In the winery it is destemmed and crushed, often with pre-fermentation maceration, sometimes with some whole bunches; fermentation is in open-top steel or concrete, sometimes old oak, with gentle cap management for finesse; usually it is drained off the skins at the end of fermentation. It matures in large old oak, since new-oak toast would swamp its fruit. It is rarely varietal: in hot climates it can be jammy and alcoholic, and even more heat-tolerant varieties such as Carignan and Mourvèdre add fresher fruit, tannin and colour.

Finally, rosé, almost never oaked, made in three ways. Direct pressing: black grapes are crushed and pressed as for white wine, extracting a little colour: this gives the palest rosés. Short maceration: crushed black grapes macerate to extract flavour and colour, for as long as the desired colour and tannin require, sometimes into the start of fermentation; then the juice is drained off and fermented cool like a white. Blending: a little red wine is added to white. This is not permitted in the EU, except for rosé Champagne, but some fruity, inexpensive New World rosés are made this way.

To sum up: red winemaking is all about extraction, through maceration, temperature, cap management and press wine; whole bunches bring carbonic fruit; oak is used more subtly than before; and each variety has its own rules. Rosés come from direct pressing, short maceration or, outside Europe, blending.

Why does a bottle cost what it costs? There are countless factors and they vary from market to market, but some apply everywhere: the costs of production, packaging, transport and selling, taxes, retailers' margins and, in the end, market forces.

Production costs split into grape growing and winemaking. Establishing a vineyard is very expensive: the land, especially pricey in famous regions, preparing the soil, buying and planting vines, building the trellis. And it takes many years to earn that investment back. In an established vineyard the vines need attention all year, and labour is usually the biggest cost. It can be kept down with seasonal workers, mechanisation, or by sharing labour and machines between growers. But in isolated vineyards or on extremely steep slopes, like some in the Mosel, those savings are not possible and costs climb sharply.

In the winery, the most obvious cost is equipping and maintaining it: the most advanced machines are very expensive, and even a small winery must invest heavily relative to its size. Some equipment, such as bottling lines, can be shared. Then there is time: some wines mature for months or years before release, sometimes because regulations require it. Storage facilities are costly to run, and meanwhile money is tied up in stock that cannot yet be sold: that delay has to be built into the price.

Packaging: bottles, labels, capsules, closures and cartons must be designed and bought. Heavy or unusually shaped bottles cost more. Shipping wine in bulk and bottling it in the destination market is cheaper, but only possible for large producers and not always allowed by local wine law.

Transport, distribution and sales. Very few producers sell only to visitors at the winery; almost all want to reach markets further afield, at home and abroad. This part of the trade is very complex and heavily regulated, and usually relies on other businesses: producers must choose partners who offer value for money and reliable access to sales.

Taxes. Nearly every government taxes alcoholic drinks, at levels that vary greatly between countries, and tax can add substantially to the price. It is seen as essential to control consumption by raising prices, and it is an important source of government revenue.

Retailers. Most wine is sold through shops or restaurants, which need to make a profit. Wine costs more in restaurants: they expect a bigger margin, and the price also reflects the occasion, the setting and the service.

Market forces. Ultimately, the price depends on what the destination market will pay, while all costs must be covered for the product to be viable. When demand is high and supply limited, the price can far exceed the costs: in recent years, demand for top Bordeaux estates has pushed prices up considerably, though market forces may eventually reverse that trend. At the other end, some businesses struggle for lack of demand: some steep Mosel vineyards have been abandoned, because covering their costs would have meant prices consumers were not prepared to pay.

Types of producer. There are three: co-operatives, merchants and estates. None of these terms has legal meaning, and they rarely appear on labels. It is also common for one producer to bottle wines under both estate and merchant labels.

Co-operatives are owned by their members, usually grape growers, who deliver their grapes to a winery owned by the co-operative and run by a winemaking team it employs. Growers benefit from a guaranteed buyer; the winemaker may find it challenging, as they do not always control the quality of grapes supplied by their own employers. But co-operative wines are not necessarily inferior, and in some regions the local co-operative makes some of the best wines. They are very common in Europe, where growers' holdings are so small on average that making and marketing their own wine is rarely economical; elsewhere they exist but are less common.

Merchants buy grapes, juice or wine from growers or co-operatives under contract, and in theory have more control over their raw material: they can reject substandard grapes, though where grapes are in high demand or short supply, a steady supply is hard to guarantee. They can be small and focused on premium wine, or large with ranges at several quality levels. They are found everywhere, but especially outside Europe, where growers have far larger holdings and dealing with a few suppliers is convenient: many big brands are made this way. They are sometimes called by the French name, négociant.

Estates make wine only from grapes they grow themselves. So they are usually fairly small, but they control the whole process, and in most regions they make the best wines. The drawback: relying only on their own crop gives fewer blending options, which is a challenge in a year hit by frost or hail. Estates exist throughout the wine world and are sometimes called by the French name, domaine.

To sum up: vineyard, winery, maturation time, packaging, transport, taxes and retail margins make up the cost; the market sets the price; and behind each bottle stands a co-operative, a merchant or an estate.

Where alcohol is legal, wine law deals with three things: making sure wine is safe to drink, making sure the label accurately describes what is in the bottle and, because alcohol is toxic and addictive, reducing the harm it can do to individuals and society.

Food safety comes first: whatever is sold must be safe and fit to consume. It is a technical area covering the many processing aids and chemicals used in vineyards and wineries, which hardly ever appear on labels. The clearest example is sulfur dioxide: almost universal in winemaking, it is toxic at very high doses. Levels in wine are tiny, but its use is tightly regulated, and in most countries the words contains sulfites must appear on the label above a certain level. Because fermentation produces a little naturally, the statement is likely to be needed even when none is added.

Label integrity. Whoever puts a product on sale is responsible for its description and claims being accurate, which means clear and verifiable. Wine has many labelling rules, and some matter more than others.

Geographical indications, or GIs, name a wine's place of origin and are very common on labels, because where grapes grow has a defining influence on style and quality. A GI is a designated vineyard area within a country: it can be huge, like Bordeaux, or tiny, like a single vineyard such as La Romanée in Burgundy. Their use is tightly controlled, because fraud is a real risk for premium wines.

Within one country, control is fairly simple; it is harder when a producer in one country uses another country's GI. So the World Trade Organization developed a shared system, based on defined boundaries and regional names, now used by all the major wine-producing countries, making mutual recognition much easier. For example, Australian producers used to label wines Chablis; they could never sell them that way in the EU, and now, under a trade agreement, they cannot use the name in Australia either, in exchange for fairer trading terms.

Two important points. First: if a GI appears on the label, typically at least eighty-five per cent of the wine must come from it. This is a standard with exceptions: some local laws are less strict, some stricter; for PDO wines, for example, one hundred per cent of the grapes must come from the stated region. Similar rules apply to vintages and grape varieties. Second: GI law is written very differently inside and outside the EU.

In the European Union, wines with a GI fall into two categories: Protected Designation of Origin, PDO, and Protected Geographical Indication, PGI. Broadly, PDOs are smaller areas with tighter rules, PGIs larger with fewer rules. These terms are allowed on labels but rarely used: producers prefer long-established traditional terms. In France, for instance, Appellation d'origine contrôlée is used instead of the French for PDO, Appellation d'origine protégée; on the other hand, the French for PGI, Indication géographique protégée, is increasingly replacing the traditional Vin de Pays.

European GIs are unique because local laws usually also specify which grape varieties may be grown and which viticultural and winemaking techniques may be used. The system was designed to protect the identity of local wines by identifying the varieties and methods behind a region's best wines, promoting quality and preventing fraud. In theory each PDO gives a wine with a unique flavour that cannot be copied, reinforced by the rule that one hundred per cent of the grapes must come from the region. Many PDO wines do not name the grape: some of the finest Chardonnays in the world are labelled simply Chablis or Meursault.

Because PDOs are so restrictive, many producers prefer PGI, which allows non-traditional varieties, such as Sauvignon Blanc in the south of France, and less strict rules, though yields and volumes are still usually limited. It is a very diverse category: exceptional wines from vineyards just outside PDO boundaries, as well as high-volume inexpensive wines from international varieties like Chardonnay and Merlot. Unlike PDO wines, they usually state the grape variety.

Wine without a GI has the most flexible rules: brand owners can blend grapes from all over a country, or even from several EU countries. There are no limits beyond those needed for safety and accurate labelling.

Outside the EU, nearly all internationally traded wines are wines with a GI. Each country divides its vineyards in its own way: sometimes by political boundaries, more often into regions, zones, districts and so on. But, crucially, no laws define or limit which grape varieties can be planted. And unlike in the EU, the legal terms, such as AVA, Zone or Ward, rarely appear on labels. Compare two Chardonnay labels: the Chablis does not name the grape but shows its legal category clearly; the Californian puts Chardonnay front and centre and does not show the AVA category.

There is also a set of EU quality and style terms defined by law and observed across the Union, which the EU is keen to stop other countries copying. Australia, for instance, has a long tradition of Sherry-style fortified wines that it used to label Fino or Amontillado: that is no longer allowed.

Safe consumption. In moderation, alcohol is not regarded as harmful to health. But drinking too much can change behaviour, sometimes dangerously; for some people it is highly addictive, and excess harms health in the short and long term. In some cultures alcohol is not accepted and is banned. Where it is permitted, the law tries to control access and limit harm in two main ways. First, a minimum legal age for buying and drinking alcohol, because young people are more vulnerable. Second, a legal limit on blood alcohol when driving, expressed in milligrams of ethanol per millilitre of blood: alcohol reduces co-ordination, slows reactions and increases risk-taking, so driving or operating machinery under its influence greatly raises the risk of injury and death, for the driver and others. Many governments also publish sensible drinking guidelines, often in units of alcohol, with daily and weekly maximums for men and women, and restrict advertising and marketing, through voluntary codes, legislation or both: for example limiting lifestyle claims and requiring responsible drinking messages.

To sum up: safety, with sulfur dioxide as the example; truthful labels, with GIs, the eighty-five per cent rule and one hundred per cent for PDOs; the EU system of PDO, PGI and wine without a GI; the non-EU system with no limits on varieties; and safe consumption, with minimum ages, drink-driving limits, guidelines and advertising rules.

France produces huge volumes of wine in a vast range of styles, so it is best explored region by region: Bordeaux, the Dordogne and South West France, Burgundy, Beaujolais, Alsace, the Loire, the Northern and Southern Rhône, and Southern France. Champagne and sparkling wines come later, in their own section. In this short introduction, the key thing is the legal framework that applies throughout the country.

Protected Designation of Origin wines. The French term is Appellation d'origine protégée, AOP, but labels far more often show the traditional term, Appellation d'origine contrôlée, shortened to AC or AOC. Here we will simply call them appellation wines. One point to remember: the same plot of land is often covered by both a generic and a more prestigious appellation, and each year the producer chooses which to use, often depending on the quality of the vintage.

Protected Geographical Indication wines: in French, Indication géographique protégée, IGP. Many producers use this term, though the traditional Vin de Pays is still often seen. The most important IGPs are Pays d'Oc in the south and Côtes de Gascogne in the south-west.
Wines without a geographical indication are called Vin de France.

On the map, the regions fall into place like this: Champagne and Alsace in the north-east, the Loire along the great river towards the Atlantic, Bordeaux and the South West on the Atlantic side, Burgundy and Beaujolais in the centre-east, the Rhône running down towards the Mediterranean, and Languedoc and Roussillon along the Mediterranean coast.

To sum up: AOC, or AOP, for appellations; IGP, or Vin de Pays, for geographical indications; Vin de France for wines without one; and the option for a single vineyard to choose each year between a generic and a more prestigious appellation.

Bordeaux is France's largest appellation, by area and by volume, and home to some of the world's most prestigious wines. Yet those represent a tiny share of production, and there is a huge gap between a few very wealthy producers and the great majority of growers.

Climate and grape growing. Bordeaux has a moderate maritime climate, warmed by the Gulf Stream, which lengthens the growing season: spring frosts are rarely a problem and ripening can continue well into October. But the Atlantic also brings rain and humidity. The Landes forest and coastal dunes to the west shelter the vineyards from the worst storms. Rain falls steadily through the year, which can disrupt flowering and fruit set, encourage rot and dilute flavours at harvest. So vintages vary a lot in Bordeaux, although the best producers minimise the differences by removing unhealthy or unripe berries. Climate change and new canopy management techniques have given healthier grapes, with fewer chemical treatments, and markedly higher sugar and flavour development at harvest.

Grape varieties and winemaking. Almost all Bordeaux, red and white, is blended. With such variable weather, and above all the rain, relying on one variety would be risky: several varieties flower and ripen at different times, so a frost or a downpour cannot wipe out the whole crop.

Black grapes. Cabernet Sauvignon truly dominates only in the Haut-Médoc, though it is widely planted in the Graves too: the gravelly, stony soils are warm and free draining, helping this late ripener, especially on cooler sites and in cool, wet vintages. It can make up three quarters of the blend in the best wines of these areas. Cabernet Franc is very common in Saint-Émilion and, less so, in the Médoc and Graves: it gives wines with less body and tannin than Cabernet Sauvignon; underripe it shows leafy, almost woody notes, but ripe it adds vibrant fruit and floral character. It also likes free-draining soils. Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted variety, vital to the great wines of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol because it ripens so well on their cooler clay soils; and, being soft, it often leads inexpensive high-volume Bordeaux. Petit Verdot is far less common: it needs a lot of heat to ripen and gives deeply coloured, tannic wines that age slowly; it is always a small part of the blend, adding tannin, colour and spice.

Winemaking practices vary a lot. To widen their options, some of the best producers use traditional wooden vats alongside concrete and stainless steel. Blending usually happens the spring after harvest, though some keep lots separate until maturation ends. Most leading châteaux now make a second wine, sometimes a third, from lots not good enough for the grand vin, protecting its style and quality; some wine may also be sold to merchants. The best reds mature in two-hundred-and-twenty-five-litre barriques: the most famous châteaux may use one hundred per cent new oak, more modest estates less, and generic Bordeaux usually none. Steady progress in the winery has given riper, fruitier, more concentrated wines, even in difficult vintages.

White grapes. Semillon is the main variety for sweet wines, thanks to its thin skin and affinity for noble rot; it is also blended with Sauvignon Blanc in the top dry whites of Pessac-Léognan and Graves, adding body. Sauvignon Blanc gives citrus and green fruit; it is increasingly used alone for dry whites, an exception in a region of blends, and brings acidity to sweet wines. Muscadelle has pronounced grapey, floral aromas and plays a small role in both dry and sweet whites. Dry whites come in many styles too: entry-level wines are fresh and fruity, fermented in temperature-controlled inert vessels with minimal maturation, though some show toasty notes; dry Pessac-Léognan is often fermented and matured in new barriques and very rich, with nutty notes and concentrated fruit. The great sweet wines come from nobly rotten grapes, and the best ferment and mature for up to three years in new barriques.

Classifications. In Bordeaux they are not tied to the appellation system, except in Saint-Émilion, and they rank estates, the châteaux, not vineyards. Estates can grow or shrink by buying and selling plots, so a château name is more a brand than a defined vineyard.

Médoc and Sauternes: in eighteen fifty-five, for the Paris Universal Exhibition, the Bordeaux Chamber of Commerce drew up an official list of the best red wines of the Médoc and the sweet whites of Sauternes: the eighteen fifty-five classification. Since then the size, ownership and quality of the châteaux have changed a great deal, and its relevance is constantly debated, but it has hardly ever been altered. Classified châteaux are called crus classés. In the Médoc there are five tiers: the first includes Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux and Mouton Rothschild, plus Haut-Brion in the Graves. Sauternes has only three tiers, the highest occupied by Château d'Yquem alone.

Because the eighteen fifty-five classification includes only a small number of Médoc estates, a Cru Bourgeois classification was later created for the other châteaux. Today it has three tiers: Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and, the most prestigious, Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel, and it is revised every five years.

Graves, now Pessac-Léognan: two parallel but separate lists, for reds and for whites. There is no hierarchy: every wine on the list may simply call itself cru classé. All of them now lie within the Pessac-Léognan appellation, created after the classification.

Saint-Émilion: here the classification sits within the appellation system. There is a Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, and within it a classification of only the best châteaux, since many grand cru wines are not classified. The base is Saint-Émilion Grand Cru Classé, above it Premier Grand Cru Classé, split into A, the best, and B. It is revised every ten years, with promotion and demotion possible.

Regions and wines. The Dordogne and Garonne meet to form the Gironde estuary and divide Bordeaux into three broad areas. West of the Gironde lies the Médoc, and south of the Garonne the Graves and Sauternes: together, the Left Bank. Between the two rivers lies the large Entre-Deux-Mers appellation. North and east of the Gironde and Dordogne is the Right Bank, with Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Bordeaux has over fifty appellations, from very large to tiny, so it is best to think in styles.

The generic appellations, Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, which has slightly stricter rules and a higher minimum alcohol, make mostly reds, but also whites, rosés and clairet. Their quality keeps improving, as more producers target exports and compete with similarly priced wines from around the world. The best generic reds are for early drinking, medium-bodied, with ripe red and black fruit and sometimes cedar from oak; the cheapest are lighter, with more astringent tannins. The best rosés are fresh and fruity. Clairet appeals mainly to the French market: it macerates longer than a typical rosé, with deeper colour and more body. Generic whites are increasingly led by Sauvignon Blanc, with intense fresh-grass notes.

Red wines of the Médoc and Graves. The Médoc lies north of the city. The Médoc appellation covers the northern part, lower and more clay-rich, with generally simpler, earlier-drinking wines. From Saint-Estèphe southwards lies the more highly rated Haut-Médoc, containing several commune appellations where most of the classified châteaux are found. From north to south, the four most famous are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux. These wines have a high proportion of Cabernet Sauvignon, a core of blackcurrant with cedar from oak, grippy tannins in youth and often long ageing potential. Just south of the city is Pessac-Léognan, the most highly rated part of the Graves: gravelly soils suited to Cabernet Sauvignon, as in the Haut-Médoc, but wines that are generally a little lighter and more fragrant; the top châteaux work with as much care as any in Bordeaux, with prices to match. Further south, the Graves appellation makes similar reds, less concentrated and complex, usually with more Merlot.

Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Right Bank wines are dominated by Merlot and, to a lesser extent, Cabernet Franc. Saint-Émilion is the larger of the two and has three groups of vineyards on different soils. The plateau north and west of the town, with warm, well-drained gravel and limestone, encourages Cabernet Franc and occasionally a little Cabernet Sauvignon. The escarpment to the south and east, on clay and limestone. The most prestigious wines come from these two areas: medium to high tannins but, compared with the more structured Left Bank, a soft, rich palate with red berry and plum, developing tobacco and cedar with age. Finally, the sandy vineyards at the foot of the slope usually give lighter, less prestigious wines. Neighbouring Pomerol has an equally high reputation: its wines tend to be richer and spicier, with blackberry fruit. The Right Bank also saw the rise of very full-bodied, incredibly ripe wines made in tiny quantities from small plots, with no expense spared; they were once called vins de garage, their makers garagistes, but many are now famous and classified within Saint-Émilion. Some remain, but many producers have moved away from that over-ripe style towards more freshness. Around Saint-Émilion and Pomerol lie lesser appellations making similar Merlot-based wines.

Côtes de Bordeaux: several lesser-known red appellations agreed to share this name, and Blaye, Cadillac, Castillon and Francs may put their own names in front of it. These are Merlot-based wines for early drinking, and the best can be excellent value. Producers in Côtes de Bourg, with similar wines, chose not to join. Note that Premières Côtes de Bordeaux is a sweet wine appellation with no connection to the Côtes de Bordeaux group.

Premium dry whites. Only a few appellations may make them. Entre-Deux-Mers, between the Garonne and the Dordogne, can only make white wine; reds from there must use a generic appellation. Graves and Pessac-Léognan make both reds and whites. Whites from Graves and Entre-Deux-Mers tend to be unoaked Sauvignon Blanc. Pessac-Léognan is home to many of the very best dry whites, which can be cru classé: blends of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, fermented or matured at least partly in new oak, medium to full-bodied with toasty notes. Some châteaux in the Médoc and Sauternes make premium dry whites, but cannot use those appellations and sell them as generic Bordeaux.

Sweet wines. The top appellations cluster along the Garonne and its tributary, the Ciron, whose waters create the misty autumn conditions that let noble rot develop on fully ripe grapes. The amount of noble rot varies each year, and when there is little, drying on the vine helps concentrate sugars. The best come from Sauternes, on the west bank of the Garonne, which includes the village of Barsac: Barsac producers may use either the Barsac or the Sauternes appellation. Semillon dominates, thanks to its thin skin and susceptibility to botrytis; Sauvignon Blanc adds refreshing acidity and fruit, Muscadelle, where used, an exotic perfume. Botrytised grapes cannot be machine harvested: they are picked selectively by hand, in several passes. The best wines are high in alcohol, sweet yet balanced by high acidity, with the apricot and citrus peel of noble rot plus toast and vanilla from oak. Several other nearby appellations make sweet wines in a similar style.

To sum up: a maritime climate, variable vintages, blending; Cabernet Sauvignon on the Left Bank, Merlot and Cabernet Franc on the Right; the eighteen fifty-five classification, the three-tier Cru Bourgeois classification revised every five years, the Graves list and Saint-Émilion revised every ten; the dry whites of Pessac-Léognan and the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac.

These wines fall into two groups. On one side, the wines of the Dordogne, mostly made from the same varieties as Bordeaux. On the other, several regions that use varieties never seen in Bordeaux, in very different styles: the wines of South West France.

The Dordogne. East of Entre-Deux-Mers lie the vineyards of the Dordogne. The climate resembles Bordeaux's, but with less moderating maritime influence. The main appellation is Bergerac, for reds and whites made from the Bordeaux varieties. Monbazillac is a source of good-value botrytised sweet wines from Semillon and Sauvignon Blanc.

South West France. Cahors lies east of Bordeaux, on both sides of the river Lot. Its wines were once called black wines: very tannic and long-lived. Today a broad range of styles is made, depending on whether the vines grow on the fertile valley floor, the poorer soils of the slopes or the plateau above. The main variety is Malbec, with Merlot and Tannat. At their best, the wines are oak-aged, deeply coloured, high in tannin, with intense dark berry fruit, slowly revealing cedar and earth.
South-east of Bordeaux there is large production of IGP wines, the most important being Côtes de Gascogne: dry, light-bodied whites with green apple aromas, generally made from Ugni Blanc.

Further south towards the Pyrenees, Madiran makes reds led by Tannat, a deeply coloured, high-tannin variety that traditionally needed long bottle ageing to soften. Today, riper grapes and modern winemaking mean the best wines have concentrated black fruit and high but riper, softer tannins.

Right in the foothills of the Pyrenees, Jurançon makes dry and sweet whites. The most important are complex sweet wines from high-acid Petit Manseng. The grapes are not botrytised but dried on the vine, and the wines have pronounced apricot and grapefruit aromas, sometimes with spicy notes from new oak.

To sum up: Bergerac and Monbazillac in the Bordeaux mould; and the South West with its own varieties: Malbec in Cahors, Ugni Blanc in Côtes de Gascogne, Tannat in Madiran and dried Petit Manseng in Jurançon.

With its countless producers and appellations, Burgundy can seem very complicated. In essence it is simple: it is the home of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and it remains the benchmark against which these varieties are judged worldwide.

Climate and grape growing. Burgundy covers a wide area, and the climate ranges from cool continental in the north, around Chablis, to moderate continental further south. Rain often disrupts flowering in early summer and harvest in autumn. Pinot Noir is particularly prone to grey rot, a problem in wet seasons. Other hazards: spring frosts, especially in Chablis, where they can strike as late as May, and localised summer hailstorms that can destroy a large share of a grower's crop.

A vineyard's position decides its place in the appellation hierarchy. Basic village-level vineyards tend to be on flat land or at the foot of slopes, while premier cru and grand cru sites are usually mid-slope, less prone to frost. The best face south or east, sheltered from the prevailing westerly winds. Soils are very varied: many small geological faults, combined with erosion, mean the soil changes significantly over short distances. These variations are often linked to subtle differences in style, though the exact role of soil is much debated. What is certain is that hillside soils are shallower and better drained, while those on the flat are deeper and more fertile.
Grape varieties and winemaking. Most wine is made from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, though Aligoté and Gamay are also grown.

Pinot Noir covers over a third of the vineyard area, everywhere but most importantly in the Côte d'Or. Classic Burgundian Pinot shows red fruit in youth, evolving into earth, game and mushroom. Acidity is usually high and tannins low to medium, depending on vineyard, producer and vintage. Techniques vary widely, and whole bunches have become increasingly popular. For the best wines, sixteen to eighteen months in barrel is normal, usually with some new oak, depending on the producer.

Chardonnay covers nearly half the vineyard area. Its style varies dramatically: from the lean, steely, high-acid wines of Chablis in the north, via the often fabulously complex, expressive wines of the Côte d'Or, to the fuller, riper wines of the Mâconnais in the south. Burgundian winemakers pioneered the techniques now linked with premium Chardonnay everywhere: barrel fermentation, barrel ageing, typically six to nine months, malolactic for whites and lees ageing. Some of the most expressive and sought-after examples come from the Côte d'Or. Debate continues about how much new oak and what toast level are ideal. Whatever the method, the best are balanced, complex and able to age a decade or more.

Around twenty years ago, it was noticed that some white Burgundies were not ageing as expected: bottles of top wines showed premature oxidation. The problem still exists, and not only in Burgundy, but today its frequency has fallen markedly compared with the previous decade. Several causes, in the vineyard and the winery, have been suggested, and producers are adapting their practices to avoid it.

Other varieties. Aligoté is a white grape giving fairly neutral, high-acid wines; it can be very good where it ripens fully, but those sites are usually kept for more profitable Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, so such wines are rare. Gamay gives early-drinking reds with ripe berry fruit and low tannin; it is allowed in some regional appellations, but only Pinot Noir is permitted for reds at village level and above.

The appellation hierarchy is based on site quality. At the base are the regional appellations, half of the region's production. Most come from vineyards with no right to anything higher, but some wines are declassified, because of excessive yields or because a quality-minded producer wants to protect the prestige of the higher appellation. Bourgogne Rouge and Bourgogne Blanc are the most generic and can come from anywhere in Burgundy, usually from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Other regional appellations cover smaller areas: Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits, Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Beaune, Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise and, new in this edition, Bourgogne Côte d'Or, a recently created appellation for reds and whites from any village in the Côte d'Or. In the Mâconnais, the regional appellations are Mâcon, red or white, and Mâcon-Villages, white only.

Next come the commune appellations, such as Chablis or Gevrey-Chambertin, about a third of production. Usually only the commune name appears on the label; occasionally a vineyard name too, if all the wine comes from a single vineyard that is not a premier or grand cru. They are also called village appellations.

Then the single-vineyard appellations: premiers crus and grands crus, sites that have consistently made outstanding wine. They rarely have a single owner, a monopole: most are divided among several estates, each farming its own parcels. There are over six hundred premiers crus, about a tenth of production. The label must say premier cru, with the vineyard name if the wine comes from one site; producers may also blend several premiers crus from one village, with no vineyard name. At the top are the grands crus, little more than one per cent of production: thirty-two in the Côte d'Or and one in Chablis, divided into seven climats. They are recognisable because only the vineyard name appears on the label, with the words grand cru.

Chablis is a village appellation in the Serein valley in the far north. Only Chardonnay is permitted. The main climatic problem is frost, fought with sprinklers and heaters. Village Chablis often comes from north-facing slopes and flatter land; premiers and grands crus sit on south-facing hillsides, giving more concentration and ripeness. Some lesser vineyards make up Petit Chablis. Petit Chablis and Chablis can be very austere, with green fruit and high acidity, though better examples show riper fruit. Premiers and grands crus have riper, more concentrated fruit, citrus rather than green apple, and more body, still balanced by high acidity. Some producers ferment or age part of their grands crus, sometimes premiers crus, in old oak for a rounder texture and subtle flavours; others prefer the purity of stainless steel or concrete.

The Côte d'Or is Burgundy's heartland. The Massif Central runs along its western edge, giving east and south-east facing slopes. It splits in two. The Côte de Nuits makes many of the fullest-bodied, longest-lived Pinot Noirs. The Côte de Beaune, further south, also makes Pinot Noir, generally fruitier, but is most famous for the region's finest Chardonnays. The appellation system reflects this: all the red grands crus but one are in the Côte de Nuits, and all the white grands crus but one in the Côte de Beaune.

From north to south, the key Côte de Nuits villages, with their most famous grands crus, are Gevrey-Chambertin, with Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze; Vougeot, with Clos de Vougeot; Vosne-Romanée, with Romanée-Conti, La Tâche and La Romanée; and Nuits-Saint-Georges. In the Côte de Beaune: Aloxe-Corton, with Corton and Corton-Charlemagne; Beaune; Pommard; Volnay; Meursault; Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet, which share the grand cru Montrachet. All make white as well as red, except Pommard and Volnay. The three villages most famous for white wine are Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet.

Côte de Nuits-Villages can be red or white, from Côte de Nuits vineyards that do not qualify for the more famous village names. Côte de Beaune-Villages must be red and can come from one or several Côte de Beaune villages, with some exceptions. The Hautes-Côtes de Nuits and Hautes-Côtes de Beaune lie west of, and higher than, the main strip: windier and cooler, they give wines with slightly less body and concentration.

The Côte Chalonnaise, south of the Côte d'Or, also grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, but higher altitude delays harvest and makes ripening less reliable, and the slopes do not always face east: the wines are lighter, mature earlier and are seen as less prestigious. There are four village appellations: Rully, with more white than red and an important sparkling wine centre; Mercurey, whose reds have the highest reputation here; Givry, the smallest, with much-admired reds; and Montagny, white only. All have premiers crus but no grands crus. Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise is the area's regional appellation.

The Mâconnais. Chardonnay is the most planted grape; reds are mostly Gamay, with some Pinot Noir still grown. Mâcon, the regional appellation, can be red or white: the best whites balance fresh apple or citrus, medium acidity and medium to full body, sometimes with a creamy touch from malolactic; reds are light, fruity and for early drinking. Whites labelled Mâcon-Villages, or Mâcon plus a village name, are generally excellent value; some villages, such as Lugny, have a strong following. Mâcon-Villages can come from one or several villages and resembles white Mâcon with more ripeness, body and character. The two most famous village appellations are Pouilly-Fuissé, which now has a number of premier cru vineyards, and Saint-Véran. The best show ripe stone and tropical fruit and are usually barrel-matured for texture and complexity. The vines grow on the limestone slopes of the Roche de Solutré, facing east and south-east: natural amphitheatres that trap the sun and give some of Burgundy's richest, ripest Chardonnays, often with toasty oak.

To sum up: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; a four-level hierarchy of regional, village, premier cru and grand cru; the Côte de Nuits for great reds, the Côte de Beaune for great whites; Chablis in the north, the Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais in the south; and the news in this edition: Bourgogne Côte d'Or, premiers crus in Pouilly-Fuissé and a decline in premature oxidation.

Red, rosé and white wines can all be made in Beaujolais, but production is dominated by reds from Gamay, so those are the only ones we'll look at. Styles range from light, fruity wines for drinking young to wines that gain complexity with some years in bottle.

Grape growing. The climate is similar to the southern Mâconnais and ideal for Gamay, an early-budding, early-ripening variety. But Gamay needs managing: left to itself it gives large yields and lesser wines. That is why the best wines come from the granite soils, low in nutrients, which limit yields and concentrate flavour in the grapes.

The traditional pruning method is the gobelet, or bush vine: spurs are left around the head of the vine, then the shoots are tied together to hold them upright. However, more and more growers are training their vines along wires, to allow mechanisation.
Gamay gives fragrant wines with raspberry and cherry aromas. They rarely have more than medium tannin and body, and the lightest can even be served lightly chilled.
The appellations form a hierarchy: at the base the regional Beaujolais appellation, then Beaujolais Villages, and at the top the individual appellations of the Beaujolais crus.

Beaujolais and Beaujolais Nouveau. Beaujolais is made mainly on the alluvial plain of the river Saône, in the east and south of the region, largely by carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration. This is also the main source of Beaujolais Nouveau, a wine made specifically for early drinking. It cannot be released before the third Thursday of November after the vintage, and growers and négociants cannot sell it after the following thirty-first of August. Nouveau can only be of Beaujolais or Beaujolais Villages quality, never one of the ten crus. Both are light in body and tannin, with red berry fruit and often, from carbonic maceration, notes of kirsch, banana and cinnamon-like spice.

Beaujolais Villages and the crus. In the north and west, the vines are planted on rolling hills with granite soils. Thirty-nine villages may call their wine Beaujolais Villages. Village names rarely appear on labels, as these wines are usually blends from several villages.

Ten villages have their own appellation: these are the Beaujolais crus. The four biggest producers are Brouilly, Morgon, Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent. Moulin-à-Vent and Morgon often give the most structured wines: concentrated fruit and tannin let them improve in bottle. Brouilly and Fleurie tend to be lighter and more perfumed.

Techniques for the crus vary. Many undergo a conventional crushed-fruit fermentation. Some are aged in oak, often large vats rather than barrels, so new oak flavours are rarely pronounced. Other producers use semi-carbonic maceration or a small share of whole bunches for brighter fruit.

To sum up: Gamay, which loves poor granite soils; a three-level hierarchy of Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages and ten crus; carbonic maceration, with its kirsch, banana and cinnamon notes; Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November; and Moulin-à-Vent and Morgon, the most structured crus.

On the border between Germany and France, Alsace is unusual for a French region: most of its wines are labelled by grape variety. Its still wines are mainly aromatic whites, dry, off-dry or sweet, plus a little red.

Climate and grape growing. The climate is cool to moderate continental. The Vosges mountains shelter the vineyards from rain-bearing westerly winds, and the clear skies give sunny summers and dry autumns. So grapes reach high sugar ripeness, although in the driest years drought can be a problem.

The best vineyards are on the steepest slopes, facing east and south-east. The north of the region is cooler and less protected by the Vosges. Lesser vineyards lie on the plain between the Vosges foothills and the Rhine, and their grapes often go into Crémant d'Alsace, the local sparkling wine.

Alsace has had a dramatic geological history, leaving a great variety of soils in the foothills. This complexity goes a long way to explain the range of styles, and the influence of geology on wine is clearer here than in many regions.

Practices depend on the site. On the slopes, vines are trained low to benefit from heat radiated by the soil, rows are oriented to maximise sun exposure, and harvesting is by hand. On the plain, vines are trained high to avoid spring frosts. Organic and biodynamic viticulture are widespread, partly because the sunny, dry conditions mean low disease pressure.

Harvest is a logistical challenge: many growers have lots of small plots of different varieties that ripen at different times. So picking often runs from mid-September to the end of November, or even early December for late-harvest and noble rot wines.

Appellations. The system is very simple: just two main appellations for still wine, Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru. On top come two terms, Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles, which depend on sugar ripeness and can be used by both. The downside of this simplicity is that producers use phrases like Réserve Personnelle or Cuvée Spéciale to distinguish their qualities, and these have no legal status.

The Alsace appellation accounts for the vast majority of production. Most wines are single-variety and labelled as such, and the named variety must then be one hundred per cent. A few blends are made, without a varietal label. Some villages may add their name for certain styles, but these wines are rare.

Alsace Grand Cru. Over fifty vineyards each have their own grand cru appellation. With a few exceptions, the wine must come from a single noble variety: Riesling, Muscat, Gewurztraminer or Pinot Gris. The label must show the vineyard name, the vintage and, where appropriate, the variety. The appellation has been controversial from the start, mainly over boundaries: some top producers and commentators feel many grands crus are far too large and include land unworthy of the name. So some producers choose not to label their wines grand cru even when entitled to.

Vendanges Tardives, or VT, means late harvest: only from the four noble varieties, with a minimum sugar ripeness depending on the variety. In the best, the grapes are shrivelled on the vine, sometimes with a little noble rot. Sélection de Grains Nobles, or SGN: same varieties, higher minimums, usually reached through noble rot. Not made every year, and only in small quantities.

Winemaking and styles. Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the so-called noble varieties, and generally the only ones allowed for VT, SGN and grand cru. Almost all wines are single-variety. Blends tend to be inexpensive, made from juice not selected for varietal wines, and labelled Edelzwicker or Gentil, or with a brand name. A few very high-quality blends exist, even from grands crus, but they are very rare.

Because most varieties are aromatic, winemaking aims to preserve the grape's aromas. Traditional producers ferment in large old oak casks, often over a century old, lined inside with a thick tartrate deposit so the wood has no influence. Modern cellars more often use stainless steel, which makes temperature control easier. Malolactic is usually avoided, as it would mask the pure fruit. Bottling happens the following spring, while the wine is young and fresh. Most are ready to drink then, but many can evolve further in bottle.

Apart from VT and SGN, the best wines were traditionally dry, but in recent years more and more, especially grands crus, have noticeable sweetness. VT can range from dry to medium-sweet, while SGN is always sweet. For a long time nothing on the label told consumers whether a wine was dry or sweet. Big news in this edition: from the twenty twenty-one vintage, all producers must show the sweetness level on the back label, using standard terms set by European regulation: sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux, in increasing order of sweetness.

Riesling is the most planted noble variety. The best are medium- to full-bodied, dry, with medium alcohol, high acidity, citrus and stone fruit and often a stony, steely character. Many now have some residual sugar. Compared with German examples, they tend to be less floral.

Gewurztraminer is famous for its pungent, spicy nose: lychee, rose and sweet baking spice. The lightly pink skin gives some wines a golden colour. It is often full-bodied, with a rich, oily texture, low to medium acidity and high alcohol: fourteen per cent is not unusual.

The best Pinot Gris are rich, full-bodied and high in alcohol, but often with more acidity than Gewurztraminer. The colour can be similar, the nose less aromatic. On the palate they have a rich texture and intense fresh and dried fruit with a honeyed note.

Muscat. Two Muscats are grown here. The best wines come from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains: intensely aromatic, with orange blossom, rose and grape, light to medium body and low to medium acidity. But it is prone to poor fruit set and rot, so the less aromatic but more reliable Muscat Ottonel is more widely planted.

Other varieties. Pinot Blanc is widely planted, mostly on the fertile soils of the plain. It is much used for crémant; as a still wine it is light, simple, refreshing and non-aromatic. Auxerrois is similar, slightly spicier and fuller, and the two are sometimes blended. Sylvaner, once widely planted, has given way to the noble varieties; it gives delicately perfumed wines for drinking young. Finally, Pinot Noir is the only black grape permitted. Another change in this edition: it used to lack body and concentration and was at its best as rosé or light red; but rising temperatures and local demand have improved quality, and some producers now make more concentrated wines with new oak flavours.

To sum up: varietal labelling; two appellations, Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru, and two terms, VT and SGN; four noble varieties, Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat; and two changes: compulsory sweetness labelling on the back label from the twenty twenty-one vintage, and increasingly concentrated Pinot Noir.

The Loire is France's longest river, but its most important vineyards lie only along the last few hundred kilometres, towards the Atlantic. It is a very varied region, with a great many appellations and no single signature style: instead, a remarkable range of still whites, reds and rosés.

The valley is loosely grouped into four sub-regions, from east to west: the Central Vineyards, Touraine, Anjou-Saumur and the Nantais. These are not appellations, and unlike most French regions there is no generic appellation for the whole Loire. Rosé de Loire is made mostly in Anjou, Crémant de Loire mostly in Saumur. There is, however, an IGP Val de Loire covering the whole region: straightforward, fresh, light and fruity wines.

Climate and grape growing. Overall the climate is cool, but the Central Vineyards, well inland, are continental, while the coastal Nantais is maritime. The vineyards are at the northern limit for their varieties, so vintages can differ widely. High rainfall encourages fungal disease. As in many cool climates, the best sites are the warmest and sunniest: south-facing, mid-slope and facing the river for extra heat and reflected light.

White wines. Sauvignon Blanc is grown mainly in the Central Vineyards and Touraine. The Central Vineyards have by far the smallest production, but contain two of the most prestigious Sauvignon appellations: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, on very chalky, stony, well-drained soils. The wines are dry and high in acidity, with green apple and wet stones; Pouilly-Fumé is often said to have subtle smoky notes. Some villages, such as Chavignol, and vineyards, such as Les Monts Damnés, in Sancerre, have a high reputation for particularly expressive wines. Some can evolve in bottle, but most Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are not for ageing.

Techniques vary. Gentle pneumatic pressing and temperature-controlled stainless steel give fresh, fruity wines. Some producers ferment and mature in old oak and keep the wine on its lees for a broader texture; new oak is rare. Malolactic depends on the style wanted, and is more likely in cool vintages to soften acidity.

South-west of Sancerre, on tributaries of the Loire, the main appellation is Menetou-Salon, a source of more moderately priced wines in the Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé style. But most Sauvignon comes from Touraine, under the generic Touraine appellation, often labelled Sauvignon de Touraine: less concentrated, simple and fruity.

Chenin Blanc is a high-acid, non-aromatic grape behind the greatest whites of Touraine and Anjou-Saumur. A quirk: grapes in the same bunch often ripen unevenly, which can give green, herbaceous aromas unless unripe berries are excluded. So several passes through the vineyard may be needed.

Chenin makes dry or sweet, still or sparkling wines, and the style depends directly on ripeness at harvest. Barely ripe grapes, enough for ten or eleven per cent alcohol, go into sparkling wine; dry, medium and sweet still wines use increasingly ripe berries, up to shrivelled or nobly rotten ones. In recent years growers have sought more ripeness even for dry wines, giving higher alcohol and often a few grams of residual sugar. Young, they range from fresh apple to tropical fruit; dry wines can be steely and smoky, sweet ones show the apricot and citrus peel of noble rot. Dry or sweet, they can age for decades, becoming richer and rounder, with honey, toast and hay, balanced by their high acidity.

Climate and soil shape the style. Vouvray, east of Tours, makes still and sparkling Chenin; the still wines range from dry to lusciously sweet depending on the vintage. The cool climate and clay soils give light- to medium-bodied wines, fresh, fruity and floral, rarely in new oak. To the west, Saumur and Anjou have similar climates and soils: Saumur is known for traditional-method sparkling Chenin, Anjou for dry wines, sometimes matured in new oak.

Savennières and Coteaux du Layon lie in the west of Anjou-Saumur. The warmer, drier climate than Touraine gives medium- to full-bodied, less floral wines.
