Savennières makes full-bodied dry Chenin: air circulation around these exposed vineyards hinders noble rot but allows late-harvested grapes to make full, complex dry wines that can age for decades. Coteaux du Layon, in the sheltered Layon valley south of the Loire, where noble rot develops well, makes some of the region's most renowned sweet wines. The two most favoured sites, Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux, have their own appellations and rank among the world's greatest sweet wines.

Melon Blanc, also called Muscadet or Melon de Bourgogne, ripens early and resists frost, suiting the cool climate. It is grown mainly in the Nantais, south of the Loire near the Atlantic. The wines are known as Muscadet, in several appellations. Muscadet covers the widest area, but most comes from the more highly regarded Muscadet Sèvre et Maine. All are dry, with medium alcohol, according to the new edition generally around twelve per cent. Once fermented in large old oak, they are now mostly made in concrete or stainless steel. They are light, high in acidity, with subtle green fruit, and should be drunk young. The local speciality is Muscadet sur lie: bottled in spring after a winter on its lees, which gives a richer texture; it is handled very little to keep delicacy and freshness.

Red wines. Cabernet Franc comes in a range of styles depending on climate, soil and winemaking. In Touraine it is grown in Chinon, south of the Loire, and Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil to the north. Everywhere, sandy soils give light, fruity wines for early drinking, and south-facing clay-limestone slopes fuller, more tannic wines. Some producers use oak, and the best can age for many years.

To the west, Saumur and Saumur-Champigny also make Cabernet Franc. Many are lighter, best drunk young and often served chilled. Saumur-Champigny shows a marked floral, violet character. And, new in this edition, many producers now also make a fuller, more tannic style able to age.

Gamay is the Loire's second black grape, mainly in Touraine and Anjou, for fruity, usually early-drinking wines. A little Pinot Noir grows in the Central Vineyards, but the best sites go to Sauvignon Blanc, so these reds are rare and generally light.

Rosés come mainly from Anjou-Saumur, but also from Touraine and Sancerre. Rosé de Loire is always dry, with at least thirty per cent Cabernet Franc or Cabernet Sauvignon. Anjou has two more rosé appellations: Cabernet d'Anjou, the highest quality, off-dry to medium-sweet, from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon; and Rosé d'Anjou, less sweet, mainly from Grolleau, a high-yielding local grape, with Cabernet Franc and other local varieties. Touraine rosés, from many varieties, are generally dry, fresh and fruity. Sancerre rosé must be Pinot Noir and is pale, light and dry with delicate fruit. Rosés are made by direct pressing or a short skin maceration, and fermented in inert, temperature-controlled vessels to keep the fruit.

To sum up: four sub-regions, the Central Vineyards, Touraine, Anjou-Saumur and the Nantais; Sauvignon Blanc from Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé; Chenin Blanc from Vouvray, Savennières and Coteaux du Layon; Muscadet sur lie; Cabernet Franc from Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny; and the rosés of Anjou.

Many Northern Rhône vineyards sit on steep slopes beside the river, between Vienne in the north and Valence in the south. They account for only a small percentage of total Rhône production, but are home to many of its premium wines.

Climate and grape growing. Here the valley is narrow and steep. The vineyards are mostly close to the river, and the best sites are steep, south-facing slopes, often in side valleys feeding into the Rhône. These valleys also protect the vines from the mistral, a cold, violent north wind that can easily damage them. Each vine is supported by its own stake, or by several stakes arranged like a tepee. The climate is similar to Beaujolais: moderate continental, noticeably cooler than the Southern Rhône.

Grape varieties and winemaking. The Northern Rhône is best known for powerful reds from Syrah. Very little white is made, but it has a big reputation, largely thanks to Viognier's popularity among fine wine drinkers.

Syrah is the only black grape permitted. At this latitude, and with the cooling mistral, it is at the northern limit of ripening. So the most prized sites are very steep, south-facing slopes, especially in the cooler north. The wines are deeply coloured, with medium to high tannin, black fruit and sometimes black pepper or floral aromas. Oak use depends on the winemaker: some use plenty of new oak for their best wines, others prefer older oak or larger vessels. Several crus used to co-ferment Syrah with white grapes, but today most wines are pure Syrah. White grapes can help stabilise colour, and Viognier in particular adds aromatic intensity.

Viognier gives full-bodied whites with blossom and apricot perfume and stone fruit flavours. They tend to have low acidity and high alcohol, because the grape only develops its signature aromas very late, at very high sugar levels. It needs careful handling in the winery to avoid an oily character that swamps its aromas. New oak is increasingly used, but also with care. A few off-dry wines are made from late-harvested grapes.

Marsanne and Roussanne are also grown, usually blended: Marsanne brings richness and weight, Roussanne acidity and perfumed fruit. They lack Viognier's aromatic intensity, but age well and develop complex hazelnut notes.
Regions and wines. Most wines come from the crus, though generic Côtes du Rhône can be made here too. Most crus are tiny; only Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage cover a significant area.

Côte-Rôtie, around Ampuis, is the most northerly appellation in the valley; its name, roasted slope, says a lot about its sun exposure. It makes only red, which may include up to twenty per cent Viognier, though in practice little is used, rarely more than a small percentage. The wines are deeply coloured, full-bodied and spicy, and the best have a floral freshness and textural elegance that set them apart from Hermitage.

Condrieu is a white made solely from Viognier. Its area has grown a lot in recent decades, and the best wines come from low-yielding old vines on steep, well-exposed terraces. Château-Grillet is a single-property appellation within Condrieu, in a similar style.

Saint-Joseph runs along the west bank from Condrieu in the north to Tournon in the south. It is mostly red Syrah, with some white from Marsanne and Roussanne. The best come from terraces near Tournon, with an intensity and structure similar to Hermitage, and excellent wines are also made just south of Condrieu. Large volumes of lighter reds, often partly from carbonic maceration, come from the flatter, more fertile sites on the valley floor and the plateau: among the lightest in the Northern Rhône, they show Syrah's peppery side.

Hermitage occupies a steep south-facing slope behind Tain-l'Hermitage. It is divided into lieux-dits, named sites outside the appellation system, varying in steepness and aspect and giving subtly different styles and body. The best Hermitage has traditionally been a blend of these sites, but some producers now release single lieu-dit wines. Red Hermitage is generally the fullest-bodied Northern Rhône red and ages well. Up to fifteen per cent Marsanne and Roussanne may be co-fermented with Syrah, but this is rare: instead they make white wines, about a fifth of production.

Crozes-Hermitage is the most important appellation by volume, on mixed terrain around the hill of Hermitage: slopes to the north, mostly flat plain to the south. Reds are Syrah, with up to fifteen per cent Marsanne or Roussanne allowed. Quality, style and price vary greatly: flatter, higher-yielding sites in the south give lighter wines, steeper northern slopes more concentrated, complex and tannic ones. Some pricier wines are oak-aged. Overall, though, Crozes-Hermitage lacks the reputation of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie. A little white is also made.

Cornas is the most southerly red cru and by far the warmest, on sheltered, south-facing slopes of many side valleys. Unlike the others, Cornas must be one hundred per cent Syrah. The wines are deeply coloured and full-bodied, similar to Hermitage in style and quality.

To sum up: steep slopes, the mistral and a continental climate; Syrah, the only black grape; Viognier in Condrieu; Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage and Cornas for great reds; Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage for volume.

The Southern Rhône vineyard is far larger than the northern one and makes an impressive range of wines, from inexpensive high-volume to premium. Red dominates, but there are some high-quality whites and rosés too.

Climate and grape growing. South of Valence the valley opens out and the vines are planted on much flatter land. Many of the best sites, though not all, have very stony soils: the stones absorb the sun's heat and warm the vineyard, helping ripening. In places, especially in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, these stones, or galets, completely cover the ground. The climate is Mediterranean: mild winters, warm dry summers, sometimes with drought. Here the mistral picks up speed and can cause extensive damage. With few slopes to shelter the vines, windbreaks have to be planted. Grenache is mostly bush-trained low to the ground, to resist the wind and benefit from the soil's warmth. Syrah, more easily damaged by wind, benefits from trellising.
Grape varieties and winemaking. Instead of one or two varieties as in the north, southern wines are often complex blends, sometimes of a dozen varieties or more.

Grenache dominates most reds and is by far the most planted variety. The warm summers let it ripen fully, giving concentrated spiced red fruit; in very hot years the fruit can become baked and jammy. Syrah and Mourvèdre play supporting roles. Syrah adds colour and tannin but can struggle in the hottest sites. Mourvèdre, by contrast, is at the northern limit of ripening here and thrives: deeply coloured and very tannic, when fully ripe it develops dense black fruit and gamey, meaty notes prized by many top producers, especially in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Cinsault can also support red blends, adding red fruit rather than tannin or colour, but is best known as Grenache's partner in fresh, fruity rosés.

Winemaking varies as much as the grapes, so it is almost impossible to describe a typical Southern Rhône red. But every winemaker must manage potentially high tannin and alcohol to make a balanced wine. Techniques range from cold pre-fermentation maceration and stainless steel to warm, extractive fermentations in traditional open vats and maturation in large old oak. Often the final blend combines wines made in different ways. Some use new oak, though some traditional producers believe it overwhelms Grenache. Styles range from light- to medium-bodied, fresh, fruity, low-tannin wines to full-bodied, highly tannic reds with spice, meat or earth.

Whites remain a minority, and there is no southern equivalent of Condrieu. Clairette, Grenache Blanc and Bourboulenc join the northern trio of Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne, which are also grown here. The best whites are richly textured, full-bodied and high in alcohol, with low to medium acidity and subtle fruit. New oak is rarely used.
Regions and wines. Production is divided between regional appellations, village appellations and crus.
Côtes du Rhône accounts for more than half of all Southern Rhône appellation wine, mostly red: medium-bodied, fruity but simple. Fruity rosés and whites are made too.

Within Côtes du Rhône, a number of villages may sell their reds, and sometimes whites and rosés, as Côtes du Rhône Villages. They must meet a higher minimum alcohol, lower maximum yields, and a greater share of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre. Some villages can add their name if all the wine comes from that village, for example Côtes du Rhône Villages Séguret, the example the new edition uses. These are the best wines outside the crus, with more body, structure and spiced red fruit than generic Côtes du Rhône. All these named villages can apply for cru status.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape, on the east bank, is by far the largest cru in the valley. It has a special place in French wine history as the first area to gain appellation contrôlée status. The vineyards are fairly flat, but small differences in aspect matter a lot for Syrah and Mourvèdre. With its size, range of soils and aspects, and thirteen permitted varieties, its famous reds are very diverse. Grenache dominates: some top Châteauneufs are one hundred per cent Grenache, others make much more of Mourvèdre's gamey, meaty character. The best are full-bodied and richly textured, with concentrated spiced red fruit balancing high alcohol. The downside: this diversity also means a lot of mediocre Châteauneuf, dilute and unbalanced by alcohol. A little white is also made.

Tavel and Lirac are the only two southern crus on the west bank. Tavel makes only rosé: mainly Grenache and Cinsault, fuller-bodied than Provence rosés, intense and able to gain complexity in bottle. Lirac also makes rosé, but according to the new edition it is best known for high-quality reds and whites in the style of Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

Other villages in the hills east of Châteauneuf have been promoted to cru. Gigondas and Vacqueyras are the longest-standing: reds, usually Grenache-led, full-bodied and spicy like Châteauneuf, and often as good, though likely to stay in their famous neighbour's shadow. Some crus also allow rosé and white. Beaumes-de-Venise has a separate appellation for its fortified Muscats, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, a sweet fortified wine.

To sum up: a Mediterranean climate, the mistral and galets; Grenache-led blends with Syrah and Mourvèdre; Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages and the crus; Châteauneuf-du-Pape and its thirteen varieties; Tavel for rosé; Gigondas and Vacqueyras.

The vineyards of southern France run along the Mediterranean from Italy in the east to the Spanish border in the west. They split into three broad areas: Languedoc and Roussillon west of the Rhône, and Provence to the east. With the regional IGP Pays d'Oc, so important in Languedoc-Roussillon, alongside many more traditional appellations, there is great diversity of style.

Climate and grape growing. The climate is warm Mediterranean: summers often above thirty degrees, mild winters and low rainfall, especially in the growing season. So in most years conditions are ideal for grapes.

But the region is far from uniform. Inland, in the foothills of the surrounding mountains, vineyards are noticeably cooler than on the coastal plain, often with less fertile, well-drained soils better suited to quality. Winds matter a lot: cool, dry winds from the north cool the eastern and western ends; the mistral blows down the Rhône valley, and the tramontane through the gap between the Massif Central and the Pyrenees. In this warm, dry climate, the biggest challenge is drought, while fungal disease is less of a problem than anywhere else in France. The region can, however, occasionally suffer summer floods.

Grape varieties and winemaking. Black grapes dominate. The vineyard has changed dramatically, over the last thirty years according to the new edition, and today both reds and whites mix local and international varieties.

Among local black grapes: Grenache, at home in the hot, dry summers, and Syrah, better in cooler sites. Carignan is widely grown: naturally high in tannin, acidity and colour, it can lack fruit and finesse, though old vines on poor soils can make quality wine. It was once prized for its enormous yields; it is now far less widely planted, but still permitted in all the appellations. Cinsault is used for rosé or to add red fruit to red blends. Mourvèdre ripens only in the warmest sites and adds richness, colour and complexity. International varieties, especially Merlot but also Cabernet Sauvignon, are widely planted for IGP wines.

Most wines have benefited from investment: modern equipment, better hygiene, temperature and oxygen control, and judicious use of new and old oak. Some producers use semi-carbonic maceration, which helps soften Carignan's tannins.

Among whites, varieties not traditionally grown here now dominate: Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, the most planted, for IGP wines, with significant Viognier too. The most planted local varieties are Muscat, for sweet fortified wines but also some dry, grapey wines, and Grenache Blanc, which gives soft, peachy, full-bodied, low-acid dry wines that oxidise easily; it is often blended with other local or Rhône varieties. Some local grapes shine in their own areas: Picpoul in Pinet, Mauzac in Limoux, Maccabeu in Roussillon, Rolle in Provence and Clairette in Languedoc and Provence. The best known is probably Picpoul, with refreshing, high-acid wines showing green fruit and citrus.

Languedoc and Roussillon. Most southern French wine comes from the Aude, Hérault and Gard, traditionally called Languedoc, and the Pyrénées-Orientales, called Roussillon. A large coastal plain stretches between Béziers and Montpellier; inland and towards Spain, the vineyards become hilly and rugged.

Appellations. The generic Languedoc appellation covers all appellation vineyards from the Spanish border to Nîmes. Above it are more specific appellations, such as Côtes du Roussillon and Minervois, with their own rules, and some areas recognised for quality now have their own appellation, such as Minervois-La Livinière. The system keeps evolving as more areas apply for full AOC status.

Most appellations allow red, white and rosé, but the vast majority is red, based on the quartet of Carignan, Grenache, Syrah and, to a lesser extent, Mourvèdre. A typical wine is hard to describe, because of blending and because appellations are large, with varied climates and soils. Cooler areas give more finesse, lighter tannins and often the best Syrahs; warmer areas suit Mourvèdre and give fuller wines with meaty, gamey notes. The best are full-bodied, with concentrated spicy red fruit, often oaked. Rosés are soft and fruity.

A few examples. Côtes du Roussillon is more rugged and mountainous: bright sun, low rainfall and strong winds give concentrated wines, and the best northern vineyards qualify for Côtes du Roussillon Villages. Fitou, just to the north, is split in two: a warm coastal strip with fuller wines, and a cooler, higher inland zone with lighter ones. Corbières covers warm coastal sites and high vineyards cooled by the tramontane; it has eleven sub-regions, and the best, Boutenac, has its own AOC. Minervois, on the slopes of the Massif Central, does not reach the coast; quality varies with altitude, soil richness and cooling Atlantic influence, and its best sub-region, La Livinière, has its own AOC.
Whites vary as much as reds. Picpoul de Pinet is near the coast, where sea breezes help keep Picpoul's natural high acidity. Limoux is cooled by altitude and makes premium oaked Chardonnay.

IGP wines. More IGP wine is made here than anywhere else in France, and it is vital to the survival of southern grape growing. Most is sold as Pays d'Oc, covering all of Languedoc-Roussillon. Its success has several causes: IGP rules allow more varieties and varietal labelling, and the warm, sunny climate makes it easy to produce large volumes of ripe, fruity wine, often excellent value.

Provence. The landscape is varied, broken up by ranges of hills that shelter against the mistral and give a great range of site climates and soils. Rosé is the vast majority of production: usually very pale, light- to medium-bodied, dry, with delicate red fruit. Reds range from fresh and fruity to fuller, barrel-matured styles, and the best whites showcase the aromas of Rolle or Clairette.

Côtes de Provence is by far the largest appellation, mostly rosé. On the coast, three isolated pockets have their own appellations. The most important is Bandol, east of Marseille: premium reds based on Mourvèdre, which ripens reliably on its south-facing terraces. Dark, full-bodied and powerfully tannic, they need bottle age to show bramble, meat and liquorice spice.

To sum up: a Mediterranean climate, drought, the mistral and the tramontane; Grenache, Syrah, declining Carignan and Mourvèdre; IGP Pays d'Oc and its varietal wines; the Languedoc, Roussillon, Fitou, Corbières and Minervois appellations; Picpoul de Pinet; and in Provence, pale rosés and Bandol's Mourvèdre reds.

Germany has the highest concentration of world-class Rieslings. Dry and steely, medium-sweet and floral, or lusciously sweet, German winemakers' mastery of this grape is beyond question. But there is more to Germany than one variety: more and more red is being made, and Pinot Noir, here called Spätburgunder, has a growing reputation for premium quality.

Climate and grape growing. Most regions have a cool continental climate, with all its problems, though Baden in the far south is noticeably warmer. Summers can be wet, but rain usually declines in autumn, during the final stage of ripening. The long, cool ripening period lets grapes reach sugar ripeness while keeping their acidity. When conditions are right, noble rot develops, and botrytised sweet wines can be made in every region. Weather varies a lot from year to year, and so do quality, quantity and style.

In such marginal conditions, small differences in site matter. Almost everywhere the best sites are steep, often stony, south-facing slopes that maximise heat and light. They must be worked by hand, and on the most extreme slopes equipment is winched into place. Vines are head-pruned, individually staked, and the canes tied at the top for maximum light and air. Near a river, reflected sunlight helps ripening, and moving air over the water helps protect against frost.

Because wines are classified by must weight, the sugar level in the juice, harvest can be spread over weeks or months. One vineyard can make a whole range of Qualitätsweine and Prädikatsweine each year: pickers pass through several times, and grapes can also be sorted after each picking.

The system and labels. The vast majority of German wine is PDO. Some PGI wine is made, labelled Landwein, and wine without a geographical indication is simply Deutscher Wein. PDO wines are Qualitätsweine, made in one of thirteen delimited regions, whose name appears on the label. Within this, Prädikatsweine are made from riper grapes and split into six levels, from least to most ripe: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese. In the new edition's table, Qualitätswein, Kabinett and Spätlese range from dry to off-dry; Auslese from dry to sweet; the last three are sweet only.

Sweetness. Dry wines may be labelled trocken, off-dry or medium wines halbtrocken. Some producers feel halbtrocken has negative associations and use feinherb instead, which is not legally defined. Often nothing is stated, but sweetness can be deduced from the category or the alcohol level.

Origin of the grapes: this is the big change in the new edition. Since twenty twenty-one, a geographical hierarchy applies to Qualitätsweine, including Prädikatsweine, with a five-year transition. A wine can name a wine-growing zone, the largest, a region, a village or a single vineyard. Regional wines must show the word Region; village wines show only the village name, for example Piesport; single-vineyard wines show the village then the vineyard, for example Piesporter Goldtröpfchen. Before this law, lower-quality regional wines could carry names that looked like single vineyards, so consumers had to know the names or rely on price. Single-vineyard wines may also be classified Erstes Gewächs or Grosses Gewächs: these must be dry and follow stricter rules, especially Grosses Gewächs.

The VDP, Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter, is an association of producers with its own classification. Its members have classified their vineyards, which include the vast majority of Germany's best sites, and impose strict rules in vineyard and winery. An eagle on the capsule identifies their wines. Single-vineyard wines come from a VDP.Erste Lage or, for the very best sites, a VDP.Grosse Lage. Dry wines from a Grosse Lage are called VDP.Grosses Gewächs, recognisable by the letters GG and a bunch of grapes embossed on the bottle neck. Permitted varieties vary by region. Note that VDP.Grosses Gewächs is a VDP trademark, not part of the wine law; even so, these are considered Germany's very best dry wines.

Grape varieties and styles. To satisfy the home market, the trend is towards dry wines, red and white, often sold simply as Qualitätsweine. Prädikatsweine are mostly white, and we'll look at them through Riesling, the most important variety.

Riesling is Germany's most planted grape. It expresses itself differently by region and even by vineyard: from delicate and floral to richer and peachy; from bone dry to lusciously sweet. Dry styles, often Qualitätsweine, range from light and fruity to very concentrated, and many of the best are Grosses Gewächs. Nearly all Prädikatsweine have residual sugar, but up to Auslese they can also be dry. The key is to see the Prädikat as an indicator of style.

Kabinett is the most delicate: light, high in acidity, green apple and citrus, often balanced by residual sugar. Sweet styles have eight to nine per cent alcohol, drier ones up to twelve. They can be sweetened after fermentation with unfermented juice, Süssreserve, but not for high-quality wines: the best sweet Kabinett is made by stopping fermentation early, giving a better sugar-acid balance.

Spätlese is made the same way, but is more concentrated and riper, with a little more body, alcohol and, where relevant, sweetness than a Kabinett from the same region; citrus and stone fruit, peach or apricot. Auslese comes from individually selected extra-ripe bunches; dry or sweet, it is richer than Spätlese, and noble rot can play an important part.

Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese. Noble rot is essential to reach the must weight for TBA; it is not required for BA, but it is typical. They are not made every year, and volumes vary a lot. Sweet and low in alcohol, with honey, dried stone fruit, candied peel and flowers, they rank among the world's greatest sweet wines. Eiswein is a genuine rarity: noble rot is not key, and the focus is varietal purity, with a very fine balance of acidity and sweetness. To keep varietal flavour, winemakers use selected yeasts, handle the juice carefully and avoid malolactic and new oak.

Other whites. Müller-Thurgau, or Rivaner, is an eighteen-eighties crossing of Riesling and Madeleine Royale. It ripens earlier but lacks Riesling's acidity and intensity; it can be floral and fruity but rarely makes high-quality wine. It is still the second most planted white, but declining with the market for cheap medium-dry wine. Silvaner, the third white, is mainly in Rheinhessen and Franken: less acidic and less overtly fruity than Riesling, sometimes earthy, it can be excellent on the right site. Grauburgunder, Pinot Gris, and Weissburgunder, Pinot Blanc, are growing, usually made dry.

Reds. Spätburgunder is the third most planted variety. It thrives in warmer areas, especially Pfalz and Baden, making dry wines that are either light and fruity or more concentrated and often oaked. Dornfelder, the other major red, gives deeply coloured wines. Then come Portugieser, Trollinger and Schwarzriesling, that is Meunier: usually light and fruity, mostly drunk at home.

Regions. Mosel covers the Mosel valley from the Rhine to the border, plus two small tributaries, the Saar and the Ruwer. Whites, especially Riesling, dominate, and only Riesling is allowed for GG. Production is concentrated in the Middle Mosel, with famous villages such as Piesport, Bernkastel and Wehlen. The best vineyards are on very steep slate slopes right by the river. Rieslings here are lighter, lower in alcohol and higher in acidity than those of Rheingau, Rheinhessen and Pfalz, with floral and green fruit notes. The cooler Saar and Ruwer are a tiny share; their best wines resemble the Middle Mosel, often with even higher acidity, and in cool vintages their grapes go into sparkling wine.

The Nahe lies between Mosel and Rheinhessen. The best vineyards line the river between Schlossböckelheim and Bad Kreuznach, on steep south-facing slopes. Riesling, the most planted and the only GG variety, gives a style between Mosel and the fuller wines of Rheingau, Rheinhessen and Pfalz: Mosel acidity with slightly riper fruit.

The Rheingau is small but prestigious. Vineyards are mainly on the north bank of the Rhine in the west and the Main in the east, facing south and sheltered by the Taunus hills. Around Johannisberg and Rüdesheim, Riesling dominates, mostly dry: medium to full body and ripe peach. Humidity from the Rhine helps make some of Germany's best BA and TBA. In the east, around Hochheim, Rieslings can be riper and fuller. Excellent Spätburgunder comes from Assmannshausen, west of Rüdesheim. GG from Riesling or Spätburgunder.

Rheinhessen is the largest region, with a broad range of varieties. Müller-Thurgau and Riesling are the most planted, and black grapes, mainly Dornfelder, Portugieser and Spätburgunder, make up about thirty per cent. Its reputation rests on the steep slopes on the west bank of the Rhine around Nierstein, the Rheinterrasse, which give some of Germany's fullest Rieslings. Recently, growers in areas without a long reputation, such as the south near Worms, have started making top wines, and the region has gained a name for innovation and excellence.

Pfalz is the second largest region. Its vineyards continue those of Alsace in a narrow eighty-kilometre strip east of the Haardt mountains, an extension of the Vosges: the driest German region, where vines can suffer water stress in hot years. Riesling is the most planted and most esteemed; Müller-Thurgau is common too, and Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder are growing. Black grapes are just under forty per cent: Dornfelder is the second variety of either colour, with Portugieser for the local market and Spätburgunder gaining an international reputation. The most established sites surround Forst and Deidesheim, the Mittelhaardt, giving ripe, full-bodied Riesling. As in Rheinhessen, young growers make top wines outside this core, and most wines are now dry.

Baden is the warmest and most southerly region, with Germany's fullest, most alcoholic wines. Its vineyards follow the Rhine to Switzerland, with nearly a third in the Kaiserstuhl and Tuniberg, opposite Colmar. The best are on the south slope of the Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano known for Spätburgunder, Baden's most planted grape. Then come Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder, Weissburgunder and Riesling.

In Franken, whites dominate, but the star is Silvaner, not Riesling. Early and frost-prone, it is planted in the warmest sites and reaches a concentration rare elsewhere. The best, on south-facing slopes around Würzburg, are dry, rich and often earthy, in distinctive flask-shaped bottles. New in this edition: high-quality Spätburgunder is also made in the west of the region.

To sum up: a cool climate and slate slopes; Riesling, from dry to sweet; the Prädikat as a style indicator; the new origin hierarchy since twenty twenty-one, with Erstes and Grosses Gewächs; the VDP and its GG; and the regions: Mosel, Nahe, Rheingau, Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Baden and Franken.

Austria is best known for its fine dry whites, from its own Grüner Veltliner and from Riesling. But it also makes excellent reds from local grapes such as Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch, and botrytised dessert wines from Welschriesling.

Climate and grape growing. The Alps cover the west of the country, so the vineyards are in the east. The climate is cool continental, with short summers and very harsh winters. Northern regions are cooled by northerly winds, while those near the Hungarian border are warmed by easterly winds. Year-to-year variation is much smaller than in northern Europe.

White grapes. Grüner Veltliner is the most planted: a high-quality grape that sets Austria apart in export markets. At high yields it gives fresh but unexciting wine; grown with care, it gives full-bodied, concentrated wines with naturally high acidity. Young, it shows citrus or stone fruit, often with a hint of white pepper, developing honey and toast with age. Most producers ferment and store in stainless steel, but old oak casks are common, and some mature part of their best wines in new barriques.

Welschriesling, not the same as Riesling, is the second white. Dry, it is fresh but simple, with citrus, green apple and high acidity; susceptible to botrytis, it also makes high-quality dessert wines. Riesling is less planted; the best come from the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal: usually dry, medium- to full-bodied, with ripe peachy fruit, and the best age well. There is also plenty of Chardonnay, Müller-Thurgau and Sauvignon Blanc, the last with a growing reputation, especially in Steiermark, or Styria, in the south.

Black grapes. Zweigelt, a cross of Blaufränkisch and St Laurent, is the most planted: deeply coloured reds with soft tannins and bramble fruit. Blaufränkisch, the most highly regarded Austrian red, gives medium tannin, high acidity, pepper and sour cherry. St Laurent, an Austrian speciality, resembles Pinot Noir. Oak ageing is common, and some producers blend these grapes with Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot.

Wine law, completely revised in the new edition. Austria makes mainly PDO wine, called Qualitätswein. PGI wines are labelled Landwein, wines without a geographical indication simply Wein. A Qualitätswein can come from a generic region or a specific region.

Generic regions are large areas covering several specific regions; the main ones are Niederösterreich, or Lower Austria, Burgenland and Wien, or Vienna. Their wines may be made from forty permitted varieties grown anywhere in the region, in any style.

Specific regions can gain DAC status, Districtus Austriae Controllatus. Introduced in two thousand and two to promote regional typicity, the system is now well established, and the vast majority of specific regions have joined. The principle: if producers agree on one or more varieties and a limited number of styles that best reflect their area, with matching rules, they can apply for DAC status. Then only wines in those styles may use the appellation name; others must use the generic region name. Within a DAC, a village or single vineyard name may also appear on the label. Specific regions without DAC status can make any style from the forty permitted varieties.

A Qualitätswein may also carry a Prädikat level, as in Germany, but in Austria these terms are mainly reserved for sweet wines. There is one extra level, Strohwein or Schilfwein: grapes dried over winter on beds of straw or reeds to concentrate sugar. Note that a Prädikatswein cannot use the name of a specific region that already has DAC status for another style; it takes the generic region name instead.
Regions. Four federal states make PDO wine: Lower Austria, Burgenland, Styria and Vienna; the first two produce the vast majority.

Lower Austria is the largest region for production and exports. Most vineyards line the Danube and run north towards the Slovak border. Of its eight sub-regions, the Wachau, now a DAC, is the most renowned for top dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling: steep, often terraced, south-facing vineyards by the Danube give highly concentrated flavours. Kamptal DAC and Kremstal DAC, just north, make wines of similar style and quality. Weinviertel DAC is Austria's largest vine-growing area and was the first DAC; only Grüner Veltliner is allowed, at two levels: Klassik, light, fresh and fruity with no discernible oak, and Reserve, with higher minimum alcohol, which may be oak-matured.

Burgenland, in the east along the Hungarian border, is best known for top sweet wines and reds; it also makes dry whites from Pinot Blanc, Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner and Chardonnay. The Neusiedlersee, a vast shallow lake in the north, is key for sweet wine: vineyards on the low ground by the lake benefit from autumn mists from the lake and surrounding wetlands, ideal for botrytis, which is almost guaranteed every year. Welschriesling is one of the main grapes. New in this edition: Ruster Ausbruch DAC covers sweet wines from grapes of TBA level grown around the town of Rust, west of the lake.

Austria's best reds come from higher ground away from the lake and the hills further south. Zweigelt is the most planted, with Blaufränkisch, St Laurent and international grapes such as Pinot Noir, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. Neusiedlersee is a DAC for Zweigelt, and there are several DACs for Blaufränkisch, including Leithaberg and Mittelburgenland.

To sum up: a cool continental climate; peppery Grüner Veltliner, Riesling from the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal, botrytised Welschriesling; Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and St Laurent; the DAC system, now covering most regions, with the Wachau, Weinviertel, Neusiedlersee and Ruster Ausbruch; and Strohwein.

The Tokaj region, whose wine is called Tokaji, lies in the foothills of the Carpathians in the far north-east of Hungary, near the Slovak border. It has long been famous for premium botrytised sweet wines, but late harvest and dry wines are increasingly popular.

Climate and grape varieties. The climate is moderate, and the best vineyards are on south-facing hillsides. The Bodrog and Tisza rivers and their many tributaries create the early-morning humidity noble rot needs.

Three white grapes, often blended. Furmint is the most planted: it gives concentrated, high-acid wines with apple in youth, developing nuts and honey with age. It can make premium dry wine, but because it ripens late and is prone to botrytis, it is best known as the main grape for sweet Aszú. Hárslevelű, also late-ripening, adds perfume to the blend, and Sárga Muskotály, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, its aromatic qualities.

Wine styles. Tokaj has long been famous for sweet wines among the world's best, but producers increasingly make top dry wines too. Dry wines come in seventy-five centilitre bottles, sweet wines traditionally in distinctive fifty centilitre bottles.

Depending on noble rot, a producer often makes several styles each vintage, and pickers sort grapes into three categories. Where botrytis is widespread, they pass through several times picking individual aszú berries. Bunches unaffected by noble rot are picked separately. And a third selection, Szamorodni, meaning as it comes, covers partly botrytised bunches. These three harvests are then used for different wines.

Dry wines without botrytis are gaining importance: they let producers make wine in years with little noble rot. Styles range from simple, unoaked wines for drinking young to concentrated, age-worthy blends, often partly fermented and matured in new oak. They are usually Furmint.

Tokaji Szamorodni is made from the szamorodni harvest and can be dry, száraz, or sweet, édes, depending on the noble rot. By nature, even the dry wines show botrytis character. According to the new edition, they must spend at least six months in cask and cannot be released before January of the second year after harvest; most are aged much longer. For dry wines, casks are not completely filled, so a flor-like yeast forms naturally and the wine develops a character like Fino Sherry. This yeast plays no part in the sweet styles, which may therefore be oxidative, though the modern trend is for less oxidative wine, with casks filled completely.

Sweet wines. Tokaji Aszú starts with a base wine from healthy grapes. Before, during or after fermentation, aszú berries are macerated in it, usually for twelve to sixty hours. Traditionally they were made into a paste, but keeping them whole avoids bitter flavours. The mixture is pressed and the wine matured in oak. The quantity of aszú berries determines sweetness. Classic Tokaji is deep amber, with high acidity and intense orange peel, apricot and honey; it grows more concentrated as sweetness rises.

The current law dates from twenty thirteen. As elsewhere in the EU, Hungary has PDO and PGI wines, and Tokaj styles such as aszú or eszencia are legally defined. Aszú sweetness used to be measured in puttonyos: a puttony is a picker's hod, and the number showed how many hods of aszú berries were added to each cask. Today puttonyos correspond to a minimum residual sugar: five puttonyos means at least one hundred and twenty grams per litre, which is also the minimum for an aszú; six puttonyos at least one hundred and fifty grams. Before the twenty thirteen vintage, less sweet wines could be labelled three or four puttonyos; now the minimum is one hundred and twenty grams. Aszú must spend at least eighteen months in oak, new or used.

Tokaji Eszencia, essence or nectar, is extremely rare and seldom seen outside the region. It is made only from the free-run juice of aszú berries. The must is so sweet it can take years to ferment, and the wine stays very low in alcohol, usually under five per cent. The legal minimum residual sugar is four hundred and fifty grams per litre, balanced by very high acidity, with enormous concentration. These wines can age and stay fresh for a century or more.

Modern-style sweet wines are made from grapes left long on the vine, often labelled Late Harvest. Some include botrytised berries, but these are fermented directly, as for Sauternes or TBA, rather than macerated as for Aszú, and they are aged for less time.

To sum up: Furmint, Hárslevelű and Muscat; mists from the Bodrog and Tisza; three harvests, aszú, healthy grapes and szamorodni; dry Furmint; dry Szamorodni with its flor; Aszú at a minimum of five puttonyos, one hundred and twenty grams, or six, one hundred and fifty; Eszencia; and late harvest wines.

Greece's most interesting wines arguably come from its many native grapes. They thrive in hot, dry conditions and give Greece a unique selling point abroad. The three best known are each linked to a region: Xinomavro in Naoussa, Agiorgitiko in Nemea and Assyrtiko in Santorini.

Climate and grape growing. The climate is hot Mediterranean: summer temperatures go well over thirty degrees, though the sea moderates the coast. Altitude and wind also cool things down; in the islands south-east of the mainland, wind can even destroy unprotected vineyards. Most of the best vineyards are in these cooler sites, away from the blistering heat associated with Greece. Rainfall varies, but even in the wetter west, the almost total lack of rain in the growing season can cause water stress. Drought is a particular worry in the east, in the rain shadow of the mountains, where there is little water for irrigation.

Wine law follows the rest of the EU: PDO and PGI. For export, producers of dry PDO wines may use Protected Designation of Origin or, less often, Appellation d'origine de qualité supérieure, a sub-category of PDO. At home, the Greek equivalent is used, Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis.

Regions and wines. Greece has over two hundred native grapes, very few grown elsewhere, well adapted to heat and drought, and many capable of high quality. Some international varieties are planted, but most PDO wines require native grapes. Three wines have the widest international reputation.

Naoussa, in Macedonia in the north. The vineyards reach four hundred metres and are noticeably cooler than the surroundings. The PDO is for reds made solely from Xinomavro, often compared with Nebbiolo: high in tannin and acidity, it has traditionally given medium-coloured wines that quickly turn tawny and lack fresh fruit even when young. Like Nebbiolo, they are long-lived and develop complex spice and earthy aromas. Some producers now make other styles: deeper in colour, less tannic, or aged in new oak.

Nemea, in the northern Peloponnese, near the isthmus joining the peninsula to the mainland. The PDO is for reds made solely from Agiorgitiko. Vineyards range from two hundred and thirty to nine hundred metres, and the best fruit comes from the middle. Lower, hotter slopes can give jammy fruit for early-drinking wines. Higher slopes give more acidity and less fine tannins: useful for freshness in a blend, but best for rosé. The best wines are deep ruby, with plenty of smooth tannin, low to medium acidity, red fruit and sweet spice; they love new oak and age well.

Santorini is a windswept volcanic island in the Aegean, where the winds are so strong that a unique training method is used: the permanent wood is coiled very low into a basket shape, and the grapes grow inside, protected. According to the new edition, the Santorini PDO covers dry and sweet whites made mainly from Assyrtiko. The dry wines are perfumed, with concentrated ripe citrus and stone fruit, balanced by the grape's naturally high acidity. The sweet wines are called Vinsanto: late-harvested grapes are sun-dried for up to fourteen days, then the wine ages at least two years in old oak, often much longer. Luscious sweetness is balanced by high acidity, and older wines show a marked oxidative character of caramel and nuts.

To sum up: a hot Mediterranean climate, cooled by altitude and wind; over two hundred native grapes; Xinomavro from Naoussa, Nebbiolo's cousin; Agiorgitiko from Nemea; and Assyrtiko from Santorini, dry or as Vinsanto.

Italy is home to a huge number of grape varieties, many rarely seen outside the country. Because of this diversity and the range of styles, it is simpler to explore Italy area by area. In this introduction we look at the wine laws that apply throughout Italy.
PDO wines. The Italian for PDO is Denominazione di Origine Protetta, but two traditional terms are more widely seen on labels.
DOC, Denominazione di Origine Controllata: wines with geographical boundaries and limits on grape varieties and production methods.

DOCG, Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita: on top of all DOC requirements, these wines are subject to stricter rules and, according to the new edition, must in most cases be bottled in their area of production.
PGI wines. The Italian is Indicazione Geografica Protetta, but the traditional term IGT, Indicazione Geografica Tipica, is commonly used.

Two more labelling terms. Classico: over time, many appellations have expanded to allow new plantings outside the original zone. Classico identifies wines made solely from the original classified land, which includes many of the best wines. Riserva: wines with higher alcohol and longer ageing than the appellation's minimums.
To sum up: DOC and DOCG for PDO, IGT for PGI; Classico for the historic heartland; Riserva for more alcohol and longer ageing.

Northern Italy makes a huge range of styles, from the full-bodied, tannic reds of Barolo to the delicate whites of Soave, thanks to diverse geography and an incredible number of local grapes. We'll cover Alto Adige, Trentino, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Veneto and Piemonte.

Climate and grape growing. The vineyards lie in the Alpine foothills and on the broad plain of the river Po. The climate is moderate overall, with dry, short summers. The Alps form a barrier along the whole northern border and shelter the vineyards from rain. Rivers, including the Po, and glacial lakes such as Lake Garda moderate inland areas. Near the sea, rainfall is higher and fungal disease can be a problem.

Traditionally, vines were high-yielding and planted at low density, often on the pergola: the canopy is trained high and horizontal, with the fruit hanging beneath. This protects grapes from sunburn and lets air circulate, reducing rot. Pergolas are still used when high acidity and low sugar are wanted, for example for sparkling wine, and for grapes to be dried, which must be free of damage and disease. But denser plantings on vertical trellising are now more common.

Alto Adige, around Bolzano in the Alpine foothills, is Italy's most northerly wine region. Vines are planted on terraces on the south-east and south-west-facing sides of the Adige valley. The climate is moderate, with short, dry summers and low growing-season rainfall. Altitude gives large day-night temperature swings, ideal for aromatic whites and elegant, light reds. The leading white is Pinot Grigio: dry, light to medium body, high acidity, citrus and green fruit. Then come Gewurztraminer, Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc. Reds are dominated by Schiava: light, fruity, low to medium tannin, raspberry and plum. Almost everything is labelled Alto Adige DOC.

Trentino, just to the south, has a wider valley, with vines on the valley floor and both slopes. The climate is similar but slightly warmer: further south, lower vineyards, and mountains to the west blocking Lake Garda's cooling influence. The main grapes are Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio: valley-floor wines are medium-bodied, with medium acidity and ripe stone fruit; higher sites resemble Alto Adige whites. Merlot and Teroldego are the main black grapes, mostly mid-slope and on the valley floor. Teroldego gives deeply coloured, medium- to full-bodied wines with medium to high tannin, high acidity and black fruit, usually oak-matured, and the best can age. Most wines are Trentino DOC.

Friuli-Venezia Giulia is in the north-eastern corner. In the north, in the Alpine foothills, the climate is moderate continental, cooled by mountain air; in the south, on the plain near the Adriatic, it is warm maritime. Many varieties give rich, ripe whites and reds, above all Pinot Grigio and Merlot. Friulian Pinot Grigio is among Italy's richest: medium- to full-bodied, with juicy peach and tropical fruit. Merlot, the most planted black grape, gives medium-bodied wines with ripe red fruit, often a hint of oak spice. Native Friulano gives medium-bodied wines with medium to high acidity, pear, red apple and herbs. New in this edition: orange wines, in small volumes, are also traditional here, with some premium examples. Wines from the plain are Friuli Grave DOC, mostly simple, fruity whites; Collio DOC and Colli Orientali DOC, in the hills, are known for premium, more concentrated whites, and Colli Orientali also for reds.

Veneto is one of Italy's largest wine regions, home to Soave and Valpolicella. It stretches from the south of Lake Garda to Venice, and from the Alpine foothills to the Po plain. The climate is warm with moderate rain. Altitude cools the foothills, with large temperature swings, and breezes from Lake Garda cool the west. The plain suffers moist air and fog from the rivers, so more sprays are needed against disease and rot.

The fertile plain supplies inexpensive high-volume brands from international grapes like Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay and Merlot, and Italian ones like Corvina, Garganega and Trebbiano: simple and fruity, labelled IGT Veneto. In twenty seventeen a new appellation, Pinot Grigio delle Venezie DOC, was created covering Veneto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia and Trentino; it is now widely used by Pinot Grigio producers who previously used local IGTs. Prosecco, a sparkling wine, comes mostly from Veneto but also from Friuli, mostly made by the tank method.

Soave, east of Verona, has two parts: foothills in the north and a plain in the south, near the river Adige. The hill soils of clay, limestone and volcanic rock are naturally cool; with altitude, they slow ripening, giving fully flavoured grapes with high acidity, and wines that can mature for years. On the plain, sandy alluvial soils aid ripening: fruitier wines with medium acidity, for drinking young. The main grape is Garganega, sometimes with a little of other whites. The wines typically have medium to high acidity, medium body, and pear, red apple, stone fruit and sometimes white pepper, rarely any new oak. The best develop almond and honey. Wines from the whole area are Soave DOC; those from the original hillside zone, Soave Classico DOC.

Valpolicella, north-west of Verona, has a similar layout: clay, limestone and volcanic hills in the north, slowing ripening for more acidity; warmer gravel and sand in the flatter south, for fruitier, less acidic grapes. The main grape is Corvina, native, thin-skinned, moderately coloured, low to medium tannin and high acidity; other local grapes can be added for colour and tannin. The whole area can make Valpolicella DOC, the original zone Valpolicella Classico DOC. These are simple, fruity, lightly tannic wines with red cherry, rarely oaked, for immediate drinking.

The passito method is widely used in Veneto to increase structure, concentration and, for reds, colour. Grapes are picked early, while acidity is high, and dried indoors to concentrate sugar and flavour; fermentation only starts in winter. There are two passito wines in Valpolicella. Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG is, according to the new edition, off-dry in style: full-bodied, high in alcohol, medium to high tannin and intensely concentrated red berry and spice, usually aged in large oak casks. Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG comes from grapes so sweet that fermentation stops naturally: a sweet wine with intense red fruit, medium to high alcohol, full body and medium to high tannin. Soave makes a sweet white the same way, Recioto di Soave DOCG.

The ripasso method uses the skins from a fermenting Amarone. Shortly before fermentation ends, the Amarone is drained off, and the unpressed skins are added to a vat of Valpolicella that has finished fermenting. Yeasts carried over ferment the remaining sugar on the skins, which give the wine more colour, flavour and tannin. The result is Valpolicella Ripasso DOC: medium- to full-bodied, medium to high tannin, stewed red cherries and plums.

Piemonte, in the north-west, lies in the rain shadow of mountains that shelter it from northern winds and rain. The climate is moderate continental, with long, cold winters and summers that can bring thunderstorms, hail and fog. The Po in the south and Lake Maggiore in the north moderate it a little. Its foothills, from one hundred and fifty to six hundred metres, give varied aspects and altitudes. The main grapes are Nebbiolo, Barbera and Dolcetto for reds, Cortese and Moscato for whites. The most famous areas are south of Turin, around Asti and Alba. Barolo and Barbaresco DOCG are the most prestigious, surrounded by many other DOCs and DOCGs.

Barolo spans several villages with steep south-facing slopes at three to five hundred metres. Barolo DOCG must be one hundred per cent Nebbiolo, a black grape high in acidity and tannin but light in colour. At this altitude it ripens slowly, developing perfumed sour cherry, herbs and sometimes dried flowers. In the best years the wines are full-bodied, with high acidity and tannin and great ageing potential. Grapes are often blended from several villages; a village name may appear if all the grapes come from it, for example Barolo Serralunga d'Alba DOCG, and the best wines come from named vineyards or crus, such as Barolo Cannubi DOCG. Dolcetto and Barbera grown here are labelled Alba DOC or Langhe DOC.

According to the new edition, Barolo DOCG must be aged for at least thirty-eight months, eighteen of them in wood, and cannot be released before January of the fourth year after harvest. Traditionally it spent years in large casks to soften harsh tannins. Today, better vineyard management and gentler extraction give smoother, riper tannins, and maturation is often shorter, in small barrels with some new oak or in larger casks, depending on style. All Barolo benefits from bottle age, developing truffle, tar and leather.

Barbaresco, smaller, is also famous for Nebbiolo. Its south-facing slopes are lower, two to four hundred metres, and a nearby river helps Nebbiolo ripen earlier: fruitier and less perfumed, with similar acidity and tannin, so it ages well too. According to the new edition, Barbaresco DOCG must be aged for at least twenty-six months, nine in wood, and cannot be released before January of the third year. The best usually come from a named cru.

Around Asti and Alba, many appellations combine a grape name with the nearest town. Barbera is the most planted: Barbera d'Alba DOC and Barbera d'Asti DOCG, often considered higher quality. Late-ripening, medium to deep in colour, low to medium tannin and high acidity, it shows red cherry and plum, sometimes black pepper, either young and fruity without oak, or barrel-aged and spicier. Dolcetto, earlier-ripening than Nebbiolo and Barbera, can go on the coolest sites; many of the finest are Dolcetto d'Alba DOC: deep, often purple, medium to high tannin, medium acidity, black plum, red cherry and dried herbs. Both can be drunk young, but the best age several years. Asti is also famous for sparkling Moscato.

Gavi, in south-eastern Piemonte, makes whites from Cortese. Altitude and sea breezes slow ripening, emphasising its natural acidity and floral character. Wines are labelled Gavi DOCG or Cortese di Gavi DOCG, and Gavi di Gavi DOCG if the grapes come from the town itself. Pale, light-bodied, high in acidity and aromatic, with citrus, green apple and pear, they are made protectively, cool-fermented in stainless steel, though some producers use old oak and lees stirring for complexity. Most are ready on release, but the best age well.

To sum up: the pergola; Pinot Grigio from Alto Adige, Trentino and Friuli, and the new Pinot Grigio delle Venezie DOC; Garganega in Soave; Valpolicella, Amarone, Recioto and Ripasso; Nebbiolo in Barolo, thirty-eight months, and Barbaresco, twenty-six months; Barbera, Dolcetto and Gavi.

This part of Italy is most associated with Sangiovese and its most famous wine, Chianti. But there is more: refreshing whites and premium full-bodied reds, from both local and international grapes. We'll cover Tuscany, Umbria, Lazio, Marche and Abruzzo.

Climate and grape growing. South of the Po valley, the region is dominated by the Apennines, running the length of the peninsula. Vines grow in their hills and valleys, where altitude moderates a hot climate; on both coasts, sea breezes cool things down.

Tuscany runs down the west coast. It divides roughly into three: the mountainous Chianti area in the north, the hills and valleys of the south, and the flat coastal plain. Everywhere, Sangiovese is the dominant and most prestigious grape, high in acidity and tannin. Late-ripening, it needs warmth. Its wines show red cherry, plum and dried herbs, and are usually aged in oak, small barrels or large casks, to soften tannins and sometimes add spice. With bottle age they develop meaty, gamey notes. Red dominates, though some white is made.

Chianti lies in the Apennine foothills between Pisa, Florence and Siena, a wide area divided into seven sub-zones. Sangiovese dominates, often with small amounts of other black grapes, French or Italian. High-volume wines from the whole area are Chianti DOCG. Better Chiantis may come from a single sub-zone, named on the label; Chianti Rufina and Chianti Colli Senesi are especially well regarded.

Chianti Classico is a DOCG in its own right, not a sub-zone of Chianti. Its vineyards are higher, slowing ripening and giving more acidity and herbal aromas. Chianti Classico must age twelve months before release; Riserva twenty-four months, at least three in bottle. Gran Selezione is the top designation: grapes from a single estate, and six months longer ageing than Riserva. There are no oak rules, but in practice nearly all spend some time in oak.

Southern Tuscany is lower and warmer, though moderated by cool south-westerly sea breezes. The best known appellations are Brunello di Montalcino DOCG and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG, often more intense and fuller than Chianti. Brunello must be one hundred per cent Sangiovese; according to the new edition, it cannot be released before January of the fifth year after harvest, with at least two years in wood. Vino Nobile may blend Sangiovese with other permitted grapes and must age at least two years. Producers can declassify, for example in poor vintages or from young vines: these become Rosso di Montalcino DOC and Rosso di Montepulciano DOC.

The Tuscan coast is fairly flat and cooled by the sea rather than altitude. Bordeaux varieties and other international grapes are widely planted. This is where the first Super-Tuscan was born: a Cabernet Sauvignon sold at a premium despite not qualifying for PDO status. Super-Tuscans were a turning point for Italy's image, re-establishing its reputation for excellence. Many producers followed, using international grapes, sometimes blended with Italian ones. Many are sold as Toscana IGT, but the newer appellations Bolgheri DOC and Maremma Toscana DOC allow wines made entirely from non-Italian grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.

Umbria has a climate like Tuscany's but more continental, with no Mediterranean influence. It is known for Orvieto DOC, a white blend of Grechetto, Trebbiano and often other local grapes: light, medium to high acidity, ripe grapefruit and peach; the best have the most Grechetto. It is made protectively, cool-fermented in stainless steel. Umbria's most prestigious red is Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG, from the thick-skinned Sagrantino grape.

Lazio, south of Tuscany, is best known for Frascati DOC. In the hills south of Rome, altitude and small lakes cool the vineyards, ideal for white grapes. It is a blend of Malvasia and Trebbiano, usually fresh and unoaked: medium body, medium to high acidity, citrus, and sometimes floral orange blossom from the Malvasia.

Marche, on the eastern side of the Apennines, is best known for whites from Verdicchio, the most famous being Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC. Verdicchio is naturally high in acidity, with green apple and lemon, sometimes fennel and almond. Many are simple and fruity, but the best are more concentrated and develop honey and almond in bottle. Reds blend Montepulciano and Sangiovese; the best known is Conero DOCG.

Abruzzo, further south, is famous for Montepulciano, which gives its name to Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC, unrelated to the Tuscan town of Montepulciano. The grape is deeply coloured and tannic, with medium acidity, black plum and cherry. Many wines are simple and fruity, unoaked, but the most concentrated often spend a short time in oak.

To sum up: Sangiovese; Chianti, Chianti Classico, Riserva and Gran Selezione; Brunello, one hundred per cent Sangiovese, and Vino Nobile; Super-Tuscans, Bolgheri and Maremma; Orvieto, Frascati and Verdicchio; and Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.

With its heat, southern Italy is best known for full-bodied reds from Aglianico, Primitivo and Negroamaro. But like the rest of Italy it offers great variety, from perfumed Fiano whites to restrained, elegant reds from the slopes of Mount Etna. We'll cover Campania, Basilicata, Puglia and Sicily.

Climate and grape growing. The south runs from Lazio to the tip of the boot, including the Puglian peninsula and Sicily. The climate is hot and dry inland, more humid near the coast. Many vineyards are on Apennine slopes, where altitude gives relief from the heat, and sea breezes cool the flatter land of Puglia. Agriculture is the main economic activity, and grapes matter most in Puglia and Sicily, which make huge volumes. Traditionally vines were bush-trained low to the ground, with leaves shading the grapes; old vines still show this, but cordon training and trellising are now the norm, allowing mechanisation on the Puglian plain.

Campania has more DOCGs than any other southern region. Its varied landscape of mountains, valleys and coastal plains suits many grapes. Fiano and Greco arguably make the best whites. Both grow elsewhere, but many of the best come from Fiano di Avellino DOCG and Greco di Tufo DOCG. Fiano gives medium- to full-bodied wines with medium acidity, stone fruit, melon and mango; often drunk young, the best are oak-matured and age, developing wax and honey. Greco has more acidity and less body, with green apple, stone fruit and passion fruit. Most ferment in stainless steel, but some use old oak and lees stirring for texture; the best develop honey and mushroom.

Aglianico is the south's most prestigious black grape: deeply coloured, high in acidity and tannin, with black fruit. Oak-matured, it ages well, developing earthy, forest-floor notes. It appears in many wines but is at its best in Taurasi DOCG.

Basilicata, south of Campania, is extremely mountainous: vineyards reach nine hundred metres, especially on the vast high plain around the extinct volcano Monte Vulture. Aglianico makes Aglianico del Vulture DOC, considered the region's best wine.

Puglia is a vast agricultural area with large volumes. The heat means black grapes dominate, especially Negroamaro and Primitivo, which is Zinfandel. At high yields they give simple, fruity wines for early drinking, sold as Puglia IGT. With controlled yields, Negroamaro makes high-quality, full-bodied wines with medium tannin and acidity, high alcohol and baked red and black fruit; many of the best are from Salice Salentino DOC. Primitivo can be excellent in a similar style: full-bodied, high in alcohol, with pronounced very ripe berry fruit.

Sicily, like Puglia, grows huge quantities, mostly sold as IGT Terre Siciliane or, with slightly lower yields, Sicilia DOC. Nero d'Avola is the dominant black grape: medium- to full-bodied, medium acidity and tannin, plum and black cherry. Often fruity and early-drinking, it is more concentrated and complex from the best producers. Local whites, varietal or blended, are usually unoaked, with citrus and stone fruit. International grapes are also planted, and Syrah has been especially successful.

There are several small appellations. Some of the island's best wines come from Etna DOC, from old, low-yielding vines at high altitude. The reds, blends of Nerello Mascalese and Nerello Cappuccio, are fragrant, high in acidity and tannin, with sour red cherry, cranberry, raspberry and sometimes dried herbs; with bottle age the tannins soften and mushroom notes appear. Fine whites are made too: medium-bodied, high acidity, citrus, often stony and steely, developing honey and wax with age.
To sum up: heat and altitude; Fiano and Greco in Campania; Aglianico in Taurasi and Vulture; Negroamaro and Primitivo in Puglia; Nero d'Avola in Sicily; and the high-altitude wines of Etna.

Spain has a long history of winemaking, but its wines have only recently risen to prominence internationally. Styles range from traditional barrel-aged reds to modern, fruity whites; and although international grapes have been planted in many regions, it is increasingly the native varieties that are celebrated.

Climate and grape growing. There are three broad climate zones. The north and north-west coast has a moderate maritime climate dominated by the Atlantic, with high rainfall and its risks. The east coast, from Catalunya down to the Levante, has a warm Mediterranean climate, moderated by the sea or altitude depending on the site, and getting hotter further south. The Meseta Central, a large central plateau, is cut off from the sea by mountains: a hot continental climate, freezing winters, very hot, dry summers, but cool nights at altitude.

Except in the north-west, heat and lack of water are the biggest challenges. Fungal disease is rare, but the vines are under heavy stress. Low-density bush vines remain the best answer, maximising water for each vine and shading the fruit. Where practical and affordable, wire training is slowly arriving to allow machine harvesting.

Red wines. They come in a wide range of styles. Inexpensive wines may be unoaked, often using semi-carbonic maceration for extra fruit. The best almost always see oak, usually with some new oak; traditionally mostly American, but French oak is now common too.

Tempranillo is Spain's premier black grape, widely grown in the north and centre, often under other names. Thick-skinned and medium in acidity, it needs warmth for flavour, but very hot climates without big day-night swings can leave it short of acidity; so it is best where sea or altitude moderate the summer. On its own, often by semi-carbonic maceration, it makes a fresh, strawberry-scented joven, an increasingly popular early-drinking style. It is also key in more concentrated, age-worthy oaked blends with the traditional Garnacha, Graciano and Cariñena, or international grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon.

Garnacha Tinta is Grenache: high-alcohol wines that tend to mature early, with notable exceptions. It is widely used for rosados, and is important in Priorat, where low-yielding old vines give intense, complex, full-bodied reds.

Monastrell is Mourvèdre: thick-skinned and drought-tolerant, but it needs heat and sun to ripen. In south-eastern DOs such as Yecla and Jumilla it ripens easily, giving very deeply coloured, full-bodied wines with high tannin and alcohol, low to medium acidity and ripe blackberry.

Other black grapes. Graciano, highly valued but hard to grow, mainly in Rioja: a little adds concentrated black fruit, acidity and tannin to help a wine age. Cariñena, which is Carignan, called Mazuelo in Rioja: high in acidity, tannin and colour, ideal in small proportions with Tempranillo, and blended with Garnacha in Priorat for structure. And Mencía, increasingly prominent: it suits moderate climates, giving fresh fruit, medium to high acidity and sometimes a hint of herbaceousness.

White wines are mostly fresh and fruity: harvesting at night or early morning and fermenting in temperature-controlled stainless steel keep the delicate fruit. Some producers use oak and lees stirring for texture.

Verdejo oxidises very easily and was once used for Sherry-like wines. Made protectively, it gives a light, high-acid wine with melon and peach, similar to Sauvignon Blanc, with which it is often blended. With skin contact and barrel fermentation it can be richer. Albariño, from the north-west, is very fashionable: thick-skinned, it resists disease in the damp climate; naturally high in acidity, it gives refreshing wines with citrus and stone fruit, sometimes richer.

Airén is Spain's most planted grape, mostly in La Mancha, because it copes with the Meseta's extreme heat and drought. It can make acceptable dry whites, but much still goes into Brandy de Jerez. Parellada, Xarel·lo and Macabeo are widely planted in Catalunya for Cava. Macabeo, called Viura in Rioja, is also used for still wines, unoaked with subtle herb and spice, and was traditionally the mainstay of heavily oaked white Rioja.

International varieties, according to the new edition, have had mixed success. In the north-east, for example Penedès and Navarra, they dominate and feature in some of the best wines. Elsewhere, their initial popularity has faded over the last twenty years in favour of local grapes.

Wine law. Spain has a hierarchy of PDO and PGI wines and also defines ageing categories. Wines outside these are simply labelled Vino. For PDO, traditional terms are used. DO, Denominación de Origen, with rules on varieties, viticulture and location. DOCa, Denominación de Origen Calificada: DOs of at least ten years' standing may apply; currently there are only two, Rioja and Priorat, which uses the Catalan term DOQ. Vinos de Pago: a small number of highly reputed single estates, which may only use their own grapes, vinified and matured on the estate. For PGI, the traditional term Vino de la Tierra.

Ageing categories. Reds: joven, no minimum; crianza, twenty-four months with six in barrel; reserva, thirty-six months with twelve in barrel; gran reserva, sixty months with eighteen in barrel. Whites and rosés: crianza, eighteen months with six in barrel; reserva, twenty-four with six; gran reserva, forty-eight with six. Many producers exceed these, gran reserva is made only in exceptional years, and white and rosé gran reservas are rare. Some regions, such as Rioja, require more; and new in this edition, Rioja uses the term genérico instead of joven.
Regions. Six broad areas: the Upper Ebro, Catalunya, the Duero valley, the North West, the Levante and Castilla-La Mancha. There are also Vino de la Tierra regions, the largest being Castilla y León.

Rioja splits into three sub-regions around Logroño. Rioja Alavesa, to the west on the north bank of the Ebro in the Cantabrian foothills, gives perhaps the lightest, most elegant wines. Rioja Alta, larger, also west but mostly south of the Ebro. Their vineyards lie between five and eight hundred metres, influenced by the Atlantic but sheltered from its worst by the Cantabrian mountains. The third, which the new edition calls Rioja Oriental, east of Logroño, mostly on the south bank: less maritime, with hotter summers, harsher winters and sometimes low rainfall.

Black grapes dominate. Tempranillo, the most planted, does best in the cooler west; it gives red fruit and medium tannin, and benefits from the body and alcohol of Garnacha, which grows best in Rioja Oriental. Mazuelo and Graciano play supporting roles. Early-drinking reds often use semi-carbonic maceration; wines for ageing are destemmed, crushed and fermented traditionally. Some producers extract heavily for deeply coloured, fruit-packed wines, but many now aim for subtlety and elegance. Oak is defining: traditionally American, with pronounced vanilla; now often French or other European oak, at least in part, for subtler spice.

Nine white grapes are now permitted in Rioja, mostly Viura. Traditional whites, aged long in American oak, became deep gold and nutty; these deliberately oxidised wines have fallen out of favour. Modern white Riojas minimise oxygen to keep fruit, and some bodegas make barrel-fermented whites in a less oxidative style.

Navarra extends Rioja up to the Pyrenean foothills, with a similar climate, cooler and wetter near the mountains. Tempranillo dominates, blended with the Rioja grapes or, increasingly, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, from good-value joven to premium gran reserva. For rosé, Garnacha is picked early, when acidity is high, and handled protectively for fresh, fruity wines. The few whites are Viura, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

Cariñena and Calatayud, south of the Ebro, have warm, dry continental climates. Garnacha dominates: inexpensive, fruity early-drinking wines, and finer wines from old Garnacha and Cariñena vines, with more intensity and structure. Note that the Cariñena grape is not the most planted in the DO of the same name.

Catalunya, in the north-east, has most vineyards south of Barcelona, on the coastal plain and nearby hills. Unlike other regions it has a generic DO, Catalunya, for all its still wines, created mainly to allow blending from different areas for large volumes of branded wine. Almost all Cava is made here too.

Penedès, south-west of Barcelona, runs from the coast into the hills, with three climates: the hottest, Mediterranean coastal plain; slightly cooler inland valleys; and moderate hills up to eight hundred metres. So styles vary widely. White plantings are mostly Cava grapes, plus Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Gewurztraminer; reds are Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, here called Ull de Llebre, and Pinot Noir.

Priorat, in the hills behind Tarragona, has long, hot, dry summers and very low rainfall, ideal for its old, late-ripening Garnacha and Cariñena vines. The best soils, llicorella, are layers of red slate with mica flecks that sparkle in the sun: they reflect and retain heat and, being deep, hold enough water. Cool nights offer relief. Bush vines and steep slopes make mechanisation almost impossible; poor soils and old vines give tiny yields, source of complexity and intensity, and these wines are never cheap. Red Priorat is deeply coloured and tannic, with medium to high alcohol, concentrated black fruit and often toast from new French oak. Some producers add international grapes, especially Cabernet Sauvignon. White and rosé exist but are rare.

The Duero valley. The river rises south of Rioja and flows through Spain to Portugal, where it becomes the Douro. Ribera del Duero is cut off from the sea by a ring of mountains: short, hot, dry summers, very cold winters, and some of the Meseta's highest vineyards, above eight hundred and fifty metres, with cool nights that preserve acidity and fruit. The DO is for red and rosé only, mostly red. Tempranillo dominates and is often the only grape in the best wines, dark and tannic; Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec and Merlot are allowed but rarely used, and Garnacha mostly goes into dry rosé. Many producers now favour long macerations and fairly short ageing in new barrels, increasingly French.

Toro, with a similar climate, makes mostly Tempranillo reds, full-bodied, intense and high in alcohol, thanks to heat, sun and often low-yielding bush vines. Jovens usually include some Garnacha; reservas and gran reservas can be extremely deep and tannic when young and age well.

Rueda, between Toro and Ribera del Duero, focuses on whites. Its continental climate with cool nights suits its traditional grape, Verdejo, along with Sauvignon Blanc. Both can be single-varietal; blends must contain at least fifty per cent Verdejo. Styles range from simple and fruity to richer, barrel-fermented versions.

The North West, cooler and wetter thanks to the Atlantic, makes many of Spain's best whites, above all Albariño from Rías Baixas. On the coast, the moderate, damp climate brings mildew and rot, so vines are trained on pergolas for air circulation, though some growers use easier systems. Albariño is mostly unoaked and refreshing, sometimes richer with a touch of oak or lees stirring. Red is permitted but a minority. Bierzo, mainly red, lies in the mountains between Galicia and the Meseta, with a moderate, maritime-cooled climate. Mencía makes elegant reds with high acidity and red fruit; many of the best come from old vines on steep, stony slopes. Some avoid oak, but many use new oak for toasty notes.

The Levante, on the coast south of Catalunya, centres on the port of Valencia, hub for wines from the Levante and La Mancha. The large Valencia DO is a source of value wines: Monastrell for reds, Merseguera for whites, and Muscat of Alexandria for Moscatel de Valencia, a sweet fortified wine. Inland, hot, arid Jumilla and Yecla are perfect for Monastrell, mostly in young, fruity styles.

Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid, produces almost half of Spain's wine. La Mancha is Spain's largest DO. Airén dominates, for neutral, fresh whites, but it is declining as growers are encouraged to plant Tempranillo, here called Cencibel, and international grapes. Thanks to investment, La Mancha is now an excellent source of inexpensive, well-made wines. It is also where the trend for top-quality pagos began, and home to most of these estates. Valdepeñas, just south, has the same climate but a better reputation; Airén is the most planted, but Tempranillo makes the reds, alone or blended, from fruity to concentrated and oak-aged.

To sum up: heat and drought, except in the north-west; Tempranillo, Garnacha and Monastrell; DO, DOCa, Vinos de Pago and Vino de la Tierra; joven, crianza, reserva and gran reserva; Rioja and its Rioja Oriental; Priorat and llicorella; Ribera del Duero, Toro and Rueda; Albariño from Rías Baixas and Mencía from Bierzo; and La Mancha.
Portugal has a wealth of local grapes giving a wide range of styles: reds that are supple and fruity or full-bodied and tannic, and whites that are usually refreshing and best drunk young.
