Climate. A small country with varied climates. The single biggest influence is the Atlantic, and much of the country is maritime. But many inland vineyards are hot, dry and continental, sometimes moderated by altitude. These temperature differences partly explain the diversity of styles.

Wine law. The Portuguese for PDO is Denominação de Origem Protegida, but the traditional DOC, Denominação de Origem Controlada, is widely used. PGI is Indicação Geográfica Protegida, but the traditional Vinho Regional is still common on labels. Wines without a geographical indication are labelled Vinho; Portugal has had great success with simple, fruity, off-dry rosés in this category.

Regions and wines. Portugal's many native grapes set it apart, but also make its wines hard to understand, especially as some grapes change name from region to region. So we focus on five main DOCs and the largest Vinho Regional.

Vinho Verde, in the north-west, has a moderate maritime climate whose key feature is high rainfall. Without careful canopy management, vines grow excessively and disease thrives. Modernisation has replaced the traditional pergola with spur-pruned vertical trellising, improving airflow, grape health and quality, and allowing mechanisation. Classic white Vinho Verde is pale lemon, high in acidity and low in alcohol, eight to eleven and a half per cent; the lower-alcohol wines are usually off-dry. If the label names a grape, a sub-region or an authorised quality term, it can reach fourteen per cent. Whites are made from local grapes such as Loureiro and Arinto, and traditionally have a slight spritz that enhances freshness. Vinho Verde Alvarinho is one hundred per cent Alvarinho, Spain's Albariño, from the small sub-region of Monção e Melgaço: slightly higher in alcohol, eleven and a half to fourteen per cent, and riper, with tropical fruit. Reds, deeply coloured and tannic, and fresh, fruity rosés are also made.

The Douro, the oldest demarcated wine region in the world, lies about eighty kilometres east of Porto, from the Marão mountains to the Spanish border; the climate is hot and dry in summer. Port dominates, but unfortified wines have always been made from the same five main grapes: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, which is Tempranillo, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão. Touriga Nacional is the most highly regarded: low yields, intense colour and flavour, high tannin. Douro reds are deeply coloured and full-bodied, with plenty of ripe tannin and rich black fruit, the best with subtle toast from new oak. Whites, especially from high vineyards, show fresh fruit and medium to high acidity.

Dão, in mountainous country eighty kilometres south of the Douro, has vineyards on gentler slopes between two and four hundred metres. Cold, wet winters, warm, dry summers and big day-night swings give excellent conditions. Reds often show delicate red fruit, soft tannins and high acidity. Replanting schemes have introduced Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Jaen, Spain's Mencía, and Alfrocheiro, which gives deeply coloured wines with blackberry and strawberry. The best whites, from Encruzado, range from light and fresh to richer, barrel-fermented styles.

Bairrada, between Dão and the Atlantic, is maritime, with rainy winters and warm summers; rain at harvest can trouble late-ripening grapes. Baga dominates: late-ripening, small and thick-skinned, it gives deeply coloured, tannic wines. Underripe, they are acidic and astringent; picked later, softer with rich black fruit. Gentler crushing and maceration, and blending with other grapes, also soften the wines. Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and international grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah are also important. Whites come mainly from Bical and Maria Gomes.

Alentejo covers eight sub-regions in the south-east. The growing season is warm, but small differences allow several styles: more elegant in the cooler, wetter north, richer in the hotter, drier centre and south. The typical red blend combines Aragonez, another name for Tempranillo, and Trincadeira, drought-tolerant, spicy, red-fruited and high in tannin; Alicante Bouschet, very high in colour and tannin, is also used, and Touriga Nacional and Syrah are on the rise. The wines are deeply coloured, with high but soft tannins, full body and expressive ripe fruit. Arinto, Antão Vaz and Roupeiro give fruity, floral whites with medium to high acidity, some fermented or aged in oak.

Vinho Regional. The largest by production is Vinho Regional Alentejano, around the Alentejo DOC but much bigger, with more liberal rules and a wider range of grapes, especially international ones. Lisboa, north of Lisbon, Península de Setúbal, to the south, and Tejo, to the north-east, are also important.

To sum up: maritime in the west, continental inland; DOC and Vinho Regional; light, spritzy Vinho Verde and Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço; Douro reds and Touriga Nacional; Dão; Baga in Bairrada; and Alentejo.

Wine is made right across the USA, but here we focus on the most important states: California, Washington, Oregon and New York. This introduction covers the wine laws that apply throughout the country.

The US system of geographical indications is based on the American Viticultural Area, or AVA. AVAs vary hugely in size: Rutherford is a very small area in Napa County, while Central Coast stretches from San Francisco in the north to Santa Barbara in the south. AVAs can cross state lines and can overlap: Santa Rita Hills AVA, for example, lies mostly within the larger Santa Ynez Valley AVA.

Federal laws set the minimum percentage of grapes that must come from a single variety, vintage or AVA for these to appear on the label. But many states have their own laws, which may differ from the federal limits.

Not all wines qualify for an AVA. For these, the name of a state, such as California, or a county, such as Napa County, may appear, and the rules on vintage and origin are often more lenient than for AVA wines.
To sum up: AVAs of all sizes, which may overlap; federal minimums for variety, vintage and AVA, which states can change; and state or county names for wines outside an AVA.

California makes the vast majority of American wine, and many of the country's most celebrated wines. Warmth, bright sun, and cooling from the ocean and altitude let its winemakers deliver a wide range of premium styles, from rich, powerful Cabernets to elegant Pinot Noirs.

Climate and grape growing. The state runs about eleven hundred kilometres from north to south, with vineyards along most of it. Yet latitude matters relatively little: the decisive factor is the exceptionally cold California Current. North of Los Angeles, where most vineyards are, the coast is mountainous, and these mountains shield much of the state from the ocean's cooling; but where it does reach, the effect is marked.

In the evening, cold ocean air, often with fog, is drawn inland, lowering night temperatures. And because the sun takes time to burn off the fog, the cooling lasts well into the day. Near the coast it can be so strong that in some years grapes struggle to ripen. Where there are gaps in the mountains, the cooling reaches far inland: valleys at right angles to the ocean, as in Monterey and Santa Barbara counties, funnel the cold air. By contrast, with no ocean exposure, as in the Central Valley, it is hot.

The other common factor is the lack of rain during ripening. Water shortage is a real concern and drip irrigation is widespread. Dry autumns have always let growers leave grapes on the vine for a long time: this extra hang time gives very ripe grapes, with very concentrated flavours and very high sugar. More recently, freshness is more appreciated, and many growers now pick slightly earlier.

Black grapes. Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted black grape. Prime sites give extremely expressive wines rivalling the world's best. Many are full-bodied, with very concentrated ripe cassis and prominent new-oak spice; some producers make a less rich style with fresher blackcurrant.

Zinfandel is seen as California's own grape and comes in many styles. It ripens unevenly, so a harvest can include both raisined and underripe grapes. Raisining gives concentrated, full-bodied, high-alcohol reds, sometimes with a little residual sugar, with red and black fruit, dried berries and liquorice; some show a subtle herbaceous note from underripe grapes. Large volumes of early-picked rosé Zinfandel are made, known as White Zinfandel: fruity, pale, medium-sweet and low in alcohol.

Merlot is widely planted too, making approachable wines with soft tannins and ripe black fruit. San Joaquin, in the Central Valley, has the most, for simple, inexpensive wines. Better Merlot now comes from cooler sites such as Monterey and the North Coast, especially Napa and Sonoma: deeply coloured, velvety, luscious, high in alcohol, with blackberry and plum.

Premium Pinot Noir comes from moderate regions such as Russian River Valley, Los Carneros and Santa Maria Valley. Styles vary: some are light, with classic gamey and vegetal notes, but most show layers of ripe red fruit, cherry and strawberry, and sweet oak spice. Syrah, planted across the state, is usually full-bodied and rich, though some make leaner, more peppery styles.

White grapes. Chardonnay is the most planted grape of either colour, and styles vary widely. Inexpensive Central Valley wines are fruity, with low to medium acidity and sometimes toast from staves or chips. In the past, top California Chardonnay was known for being very full-bodied, high in alcohol and low in acidity, with oak, hazelnut and butter beneath peach and banana. Today there is great variety, including restrained, less oaky wines from cool regions such as Los Carneros and Russian River Valley.

The best Sauvignon Blanc comes from the coastal regions: high acidity and ripe citrus. Affordable, fruity everyday wines come from warmer areas such as the Central Valley. Fumé Blanc sometimes indicates an oaked style, but some producers use it for unoaked wines.

Regions. Most California wine comes from the Central Valley, with very fertile soil and irrigation to raise yields. In the premium regions, mainly along the coast, great care goes into the vineyard to reflect each area. We'll look at three regions: North Coast, Central Coast and Central Valley.
The North Coast covers vineyards north of San Francisco Bay, strongly influenced by the ocean: fog and cool breezes flow through gaps in the coastal ranges and river valleys.

Napa Valley AVA runs about fifty kilometres north to south but is only about five wide. It has the most expensive vineyard land and some of California's most prestigious wineries. The Mayacamas Mountains to the west separate it from Sonoma County; the Vaca Mountains to the east from the Central Valley. Vineyards are on the valley floor and both sides, divided into smaller AVAs.

The key influences are morning fog and cool afternoon breezes from San Pablo Bay to the south. Los Carneros, the most southerly area, extending into Sonoma, is cool enough for high-quality Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, still and traditional-method sparkling. Moving north, it gets warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon: Stags Leap District, Yountville, Oakville and Rutherford are all renowned for premium Cabernet. Rutherford, least influenced by the bay, is warmest by day, and its reds are often considered the most powerful and structured. Merlot is widely planted too, and Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with ripe tropical fruit, are the main whites. In the north, Saint Helena and Calistoga often have the warmest days and some of the most concentrated wines in the valley; cool air through the Chalk Hill gap and much cooler nights help keep acidity. Cabernet is the focus, but Zinfandel and Syrah are grown too.

Many hillside vineyards sit above the fog, cooled by altitude instead. Aspect matters: west-facing sites such as Howell Mountain and Atlas Peak get full afternoon sun and are warmer than east-facing ones such as Diamond Mountain District, Spring Mountain District and Mount Veeder, giving fuller, higher-alcohol wines. Overall, hillside reds have more tannin and less palate richness than valley-floor wines. Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Zinfandel; Chardonnay shows citrus and stone fruit with more acidity than on the valley floor.

Sonoma County is larger than Napa, with more climates. Thanks to a break in the coastal ranges, the Petaluma Gap, Russian River Valley is very cool and foggy, best known for elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. Further north it is noticeably warmer. Dry Creek Valley is planted on hillsides and floor: above the fog, top old-vine Zinfandel; on the floor, Sauvignon Blanc; Rhône grapes and Cabernet are popular too. Alexander Valley is warmer still, with fleshier, fuller wines, especially soft, full-bodied Cabernet. To the west, the large Sonoma Coast AVA is strongly influenced by the cold Pacific, with vineyards often on south-facing slopes to ripen. In the south, Sonoma Valley, parallel to Napa, is cooled by San Pablo Bay: fine Chardonnay and old-vine Zinfandel.

North of Sonoma, Mendocino County is large and diverse. Very cool Anderson Valley supplies aromatic whites such as Riesling and Gewurztraminer, and sparkling wine. The larger Mendocino AVA is much warmer and drier, sheltered by coastal hills up to nine hundred metres: full-bodied, soft-tannin wines from Cabernet, Zinfandel and Syrah.

Central Coast. Santa Cruz Mountains, in the north, has hillside sites with poor soils and a moderate climate: some of California's most elegant Cabernets, plus fine Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Monterey AVA follows the Salinas Valley, strongly influenced by the cold Pacific: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir near the coast, where strong cool winds blow daily; further inland, Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah. On the surrounding slopes, Santa Lucia Highlands is noted for Chardonnay with citrus and tropical fruit and balanced acidity.

Further south, in San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties, the mountains run east-west, letting ocean air flow inland. Paso Robles has notable Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah, with two zones: the hot, sunny, fertile east for supple, fruity high-volume wines; the west, cooled by marine air, known for Zinfandel and Rhône grapes. Exposed coastal Santa Maria Valley is much cooler, ideal for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay: fog slows ripening, giving concentrated fruit balanced by high acidity. Santa Ynez Valley, slightly warmer, makes reds from Syrah and Bordeaux grapes, and Santa Rita Hills, at its far western end, much cooler, specialises in Pinot Noir, with Chardonnay and some aromatic grapes.

The Central Valley, covering the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys, makes the vast majority of California wine, mostly for inexpensive brands, often labelled simply California. The climate is hot and dry, with widespread irrigation. Grapes such as Rubired and Ruby Cabernet were bred here for these conditions, alongside Cabernet, Merlot, Chardonnay, Colombard, Chenin Blanc and Barbera. Lodi, in the middle, lies east of the huge Sacramento Delta and gets cooling breezes from San Francisco Bay every day; most grapes are grown, but it is home to some of the state's oldest and best Zinfandel vineyards.

To sum up: the cold California Current and fog; drought and hang time; Cabernet, Zinfandel, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon; Napa's valley-floor and hillside AVAs; Sonoma, Russian River and Mendocino; Monterey, Paso Robles and Santa Barbara; and the Central Valley with Lodi.

After California, the most important wine states are Oregon, Washington and New York. The first two lie directly north of California, in the north-west corner of the country, either side of the Cascade Mountains. New York is on the Atlantic seaboard, in the north-east.

Oregon. In the north, the Willamette Valley AVA, west of the Cascades, stretches south from Portland and has the largest concentration of wineries and vineyards in the state. The climate is moderate, cooled by Pacific breezes, with a mostly dry growing season, long sunny days and cool nights. Pinot Noir is by far the most planted grape: ripe red fruit, a hint of cinnamon spice and high acidity. Pinot Gris is also widely grown, usually fruity and dry.

In the south, the Southern Oregon AVA, directly below Willamette, includes Umpqua Valley, Rogue Valley and other AVAs. It is Oregon's warmest area, but its hills and valleys also have cooler spots, so both cool- and warm-climate grapes succeed: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Syrah.

Washington State. Most vineyards are in the vast Columbia Valley AVA, east of the Cascades, in the valleys of the Columbia River and its tributaries, which contains the smaller but important Yakima Valley and Walla Walla AVAs. Columbia Valley lies in the Cascades' rain shadow, so irrigation with river water is essential. Long days and steady summer temperatures give optimal ripeness, while cool nights keep natural acidity. A major problem is winter freeze, which can cut the crop by half or more.

The key reds are plummy, full-bodied Merlot and elegant, age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon; full-bodied, intensely concentrated Syrah is made too. Chardonnay is the most planted white, fruity, often with some oak toast. Riesling is also popular, usually dry with ripe stone fruit.

New York State. Unlike the west coast, its vineyards are dominated by American species and hybrids, used for juice and jelly but also for wine, thanks to their winter hardiness. Wine is also made from Vitis vinifera, mainly Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon. The Finger Lakes AVA is the most important: deep glacial lakes store heat into November, warming the air around the vineyards and extending the season. It is best known for perfumed Riesling, but also makes Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay, as well as American varieties and hybrids. Some lakes have their own AVAs.

To sum up: Willamette Valley Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris; warmer Southern Oregon; irrigated Columbia Valley, with Yakima and Walla Walla, its Merlot, Cabernet and the risk of winter freeze; and Finger Lakes Riesling in New York.

Canada's most important wine regions are in Ontario and British Columbia. They have a harsh continental climate, moderated by large bodies of water. Canada makes world-renowned Icewines, and steadily growing volumes of dry whites and reds.

Wine law. Canada's appellation system is the VQA, Vintners Quality Alliance, currently used by two provinces: Ontario and British Columbia. Each province is divided into DVAs, Designated Viticultural Areas, which are split into regional appellations and then sub-appellations. Every VQA wine must use one hundred per cent grapes grown in that province, and be made entirely from Vitis vinifera or selected hybrids.

The climate is continental throughout: average annual temperatures are low, but July and August days are often very hot. Large lakes moderate the extremes, but winters are cold, with long spells far below zero, ideal for Icewine.

Ontario has three DVAs, the most important being the Niagara Peninsula, on the south-west corner of Lake Ontario. The lake cools and warms more slowly than the land: it extends autumn, letting grapes ripen fully, and delays budburst in spring, reducing frost damage. Air flow helps limit fungal disease. Riesling does well, making fresh, fruity dry and off-dry whites and the finest Icewines. Vidal, a hardy hybrid, is also widely used for Icewine: dull as a dry white, it can make high-quality Icewine, though without Riesling's acid structure and aromatic complexity. Good dry Chardonnay is made, with pure fruit and restrained oak. Among reds, some producers make very fine Pinot Noir, while plantings of Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are increasing.

British Columbia has five DVAs, the most important being the Okanagan Valley. This huge DVA lies in the rain shadow of two mountain ranges: very low rainfall and a semi-desert environment. At this northern latitude, growing-season days are extremely long, extending photosynthesis and helping ripening. Large glacial lakes moderate temperatures and lengthen the season, so white grapes ripen in the north and black grapes in the south. The most planted varieties are Merlot, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and Icewine is made too, usually from Riesling or Vidal.
To sum up: a continental climate moderated by lakes; VQA and DVAs; the Niagara Peninsula, with Riesling and Vidal Icewine; and the semi-desert Okanagan Valley with its very long days.

Between the Andes to the east and the Pacific to the west, Chile has an unusual geography. It is this geography, combining cooling from the Pacific and the Andes with plentiful sun, that explains its success with a wide range of styles.

Climate and grape growing. Chile's vineyards span more than nine hundred kilometres north to south, but rarely more than a hundred east to west. Four features define the landscape: the Pacific to the west, the coastal range just inland, and to the east the Andes, which form the border with Argentina. North of Santiago the two ranges tend to merge; south of the capital a large depression lies between them, known as the Central Valley. In many places, rivers draining the Andes have cut gaps through the coastal range.

Overall the climate is warm Mediterranean. The dry, sunny growing season ensures reliable ripening and keeps disease down, and irrigation makes up for the lack of rain, though water is increasingly scarce. It gets cooler and wetter in the south. El Niño and La Niña can affect some years: rainfall can rise dramatically in El Niño years, while La Niña can bring drought.

Two influences cool the western and eastern edges of the vineyards. The cold Humboldt Current flows up from Antarctica along the coast, and prevailing winds push cool air inland along river valleys, sometimes with fog near the coast; the effect is strongest where the coastal range is lowest and in the parts of valleys closest to the Pacific. In the Andean foothills, cold air descending from the mountains at night creates large day-night swings. In between, the climate is more sheltered, and the broad flat land is easy to farm. These two influences are the reason for the labelling terms introduced in twenty twelve.
Sustainable and organic farming are widely practised by large and small estates, promoted by respected winemakers and the authorities.

Wine law. Chile is divided into Denominaciones de Origen. Four main regions, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Central Valley and Southern Region, are split into thirteen better-known sub-regions that generally follow the valleys running from the Andes to the Pacific. Based on administrative regions, they are very broad, and many contain several zones with more uniform climates. In twenty twelve a further classification was added, by distance from the coast rather than latitude: Costa for coastal areas, Entre Cordilleras for the area between the ranges, and Andes for the mountains. These are optional terms used alongside the DO. Chilean law also recognises Reserva, Reserva Especial, Reserva Privada and Gran Reserva: loosely defined, they mean little overall, but can signal quality levels within a producer's range.

Black grapes have always dominated. Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape of either colour, from simple and fruity to full-bodied premium wines, usually with very ripe black fruit and often a herbaceous note; it is frequently blended with Merlot, Carmenère or Syrah. Inexpensive, fruity, medium-bodied Merlot has done very well in export markets, though fuller, more complex versions exist. Carmenère, late-ripening, succeeds in the warmest, sunniest sites: full-bodied, often very tannic; underripe it is overtly herbaceous, but good examples balance black fruit and herbal notes. It is often seen as Chile's signature grape. Syrah is planted widely: lighter and peppery from cooler coastal or northern regions such as Elqui, more intense and fuller from hot areas such as Colchagua. Pinot Noir shows real promise in cool areas such as San Antonio and Casablanca.

Whites are dominated by Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. Sauvignon does especially well in cool sites such as Casablanca and San Antonio: high acidity, intense fruit, ripe apple, citrus and tropical notes, sometimes herbaceous; some gain richness from lees and oak. Chardonnay has mostly been made in a modern international style, ripe fruit and oak, but quality and range keep growing: Limarí Valley in particular gives structured, elegant, restrained wines, as do Aconcagua, Casablanca and others. Muscat of Alexandria, the third white, mostly goes into Pisco, a grape brandy. Small plantings of Viognier, Riesling and Gewurztraminer give fresh, fruity wines in cool regions such as Biobío and Itata.

Coquimbo, bordering the Atacama Desert, is the most northerly main region, with three sub-regions: Elqui, Limarí and Choapa. Plantings are small but quality is often high: brilliant sun and marked cooling from sea breezes or mountain air, with some vineyards now at very high altitude. The big challenge is lack of water, making irrigation expensive. Elqui is already known for Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah, and Limarí makes some of Chile's best Chardonnay.

Aconcagua, though well known, is the second smallest region, in three sub-regions. The Aconcagua Valley is narrow and steep-sided; despite some cooling from ocean and mountains, the fertile valley floor is among Chile's warmest sites. It is classic red wine country, long dominated by Cabernet, but Syrah, pioneered in Chile in this valley, and Carmenère are increasingly important. Producers now seek lower alcohol and more freshness, planting on slopes or towards the coast.

Casablanca and San Antonio, neighbours, lie between the coastal range and the Pacific: morning fog and afternoon winds make them noticeably cooler, and white grapes dominate. Sauvignon Blanc is the star, especially in San Antonio and its very cool Leyda zone, but Chardonnay is fine too. Pinot Noir is the main black grape, with red berry and herbal notes in the coolest sites, and Syrah succeeds as well, especially in warmer eastern Casablanca, structured and peppery.

The Central Valley runs from Santiago south to Itata. Vast, warm and flat, it has always held most of Chile's vineyards; grapes ripen easily, and much is inexpensive fruity wine, often Merlot and Chardonnay. It has four sub-regions: Maipo, Rapel, with its two zones Cachapoal and Colchagua, Curicó and Maule.

Maipo, next to Santiago, is the historic heartland. Almost surrounded by mountains, it gets little ocean influence. Many premium sites are in the Andean foothills, cooled by descending air, which gives elegance and structure. Its Cabernet often has a distinctive minty character. In Rapel, Cachapoal to the north is warm and cut off from sea breezes: Carmenère ripens well on the valley floor, Cabernet and Syrah in the cooler east. Colchagua, larger and more varied, is warm in the centre and partly open to the ocean: known for full-bodied reds, especially Cabernet, but also Syrah and Carmenère. Vineyards have spread onto the slopes, and some areas, notably Apalta, have a premium reputation; further west, Pacific cooling allows fine whites.

Curicó and Maule, at the southern end of the Central Valley, are warm and fertile, the main sources of inexpensive blends. Maule is cooler, and its wines keep more acidity, useful in blending. There is growing interest in the many old, dry-farmed vines in its western hills: Carignan has become the star, giving full-bodied, intensely concentrated wines from ancient, low-yielding bush vines.

The Southern Region has three sub-regions: Itata, Biobío and Malleco, getting cooler and wetter further south. Itata and Biobío are dominated by País and Muscat of Alexandria, mostly drunk locally; but, new in this edition, some producers, especially in Itata, are using old bush vines of these grapes for good-quality wines with a distinctive style. Biobío shows great promise for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic grapes, and interest in the acidity and aromatics of these regions is growing. Malleco, the smallest and most southerly, has only a few producers of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, but is attracting premium producers.

To sum up: a geography between ocean and Andes; the Humboldt Current and mountain air; the Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes terms; Cabernet, Carmenère, Syrah, Sauvignon and Chardonnay; Limarí, Casablanca, San Antonio and Leyda; Maipo, Colchagua and Apalta; old-vine Carignan in Maule; and the revival of Itata.

Cut off from Pacific influence by the Andes, Argentina's wine regions are defined by altitude: many of the best vineyards lie above a thousand metres. Two grapes have become the country's signatures: Malbec for reds and Torrontés for whites.

Climate and grape growing. Most vineyards lie close to the Andes, in a series of irrigated oases in otherwise desert land, spread over more than fifteen hundred kilometres from Salta province in the north to Río Negro and Neuquén in Patagonia. Apart from Patagonia, most are at six hundred metres or more, and in Salta, near Cafayate, they often exceed two thousand, so cool sites can be found fairly close to the Equator.

Because of the heat, vines were traditionally trained on pergolas, known as parral: grapes were lifted away from the hot ground and hung shaded beneath the leaves. Parral is still common for Torrontés, but many black-grape vineyards now use vertical trellises, with canopies arranged to shade the fruit.

In the Andes' rain shadow, rainfall is extremely low, but water comes from mountain rivers or underground aquifers. Flood irrigation was widespread, but more efficient drip irrigation is common in newer vineyards. Spring frost is occasional, but summer hail is a regular hazard, especially in Mendoza, and many producers use netting despite the cost. The traditional way to manage risk, owning vineyards in several areas, remains widespread, and also helps with blending. The dry climate means little rot or mildew, and Argentina is an important producer of organic wine.

Black grapes. Malbec is the flagship, and Argentina has the world's largest plantings. It gives deeply coloured, full-bodied wines with black fruit and often high levels of smooth tannin; some winemakers now extract more gently for elegance. Most premium Malbec is aged in new oak, with subtle spice. Grown in every region, it shows regional differences: lower altitudes give fuller wines with richer black fruit; higher sites more elegant, fresher, more floral wines. It is mostly a varietal, but also leads premium blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc or Petit Verdot.

Bonarda is the second most planted grape: late-ripening, deeply coloured, high in acidity and tannin. At high yields it makes easy-drinking wines with raspberry and blackberry; with controlled yields and full ripeness, more concentrated, structured wines. It is mainly grown in Mendoza and San Juan. Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot are widely planted too, with some Tempranillo and Pinot Noir; premium wines show concentrated ripe fruit, often with oak toast.

White grapes. Torrontés is the white signature, planted in Salta, La Rioja, San Juan and Mendoza; many of the best come from high vineyards in Cafayate. Intensely fruity and floral, with medium body and acidity, stone fruit and melon, it is fermented in inert, temperature-controlled vessels and released within the year. Chardonnay is widely planted in several styles, the best aged in partly new oak. Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon and Viognier are also grown. Pedro Giménez, not the same as Spain's Pedro Ximénez, a traditional low-quality grape for cheap domestic wine, is declining but still the most planted white.

Wine law, clarified in the new edition. The GI system splits the vineyards into three broad regions, which, except Patagonia, rarely appear on labels. Each region is divided into provinces, then departments, which may contain smaller districts, sometimes with even smaller GIs. For a GI to appear on a label, one hundred per cent of the grapes must come from within it.

Salta, near Bolivia, is the most northerly province, with some of the world's highest vineyards, above three thousand metres. The extreme climate gives wines of great purity and concentration. Torrontés dominates, highly aromatic, especially in Cafayate, where big Mendoza wineries and European companies have invested. Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon lead among reds.

La Rioja is the third largest province by area. Most vineyards are in the Famatina Valley, where irrigation allows large volumes. Torrontés is a speciality, and Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Bonarda are the main reds. According to the new edition, to avoid confusion with Spain's Rioja, exports are generally labelled La Rioja Argentina.

San Juan is the second most important area, at four hundred and fifty to fourteen hundred metres, like Mendoza, but hotter and more arid. It is noted for Syrah, with Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Bonarda too; among whites, according to the new edition, Torrontés and Chardonnay are the most planted.

Mendoza dominates production. Vines grow in desert conditions, sheltered from rain by the Andes to the west and the vast Pampas to the east. It divides into five areas: Northern, Eastern, Central, the Uco Valley and Southern, and wines are often blended across them. The north and east focus on inexpensive volume wine, irrigated by the Mendoza river. The centre has the longest tradition of quality and many famous producers. Luján de Cuyo, at nine hundred to eleven hundred metres in the Andean foothills south-west of the city, is renowned for Malbec, and its old vines bring softness, roundness and sweet spice to blends. Maipú, to the east and lower, does well with Syrah and Cabernet; its lower eastern part supplies much volume wine, but also old-vine Bonarda and Tempranillo.

The Uco Valley, south-west of Mendoza, at nine hundred to fifteen hundred metres, has the province's highest vineyards and high-quality fruit: cool nights keep acidity and fresh fruit, sometimes with floral notes. Chardonnay, Torrontés, Sauvignon Blanc, Malbec, Cabernet, Merlot and Tempranillo all flourish, and some sites are cool enough for Pinot Noir. It includes Tupungato in the west, increasingly recognised. In the south, San Rafael is lower, but its latitude makes it one of the province's coolest areas, with the country's largest Chenin Blanc plantings.

Patagonia includes Río Negro and the newer Neuquén. Vineyards lie at two hundred to two hundred and fifty metres: here latitude, not altitude, provides the cooling. Strong desert winds are a challenge, but low rainfall and wide day-night swings keep disease low. Long days and cool nights give concentrated yet fresh fruit and medium to high acidity. Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Malbec and Merlot can all be excellent in Río Negro, and Neuquén's potential is still being explored.

To sum up: altitude and irrigated oases; hail and parral; Malbec and Bonarda; Torrontés from Cafayate; one-hundred-per-cent GIs; Salta, La Rioja Argentina and San Juan; Mendoza, Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley; and Patagonia, cooled by latitude.

Most of South Africa's wine regions lie on or near the Cape coast, where they benefit from the cooling Southern Ocean. With a dramatic mountain backdrop, this landscape lets winemakers produce a broad range of styles.

Climate and grape growing. Between twenty-seven and thirty-four degrees south, South Africa should be hot. Some inland areas regularly exceed thirty degrees in summer, but many vineyards are cooled, above all by the ocean: the cold Benguela Current flows up from the Antarctic along the west coast. This is magnified by strong south-easterly summer winds, the Cape Doctor, which push cool air inland and can lower temperatures by a further couple of degrees.

The other defining feature is the mountain ranges running through the wine regions: a wide range of altitudes, aspects and soils, so many different site climates. Valley floors are much warmer than mountain sites. As elsewhere in the Southern Hemisphere, vines may be planted on south-facing slopes for coolness. Mountains can also cast shade at certain times of day, and near the coast they channel winds through the vineyards.

Black grapes. Cabernet Sauvignon, the most planted, is made as a varietal or blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in Bordeaux-style blends. Merlot alone can give full-bodied, plummy wines. Syrah is widely planted: in hot climates rich, full-bodied, often high in alcohol, with ripe black fruit, sometimes earthy or meaty; in cooler areas lighter and peppery. Pinot Noir dislikes the heat and is planted in small amounts in the coolest coastal areas. Most premium reds are oak-matured, with some new barrels.

Pinotage, a cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault developed in South Africa and hardly grown anywhere else, is a real point of difference. It comes in many styles. It is sometimes blended with international grapes into a Cape blend. Alone, it can be light and fruity with red berries or, from old bush vines, very full-bodied with rich, spiced fruit. Fermented or stored with heavily toasted oak staves, it takes on intense coffee or chocolate aromas, a style popular with some consumers.

White grapes. Chenin Blanc is the most planted grape of either colour. Its importance has declined, but growers now make better use of its versatility, dry and sweet. At a basic level it gives easy-drinking wines with simple stone fruit; but more and more producers use old bush vines for more concentrated, complex, fuller wines, some barrel-fermented and aged. Colombard remains the second white, much of it for brandy. Sauvignon Blanc is widely grown, often herbaceous; the best, from the coolest regions, show very pure citrus and green fruit; in warmer areas grapes must be picked early to keep these flavours and acidity. Chardonnay can be exceptional in cooler sites, often with Burgundian barrel fermentation and lees stirring. Muscat of Alexandria, here called Hanepoot, is used for late-harvest dessert wines, sometimes with noble rot. Viognier has expanded dramatically, making rich, perfumed wines with a hint of oak. And high-quality white blends have emerged, especially from Swartland, based on Chenin with Rhône grapes: Marsanne, Roussanne, Grenache Blanc and Viognier.

Wine law. The GI system is the Wine of Origin scheme, or WO, with a certification seal on every bottle. It recognises four sizes of area. The largest is the geographical unit, a catch-all appellation allowing blends of several regions; the only important one is the Western Cape, widely used even for premium wines, since it lets producers blend the best parcels from different areas. The Western Cape is divided into regions following major geological features: mainly Coastal Region, Breede River Valley and Cape South Coast, split further into districts and then wards. Estate Wines must come from a single estate, with vineyards in one area and facilities on site up to and including bottling; so a top producer can release Estate Wines and other WO wines under the same brand. There is also a voluntary sustainability scheme, Integrated Production of Wine, whose credentials can appear with the WO seal.

Regions. Well over ninety per cent of the wine comes from the Western Cape; most of the rest comes from the very hot, irrigated Orange River, mainly cheap whites rarely exported. Some wineries source grapes from outside their district or ward: their wines then carry a region, such as Coastal Region, or a geographical unit, such as Western Cape, and a number of premium wines are made this way.

In the Coastal Region, the Stellenbosch district, from near the coast at Somerset West up into the mountains around the town, has long been the hub of South African fine wine. The climate is moderate to warm depending on site, with enough winter rain and summers rarely too hot thanks to cool winds from False Bay funnelled by the mountains. But its key strength is the variety of altitude, aspect and soil in a small area, reflected in its many wards. It is renowned for top reds, especially Cabernet and Merlot, often in Bordeaux-style blends, Syrah and Cape blends, and cooler sites give fine Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

Paarl, to the north and further inland, is hotter in summer, though nights are cooler. Like Stellenbosch, it offers varied altitude, aspect and soil. The main reds are Cabernet, Syrah and Pinotage, the main whites Chenin and Chardonnay.

Constantia, in the Cape Peninsula, has some of the Cape's oldest vineyards, on the eastern flanks of Table Mountain, constantly cooled by the Cape Doctor; it is known for Sauvignon Blanc, and one estate still makes Vin de Constance, a sweet wine from late-harvested Muscat. Further south towards Cape Point, vineyards exposed to the ocean specialise in Sauvignon and Semillon, with some Shiraz and Cabernet in warmer spots.

North of Cape Town, Swartland, once a source of cheap grapes, has become a centre of innovation and premium wine. It is known for old-vine Chenin and high-quality Syrah, often dry-farmed, lowering yields and concentrating fruit, and for premium red and white Cape blends. Darling, to the south-west, nearer the coast and cooled by sea breezes, built its name on Sauvignon and also has old vines. Durbanville, in the Tygerberg district, has hillside sites cooled by sea breezes and a reputation for Sauvignon Blanc.

In the Breede River Valley, Worcester is hot and dry, irrigated from the river, with fertile soils: a large share of national production, mainly Chenin and Colombard whites, much of it distilled, but also reliable wines for high-volume brands. Robertson, further east and slightly cooler thanks to south-easterly winds, also supplies reliable branded wines, but cooling and less fertile soils also allow excellent Syrah and full-bodied Chardonnay.

The Cape South Coast, well exposed to the ocean, regularly supplies some of the best fruit. Walker Bay, with the Hemel-en-Aarde wards, has long been home to some of the country's best Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and also does well with Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah. Elgin, to the north-west, also cooled by altitude, is known for intense, fresh Sauvignon and shows promise for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah. To the south-east, Elim, in the Cape Agulhas district, is known for pungent, herbaceous Sauvignon, and Syrah shows promise.

To sum up: the Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor; mountains and their site climates; Cabernet, Syrah and Pinotage; old-vine Chenin; the Wine of Origin scheme; Stellenbosch, Paarl, Constantia and Swartland; and cool Walker Bay, Elgin and Elim.

Australia has been remarkably successful at turning international grapes into unique new styles: full-bodied Shiraz, lime-scented Riesling, elegant Cabernet and subtle Semillon that evolves for decades. And the diversity keeps growing, as new regions, grapes and styles are explored.

Climate and grape growing. The country is as big as the USA and bigger than Europe, so climates vary widely. But because of its latitude, the main regions are warm or hot. Many are moderated by the Southern or Indian Ocean or the Murray River system; others, such as Adelaide Hills and Eden Valley, by altitude. Rainfall is often low and irrigation essential. Drought can be serious: in extreme years even the Murray, vital for Riverland and Murray-Darling, can run low. Dry heat makes bush fires a real risk: even if vines escape, smoke can leave a pungent taint in the wine. Many producers are seeking cooler sites, at altitude on the mainland or in Tasmania, further south.

Black grapes. Shiraz is Australia's leading grape of either colour, planted almost everywhere. Hot regions such as Hunter Valley and warm ones such as Barossa Valley give full-bodied, intensely fruity Shiraz, often earthy or spicy, developing leather with age; some winemakers now make more restrained styles by controlling extraction. Cooler regions such as Geelong and Heathcote give a leaner, more peppery style, and these qualities can be combined in multi-regional blends. Shiraz also adds softness and body to Cabernet blends, a role like Merlot's in Bordeaux. Australian Cabernet Sauvignon is darker, firmer and more acidic than Shiraz, with ripe blackcurrant and black cherry, often over toasty oak; classic regions are Coonawarra and Margaret River. Merlot is mostly used in blends with Cabernet, for body and fleshy fruit.

Pinot Noir is grown in several regions, and the best come from cool or moderate sites such as Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula and Tasmania: medium body and alcohol, medium to high acidity, cherry and strawberry. Hot regions suit late-ripening grapes such as Grenache, Petit Verdot and Mataro, which is Mourvèdre; and Italian and Spanish grapes such as Sangiovese and Tempranillo are gaining ground, well suited to heat and limited water.

White grapes. Chardonnay is the most planted white, in a wide range of styles. Basic Chardonnay is often a multi-regional blend, unoaked and peachy, or with chips or staves for toast and vanilla. At the other end, top Chardonnays from cool to moderate regions such as Adelaide Hills, Mornington Peninsula and Yarra Valley, and even warmer Margaret River, are often beautifully balanced, with fresh, vibrant fruit and subtle use of lees, malolactic or oak.
Sauvignon Blanc, very popular, is now widely planted; moderate Adelaide Hills has become the benchmark: concentrated passion fruit and refreshing high acidity.

Semillon makes a style unique to Australia, classically from Hunter Valley. It is picked early, with low sugar and high acidity, protected from oxygen and fermented and stored in inert vessels. On release it is light and almost neutral, but with age develops extraordinary honey and toast, and the best last twenty years or more. Western Australia makes a much more herbaceous style, close to Sauvignon. Barossa traditionally made a fuller, softer Semillon, but early-picked, unoaked versions are increasingly common.

Riesling also has a unique Australian style: pronounced citrus in youth, lime, lemon and grapefruit, developing quickly into toast, honey and petrol. Unoaked and high in acidity, it is usually dry or just off-dry, with some sweet wines. Classic regions are Eden Valley and Clare Valley; according to the new edition, Great Southern in Western Australia and Tasmania also have a growing reputation, with less citrusy, more floral wines.

Wine law. Australia has a hierarchy of GIs: zones, regions and sub-regions. Zones are large areas with no particular qualifying attributes: a state, such as South Australia, or several, such as South Eastern Australia; they rarely appear on labels, except perhaps Barossa. Regions, such as Coonawarra, Clare Valley and Margaret River, are smaller and must have distinct qualities from their neighbours, and many are split into sub-regions. A region can sit within nested zones: Eden Valley is in the Barossa zone, within South Australia, within South Eastern Australia. This gives producers many blending options.

South Eastern Australia is a super-zone covering all GIs in South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. Most wines using it are high-volume brands sourcing from the fertile, irrigated vineyards of Riverland, Murray-Darling and Riverina: high yields of healthy grapes, but lacking concentration, which can be lifted with fruit from Barossa, Adelaide Hills or McLaren Vale. Riverina also specialises in botrytised Semillon, thanks to autumn mists.
South Australia makes most of Australia's wine. Some of the country's most prestigious and expensive wines blend across regions and are simply labelled South Australia.

Barossa Valley, north of Adelaide, is the heartland of fine wine. In its warm, dry climate, old bush vines give outstanding Shiraz, Cabernet and Grenache. Classic Barossa Shiraz is full-bodied, with soft tannins and ripe black fruit plus sweet American oak, developing leather and spice. The main white is Semillon, increasingly fresh and unoaked. Wines labelled Barossa come from the zone and can blend Barossa Valley and Eden Valley.

Eden Valley, in the hills to the east, is cool to moderate depending on altitude. Its cooler sites give outstanding Riesling, with intense lime and grapefruit and a steely character, developing marmalade and toast after ten years; Shiraz, Chardonnay and Cabernet also do well.

Adelaide Hills, twenty-five kilometres east of Adelaide, has a moderate climate with all vineyards above four hundred metres. Rain falls mainly in winter, and soils hold little water, so irrigation is often needed. It specialises in refreshing Sauvignon and elegant, high-acid Chardonnay with citrus and peach; Pinot Noir is grown for reds and, with Chardonnay, for sparkling wine.

Clare Valley, north-west of Barossa, is also Riesling country. Its warm climate is tempered by cool afternoon breezes and cold nights, with many vineyards at three to four hundred metres, some up to five hundred and seventy. Its Rieslings are dry, with intense citrus and lime and high acidity, developing honey and toast. Shiraz is fragrant, powerful and structured, and Cabernet excellent; the best reds age for a long time.

McLaren Vale, on the coast south of Adelaide, is tempered by afternoon sea breezes. It makes mostly reds from Shiraz, Cabernet, Merlot and Grenache, intense, dark-fruited and soft-tannined, and old-vine Shiraz and Grenache give depth and complexity.

Coonawarra is a narrow strip about one and a half kilometres wide and fifteen long, with red terra rossa soil over limestone, four hundred kilometres south-east of Adelaide. Cold Antarctic currents give a moderate maritime climate, and cloud cover tempers summer heat. Cabernet dominates, concentrated and structured, with cassis and eucalyptus or menthol, and the best age very well; Shiraz, Merlot and Chardonnay are also grown.

Victoria has some of the mainland's coolest sites. Around Melbourne and Port Phillip Bay, sea breezes allow fine Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base. Inland, the Great Dividing Range gives varied altitude and aspect: high sites such as Macedon Ranges and Upper Goulburn give elegant Pinot and Chardonnay and aromatic Riesling and Sauvignon; lower slopes grow Shiraz and Cabernet, fresher and lighter than in hotter regions.

Yarra Valley, north-east of Melbourne, is cool to moderate and maritime, but very varied. Pinot Noir is the speciality, for still wine and excellent sparkling: rich in strawberry, plum and dark cherry, with soft, ripe tannins and careful oak, the best age-worthy. Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cabernet also succeed, never as heavy as in warmer regions.

Mornington Peninsula, south of Melbourne, is coastal and cool to moderate, home to small boutique estates specialising in Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Vintages vary, with a risk of cool, wet, windy weather at flowering and often at harvest; in the best years, a long season gives fragrant, elegant wines. Pinot ranges from light and delicate to more structured, always with very pure fruit, and Chardonnay shows citrus, pear and apple with high acidity often softened by malolactic.

Geelong, west of Melbourne, with a similar climate, is known for complex, concentrated, full-bodied Chardonnay; its Pinot can be earthy and its Shiraz fresh and peppery, and Chardonnay and Pinot also go into sparkling wine. Heathcote, in central Victoria, is cooled by altitude rather than the ocean: Shiraz with firmer structure and fresher fruit than in warmer regions, plus Chardonnay, Cabernet and promising Mediterranean grapes such as Sangiovese and Tempranillo. Warm Goulburn Valley, to the east, slightly tempered by lakes and creeks, grows mostly Shiraz, but its speciality is Marsanne, citrusy when young and honeyed with age.

New South Wales has Australia's longest winemaking history. The main region is hot Hunter Valley, but Mudgee, Orange and Cowra, at altitude on the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range, are slightly cooler, giving very concentrated Chardonnay and structured Cabernet. Hunter Valley is hot and humid; cloud and sea breezes ease the heat, but rain at harvest is common, so canopy management is vital against rot. Semillon is the most planted: light, low in alcohol, high in acidity, almost neutral young, then toast, nuts and honey with age. Chardonnay, oaked or not, is widely planted, and Shiraz, the main red, gives medium-bodied wines with blackberry and cherry, soft tannins and an earthy undertone.

Western Australia's vineyards are in the south-west tip of the state. Its wines can be blended as Western Australia, the only ones outside the South Eastern Australia super-zone. Margaret River, about two hundred kilometres south of Perth, is coastal with a warm maritime climate and relatively high rainfall, mostly in winter. Cabernet, often blended with Merlot Bordeaux-style, ranges from elegant and restrained to fruity and powerful; Chardonnay shows concentrated stone fruit and high acidity, with barrel ageing and malolactic for complexity; Sauvignon, often blended with Semillon, shows gooseberry, tropical fruit and high acidity. Further south, Great Southern, with Mount Barker and Frankland River, is known for deeply coloured Cabernet, elegant peppery Shiraz and, according to the new edition, pure Riesling with mineral notes.

Tasmania has a cool maritime climate, cooled by westerly winds off the Southern Ocean and free of extremes. Long a prime source of base wine for Australian sparkling wine, it now also makes excellent still wines: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris, and even Cabernet in the warmest, driest spots.

To sum up: heat, drought and bush fires; Australian-style Shiraz, Cabernet, Chardonnay, Semillon and Riesling; zones, regions and sub-regions; Barossa, Eden, Clare, Adelaide Hills, McLaren Vale and Coonawarra; Yarra, Mornington, Geelong and Heathcote; Hunter Valley; Margaret River and Great Southern; and Tasmania.

New Zealand is best known for fresh, vibrant Sauvignon Blanc, a style that has inspired winemakers worldwide. But its reputation for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah and Bordeaux-style blends shows there is far more to it than one grape.

Climate and grape growing. Isolated in the Pacific, nineteen hundred kilometres from Australia, the nearest land, it has a maritime climate. The South Island is cool, the North Island a little warmer. Long sunshine hours, sea-cooled nights and a long ripening period give high sugar and flavour ripeness while keeping acidity. On the South Island, vineyards are mostly on the east side, sheltered from rain-bearing westerlies by central mountains, but many still get plenty of rain, a problem during ripening. Soils drain freely, but on flat land they can be too fertile, giving excessive vigour, so New Zealand growers have become experts in trellising and canopy management. The industry is strongly committed to reducing its environmental impact, through Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand.

Wine law, new in this edition. The GI system is recent: the first GIs were registered in twenty seventeen. To name a GI, at least eighty-five per cent of the grapes must come from it. New Zealand, the North Island and the South Island are GIs, as is each of the main wine regions.

White grapes. Since the early nineteen-nineties, Sauvignon Blanc has been the flagship and makes up most production. Its pungent elderflower and passion fruit and high acidity set a world benchmark. The warmer north gives more tropical notes; the south more acidity, with green bell pepper and gooseberry. It is mostly fermented cool in inert vessels to keep the fruit, though some producers make oak-matured styles. Chardonnay is widely planted too, made in many ways, but generally with concentrated citrus and tropical fruit and subtle toast and spice from new French oak. Producers are also exploring Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris: dry autumns and cool nights give aromas time to develop, and wines range from dry to sweet, mostly off-dry.

Black grapes. Pinot Noir is the second most planted grape, throughout the South Island and in a few North Island sites: vibrant fruit, fine ripe tannins, soft texture and often fairly high alcohol, with distinct regional styles. Far behind in area, Merlot is the second red by volume; Cabernet Sauvignon adds tannin and cassis in Bordeaux-style blends noted for pure fruit, mostly in the warmer North Island. Syrah, small but growing, does best in warm sites, giving elegant wines closer to the Rhône than to Australia.

North Island. Auckland is where the industry began, and big wineries there still process grapes from all over the country. Warm and the wettest part of New Zealand, it battles fungal disease; Chardonnay, Merlot and Syrah are the main grapes, and Waiheke Island, to the east, has a growing reputation, especially for reds. Gisborne, on the east coast in a broad estuary plain, is rainy but warm and sunny: over half the vines are Chardonnay, with ripe tropical fruit, plus a little fine Gewurztraminer and full-bodied Pinot Gris.

Hawke's Bay, near Hastings and Napier, also on the east coast, is the warmest and sunniest main region, second only to Marlborough in area, and very diverse in soils, aspects and altitudes. The Gimblett Gravels, a parcel of free-draining, heat-absorbing gravel on the valley floor, are especially renowned for reds. The region made its name with Merlot and Cabernet Bordeaux blends, but premium Syrah is made too.

Wairarapa, at the southern tip of the North Island, is a scattering of small vineyard areas. The most important, around Martinborough, world-famous for Pinot Noir, now has GI status according to the new edition. Summers can be warm, but wide day-night swings suit Pinot: medium- to full-bodied, ripe, with dark plum and spice.

South Island. Marlborough is the country's main grape-growing centre, dominated by Sauvignon Blanc. Most vineyards are in two neighbouring estuary valleys: Wairau, by far the largest, and Awatere. Wairau is like Martinborough, with long sunny days, but far from uniform, with side valleys to the south offering a range of aspects and altitudes. Awatere is drier, cooler and windier: its Sauvignons have higher acidity and more herbaceous character, without the tropical fruit of some Wairau wines. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also widely planted, for still and sparkling wine; still Pinot is medium-bodied with fine tannins, cherry and cranberry, and improving as producers focus on it. Riesling and Pinot Gris also do well.

Nelson, north-west of Wairau, is cooler and wetter than Marlborough, with mostly Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris. Canterbury has two centres: the plain west of Christchurch, exposed to Pacific cooling despite slight warming from north-westerly winds, and the larger Waipara Valley to the north, sheltered from the ocean by hills, where those warm winds have more effect. Sauvignon and Pinot Noir lead, and Waipara is noted for Riesling.

Central Otago lies inland in the foothills of the Southern Alps, across several valleys with different aspects, soils and altitudes. Unlike the rest of the country, the climate is continental, with real frost risk in spring and autumn. Summers can be warm, but crucially the day-night range is large, and very intense sunlight explains the often high alcohol. Pinot Noir dominates: full-bodied, juicy, vibrant wines with concentrated ripe red fruit. Pinot Gris, Riesling and Chardonnay are also important.

To sum up: a cool maritime climate and vigour control; a new GI system since twenty seventeen, at eighty-five per cent; Marlborough Sauvignon from Wairau and Awatere; Pinot Noir from Martinborough and Central Otago; Bordeaux blends and Syrah from Hawke's Bay and the Gimblett Gravels; and Waipara Riesling.

They all fizz, but sparkling wines come in a wide range of styles: white, red or rosé, any level of sweetness, from fresh and fruity to toasty and nutty. Here we focus on white sparkling wine and the techniques used in the vineyard and winery.

The vineyard. The requirements differ greatly from still wine. First, grapes should be relatively low in sugar: the second fermentation that gives most sparkling wines their bubbles adds one point two to one point three per cent alcohol, so winemakers aim for a dry base wine of ten to eleven per cent. Second, high acidity is wanted for a refreshing style. Third, despite low sugar and high acidity, flavours must be ripe enough to have lost any green, herbaceous character.

That is hard in all but the coolest regions. In cool climates sugar and acidity change slowly, in step with flavour. In warm climates sugar rises and acidity falls very fast, and picking early for the right balance often means green, herbaceous grapes. A cool enough climate is fundamental for premium sparkling wine.

Grapes and juice must be handled with care. For the best wines, grapes are hand-picked to keep whole, unsplit bunches; in warm regions, for inexpensive wines, machine harvesting can get everything in before sugar rises too far. At the winery, grapes are pressed quickly and gently to minimise tannin and colour, especially when black grapes make white wine; whole bunches help by limiting skin contact. In most EU regions, law sets maximum pressure and the amount of juice extracted.
Methods. In some European regions law dictates the method; elsewhere, the choice depends on style, quality and cost.

The traditional method: the second fermentation takes place in the bottle in which the wine is sold. It is the method most used for premium sparkling wine, costly and time-consuming, but often giving the highest-priced wines.

Base wine: the first fermentation usually takes place in large temperature-controlled stainless steel vats, though some use oak. The wine is dry, neutral and high in acidity. Depending on style, the winemaker decides on malolactic and any oak maturation. Most base wines are used the year after harvest, but some are kept as reserve wines, important for blending.

Blending has several roles. It maintains a house style year after year, especially for non-vintage wines, by combining vineyards, varieties and vintages. It improves balance: Chardonnay brings citrus, finesse and longevity, Pinot Noir red fruit and body. And it adds complexity: old reserve wines bring dried fruit, oak-matured wines a broader texture and spice. So grapes are often fermented in many small separate parcels.

Second fermentation: a little liqueur de tirage is added to the blend, a mix of wine, sugar, yeast, yeast nutrients and a clarifying agent. The bottle is sealed with a crown cap holding a small plastic cup, and stored horizontally in a cool, constant cellar. A slow fermentation adds one point two to one point three per cent alcohol, and the carbon dioxide dissolves into the wine, building five to six atmospheres of pressure.

Yeast autolysis: once fermentation ends, the yeasts die and form a lees deposit. After some months they start to break down, releasing compounds that give bread, biscuit and toast. According to the new edition, autolysis is most active at the start; it usually lasts four to five years, sometimes longer. The longer on the lees, the more pronounced the yeast character, and once autolysis is complete the lees keep the wine fresh for years. With shorter ageing, the yeast is removed before autolysis is finished.

Riddling: the deposit must then be removed. The bottle is moved slowly from horizontal to upside-down vertical, so the sediment slides into the plastic cup. Traditionally this was done by hand on A-frame pupitres: each day every bottle was shaken, turned and tilted a little, taking up to eight weeks. Today it is mostly done by gyropalettes, cages of five hundred bottles on a hydraulic arm, completing the job in days.

Disgorgement: the neck of the upturned bottle is dipped into very cold brine, freezing the wine in the neck. The bottle is turned upright, the crown cap removed, and the pressure ejects the frozen plug with the sediment. The wine is topped up with liqueur d'expédition, wine and sugar, and sealed with a cork held by a wire cage; fully mechanised, it takes seconds, avoiding pressure loss and oxidation. The amount of sugar, the dosage, sets the final sweetness, balances acidity and aids flavour development; wines with no added sugar are labelled Brut Nature or Zero Dosage. The wine in the liqueur matters too, young and fresh, toasty from oak or developed from years in bottle: it is a second blending step that shapes house style.

Almost all sparkling wines are sealed with cork. The cork starts as a cylinder much wider than the bottle neck; heavily compressed to go in, it takes its mushroom shape afterwards, and the wire cage keeps it secure. After corking the wine rests a few months to integrate the liqueur. Most are ready on release, but some premium wines benefit from ageing. Since most are non-vintage, their age is hard to know, and some producers now print disgorgement dates on labels.

The transfer method follows the traditional method up to riddling, then avoids riddling and disgorgement: the bottles are emptied into a pressurised tank, the lees filtered out, the liqueur d'expédition added and the wine rebottled. It is cheaper and suits large, consistent batches. Labels often say bottle-fermented, whereas the more prestigious traditional method is usually named as such.

The tank method keeps the base wine's flavours, without bready notes: ideal for aromatic grapes such as Muscat and Riesling, and fruity styles such as Prosecco. Cheaper, faster and less labour-intensive, it was long seen as inferior, but with good grapes and care it makes high-quality wine. The first fermentation is in temperature-controlled steel, usually without malolactic or oak; then yeast, sugar, nutrients and clarifying agent are added, and the second fermentation takes place in a sealed pressure tank. The wine is filtered and bottled under pressure. Most show no autolytic notes; paddles can stir the lees to create some, but most producers want primary fruit.

The Asti method is used mainly for sweet sparkling wines from Asti in Piemonte, with only one fermentation. The juice is chilled and stored, then warmed and fermented in pressurised tanks: at first the gas escapes, then the tank is sealed to keep it. Fermentation is stopped by chilling at around seven per cent alcohol, when pressure reaches, according to the new edition, four to five atmospheres. The wine is filtered under pressure and bottled for immediate sale.

The ancestral method, new in this edition: a very old method that has regained popularity. Like Asti, it involves only one fermentation: the fermenting must is bottled partway through, so the carbon dioxide produced afterwards is trapped. The wines may or may not be disgorged; if not, they may be cloudy with some sediment. They are usually released young.
Finally, carbonation: carbon dioxide is injected into a still wine, bottled under pressure. It keeps the base wine's fruit, for example from Sauvignon Blanc, and is the cheapest method.

Styles. In the EU, or for sale there, sparkling wines must state sweetness using defined terms, each covering a range. For the exam, remember: Brut Nature, zero to three grams per litre, no dosage; Brut, zero to twelve grams; and Demi-Sec, thirty-two to fifty grams. In between are Extra Brut, Extra Dry and Sec, and above, Doux. Non-vintage is not a labelling term but describes wine from several years, the producer's standard and house style. Vintage: in Champagne, wine from a single year; elsewhere, a small percentage of other years may be allowed. In Champagne, vintages are made only in the best years and cost more. Rosé is made by blending red and white base wines or by short maceration, and some appellations allow only maceration. Blanc de Blancs: white grapes only. Blanc de Noirs: a white wine from black grapes only. Prestige cuvée, finally, is not a legal term but the producer's top wine, very important in Champagne.

To sum up: low-sugar, high-acid but ripe grapes from a cool climate; the traditional method, with tirage, autolysis, riddling, disgorgement and dosage; transfer, tank, Asti, ancestral and carbonation; and Brut Nature, Brut and Demi-Sec.

Champagne remains the most prestigious sparkling wine, so we'll cover it in most detail: its reputation is such that most premium sparkling wines are made the same way and from the same grapes. But Champagne is not to everyone's taste, and sweeter, less acidic sparkling wines are hugely popular. EU rules for sparkling wine are many; here we focus on permitted grapes and lees ageing. Outside the EU, producers are free of these rules, though they widely copy European techniques.

Champagne has only one appellation: Champagne AC. Some villages have cru status: forty-four premier cru and seventeen grand cru, but these are not separate appellations. Unlike Burgundy or Alsace, the whole village is rated, not specific sites, and growers there face no stricter rules such as lower yields. Inevitably some outstanding sites lie in lower-rated villages, and not every plot in a grand cru village has the same potential; still, the classification persists and the terms may appear on labels.

The vineyards are concentrated in five sub-regions. The three most famous, near Reims and Épernay, are the Montagne de Reims, the Vallée de la Marne and the Côte des Blancs. The Côte de Sézanne is about thirty kilometres south-west of Épernay, and the Côte des Bar over a hundred kilometres to the south-east.

Climate and grape growing. The climate is cool continental and viticulture is challenging: winter freeze, spring frost, rain and cloud. But even in the warmest years, sugar stays low and acidity high, ideal for sparkling wine. Against frost, most vineyards are on slopes. The soils are mainly chalk, draining well after storms but holding enough water in dry spells. Producers are fully committed to sustainable viticulture, with ambitious targets to cut synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.

Grape varieties. Three main grapes: Chardonnay, mostly in the Côte des Blancs and Côte de Sézanne, much lighter than in Burgundy, high in acidity, floral and citrus; Pinot Noir, mostly in the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar, fuller, giving the structural backbone of most blends and some red fruit; and Meunier, mostly in the Vallée de la Marne, because it buds late and escapes the more frequent spring frosts there, adding fruitiness and especially important for wines to drink young.

Winemaking. Champagne is made by the traditional method. Grapes must be hand-picked, to select and keep whole, healthy bunches. Pressing is tightly controlled: the first juice, the cuvée, is the purest, the rest is the taille, and the best Champagnes use only the cuvée. The first fermentation may be in steel, oak or both; malolactic may be encouraged or prevented, and base wines briefly aged in oak or kept in inert vessels, depending on house style. Since the weather varies a lot, blending is crucial: wines are fermented in small parcels, and big houses blend dozens of wines to keep their style.

Ageing depends on style. Non-vintage wines must age at least fifteen months, at least twelve on the lees. Vintage wines at least thirty-six months, including, according to the new edition, at least twelve on the lees. In practice, ageing is often much longer.

All Champagne has high acidity and some autolytic character. Non-vintage is lighter, with fresher fruit, the best made complex by reserve wines. Vintage wines, made in the best years, are more concentrated, with more toast and biscuit from longer lees ageing. Rosé comes in non-vintage and vintage; the best balance autolysis with delicate red berry notes. Blanc de Blancs is light to medium-bodied with citrus; Blanc de Noirs fuller with more red fruit. Many houses make a prestige cuvée, often vintage, from their best parcels, often closed and austere young, repaying years of cellaring and commanding premium prices. Brut is by far the most popular style; Brut Nature is growing, but still a very small share.

Crémant. Several French sparkling ACs are called crémant, especially Crémant d'Alsace, Crémant de Bourgogne and Crémant de Loire. Traditional method, at least nine months on the lees, generally from the grapes used for the region's still whites; in Alsace, aromatic grapes such as Muscat and Gewurztraminer are not allowed, while Chardonnay is.

Saumur and Vouvray. After Champagne, the Loire is France's next biggest sparkling centre, with two major appellations besides Crémant de Loire. Sparkling Saumur can use various local grapes plus Chardonnay, which with Chenin Blanc and Cabernet Franc goes into the best wines; red sparkling Cabernet Franc is made too. Sparkling Vouvray is made in larger volume than still Vouvray, almost always pure Chenin Blanc. Chenin's natural acidity suits sparkling wine, but it takes on less bready, biscuity character than Chardonnay or Pinot Noir: its autolytic notes tend to be smoky and toasty. Both use the traditional method with at least nine months on the lees.

Cava is an unusual DO covering several non-contiguous areas of Spain. Yet the vast majority comes from Catalonia, around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, with other areas in Navarra, Rioja and Valencia. Traditional method, at least nine months on the lees. Traditional grapes are Macabeo, or Viura, Xarel·lo and Parellada for whites, Garnacha and Monastrell for rosés. Cava from traditional grapes is usually dry, with medium acidity and an autolytic character different from Champagne's bread and toast. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, more recently allowed, add fruit and acidity, but are controversial, as some feel they erode Cava's identity. Most Cava is non-vintage, ready to drink, less acidic than Champagne and very approachable; a few producers make premium Cavas with extended lees ageing.

Asti DOCG, in Piemonte, is made from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains by the Asti method, with that grape's distinct grapey character: peach, grape and flowers. Always sweet and low in alcohol, about seven per cent, with no autolytic notes to mask the fruit, it should be drunk as young as possible.

Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, with two areas: Prosecco DOC, covering much of Veneto and Friuli, and the higher-quality Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG, on steep limestone hills between these towns north-west of Venice. Cartizze and Rive indicate exceptional sites. The grape, once also called Prosecco, has been renamed Glera to protect the appellation names. Prosecco is usually made by the tank method: medium acidity, green apple and melon. It comes as Brut, Extra Dry and Dry, usually a little sweeter than Champagne or Cava, with sugar often left by stopping fermentation through chilling and filtering. It is drunk young and fresh. New in this edition: since a rule change in twenty twenty, the DOC can make rosé Prosecco, mainly Glera with up to fifteen per cent Pinot Noir.

Sekt. Germany is a huge market, with the world's highest per capita sparkling wine consumption, mostly Sekt, nearly all made by the tank method. Base wines often come from France or Italy and are made sparkling in Germany. Deutscher Sekt, by contrast, must use only German grapes, the best from Riesling; if all grapes come from one quality region, such as Mosel, it may be labelled Deutscher Sekt b.A. A few top estates make single-vineyard, traditional-method Sekt, but it is rare.

Australia makes many styles. Cool and moderate regions such as Yarra Valley, Adelaide Hills and Tasmania give complex, elegant traditional-method wines, mostly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, in every style. Inexpensive wines come from warm regions such as Riverina, by tank or carbonation, fruity and in all sweetness levels. Sparkling reds, mostly Shiraz, have had their biggest commercial success here, though sales have fallen sharply: full-bodied, with red berry fruit, smooth tannins and some residual sugar.

New Zealand has a strong reputation for traditional-method wines from the Champagne grapes: its southerly position and cool maritime climate ripen Chardonnay and Pinot Noir slowly, giving elegant wines in all styles. They are made everywhere except Auckland, mostly in Marlborough; the North Island gives a richer style, and cross-regional blends are common. Sparkling Sauvignon Blanc is made too, by tank or carbonation, to keep its intense aromas.

South Africa. Traditional-method wines are labelled Cap Classique, while Méthode Cap Classique describes the process. Grapes come from across the Western Cape, the best wines from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. In the warm climate, site selection is crucial: south-east-facing slopes or coastal sites. According to the new edition, Cap Classique wines must spend at least twelve months on the lees, and many top producers belong to the Cap Classique Producers Association, which promotes and improves their quality. There is also a large domestic market for off-dry to sweet carbonated sparkling wine.

The USA. California makes the vast majority of American sparkling wine. The best come from cool areas such as Los Carneros and Anderson Valley, by the traditional method, mainly Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, often with long lees ageing, five years not being unusual: concentrated, complex and high in acidity. Large volumes of cheap, fruity, often medium-sweet to sweet wines are made by tank or carbonation from Central Valley grapes.

To sum up: Champagne, its crus, five sub-regions and three grapes; fifteen months for non-vintage, thirty-six for vintage, twelve of them on the lees; crémant, Saumur and Vouvray at nine months; Cava; Asti; Prosecco and its new rosé; Sekt; and the New World, with Cap Classique at twelve months.

Perhaps more than any other wine, Sherry is defined by maturation. None of its key techniques, the solera system, biological ageing or oxidative ageing, is unique to the region, but in Jerez they are exploited to the full.

The vineyards surround Jerez de la Frontera in southern Spain, which gives the region its name. New in this edition: at the time of publication, several changes to the Jerez DO were awaiting EU approval. One would allow various unfortified styles of Sherry, under conditions such as alcohol level and typical aromas. Here, however, we cover only fortified wines.

In the vineyard. The climate is hot, sunny and Mediterranean; vineyards nearer the coast are a little cooler, thanks to the poniente, a cool, humid westerly wind. Sometimes the hot, drying levante from the east sends temperatures soaring, stressing vines and damaging grapes. Rainfall is high for Spain, but low in the growing season: it is the albariza soil that lets the vines cope. Very high in chalk, it drains well, but above all, being deep, it holds plenty of water for summer. After harvest, rectangular pits are dug between rows to trap rainwater, smoothed over in spring; and in summer a hard crust forms on the surface, limiting evaporation.

Three grapes are permitted. Palomino, the vast majority: naturally low in acid and without obvious aromas, it is ideal because the style comes from ageing. Pedro Ximénez, or PX, also neutral, thin-skinned and ideal for sun-drying, is used for sweet Sherries; very little grows in Jerez, and most comes from neighbouring Montilla-Moriles, where it does better, an unusual feature the rules allow. And Muscat of Alexandria, in very small amounts, also for sweet wines.
