In the winery, dry styles. Palomino makes the dry wines. With harvest heat, grapes must reach the press fast to avoid oxidation. Fermentation is usually in large stainless steel tanks at twenty to twenty-five degrees, warm for a white, but deliberate: the aim is a neutral, dry base wine of about eleven per cent.

First classification. In autumn the wines are sorted: those for biological ageing and those for oxidative ageing, based on flavour. Typically, lighter, paler wines with more finesse go to biological ageing, darker, richer, heavier wines to oxidative. By now the film-forming yeast, flor, has started to grow on all of them. Criteria depend on house style, and nothing is left to chance: producers need certain volumes of each style for their brands. As a guide, grapes from cooler coastal vineyards or cooler fermentations suit biological ageing, those from warmer inland sites or warmer fermentations suit oxidative ageing.

Fortification and sobretabla. The wines are then fortified with neutral spirit, according to the new edition at ninety-five per cent, and left for a few months before entering a solera: this is sobretabla. Wines for biological ageing go to fifteen to fifteen and a half per cent, ideal for flor; sobretabla is crucial, as producers check that the flor develops properly, in a second classification; wines that fail are refortified for oxidative ageing or rejected. Wines for oxidative ageing go to seventeen per cent, which kills flor, so sobretabla is less critical.

Naturally sweet styles. Grapes are sun-dried to concentrate sugar, which also gives raisin flavours. They are then pressed and fermentation started, but the juice is so concentrated the yeast manage only a few degrees; the wine is then fortified to seventeen per cent.

Maturation in the solera. Sherry ages in six-hundred-litre oak casks, called butts, very old and often first used for unfortified wine so they give no oak flavour. The wood lets oxygen in, and butts are only five-sixths full. Until now, ageing was only allowed in Jerez, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María; according to the new edition, a proposed change would allow it in any bodega in the DO, except that Fino cannot be aged in Sanlúcar. Keeping wine cool is a challenge: traditional bodegas have thick whitewashed walls, high ceilings, windows facing the poniente and damp earth floors for humidity; some are now air-conditioned.

The solera system groups butts into levels of different average age, the criaderas. The oldest level is the solera. Wine for bottling is drawn from the solera, an equal amount from each butt, never emptying it. The solera is topped up from the first criadera, slightly younger: an equal amount from each butt is drawn, mixed, then used to top up every solera butt. The first criadera is topped up from the second, and so on; the youngest is filled with sobretabla wine. There can be three to fourteen criaderas. Because of this blending, only average age can be stated. The great advantage: the wine drawn is consistent every time, as new wine takes on the character of the older wine it joins, provided poor wine isn't fed in and too much isn't drawn each year. Each criadera belongs to one solera, and criaderas are often kept in different buildings to limit the risk of catastrophe.

Flor and biological ageing. Flor is a mix of yeast strains forming a thick layer on the wine. They feed on alcohol, nutrients and oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and acetaldehyde, which gives biologically aged Sherry its unique flavour. Flor needs precise alcohol, temperature and humidity: it cannot survive above fifteen and a half per cent, and prefers cool to moderate temperatures and high humidity; it grows most in spring and autumn and dies back in winter and summer. Even a butt's position in the bodega affects style. The solera sustains permanent flor in every butt; part-filled butts give it air, and the layer protects the wine from oxidation. Since it constantly consumes alcohol and nutrients, regular additions of new wine are needed, and wine is drawn frequently through the year; this also suits the style, as Fino loses freshness fast and should be drunk soon after bottling. These wines rarely exceed an average age of three to four years: by about seven, nutrients run low, the flor fails and oxidative character develops.

Oxidative ageing. Oloroso, PX and some Muscat Sherries age without flor, exposed to the air in the butts; Amontillado ages oxidatively after a biological phase. Adding young wine preserves the base character, which would otherwise become over-oxidised. These Sherries can age for over thirty years, and as water evaporates, alcohol rises to twenty-two per cent.

Blending and finishing. The solera gives consistent style, but most Sherries, including many of the best, blend several soleras; very old Oloroso, for example, is balanced with younger wine. Most are fined and filtered, but the trend is towards minimal intervention, especially for biological wines, whose vibrancy can be dulled. According to the new edition, a proposal would define the term en rama for wines that are not fined or cold-stabilised, though they may be filtered.

Dry styles. Fino and Manzanilla have only biological ageing: pale lemon, citrus, almonds, herbs and bready flor notes, a flavour sometimes called tangy or salty. They don't improve in bottle and should be drunk as fresh as possible. Wines aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda have their own DO, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda: made like Fino, but the cooler, more humid coast guarantees thick flor all year, giving a more intensely tangy aroma; the most famous style is Manzanilla fina.

Oloroso has only oxidative ageing: brown, full-bodied, toffee, leather, spice and walnut. Very old Olorosos become very concentrated and astringent, which younger wine in the solera balances. Amontillado has biological ageing first, then is refortified to seventeen per cent to kill the flor and moved into an Amontillado solera: amber to brown, less full than Oloroso, combining yeast-derived and oxidative notes, and able to age as long. Palo Cortado, rare, has the aroma of an Amontillado and the body and richness of an Oloroso; some producers identify it at the second classification, methods vary, and it can be hard to tell from the other two, but it is nearly always very high quality.

Naturally sweet styles, all oxidatively aged, are rare and used mostly to sweeten other Sherries. PX is deep brown and lusciously sweet, often reaching five hundred grams of sugar per litre, with dried fruit, coffee and liquorice. Muscat is similar, with a dried citrus peel note.

Sweetened styles. Pale Cream has a short biological ageing before sweetening, usually with rectified concentrated grape must; it looks like Fino but rarely shows much flor character. Medium and Cream are a very diverse category, from cheap to super-premium. Traditionally, Medium had to show both biological and oxidative character and Cream only oxidative; according to the new edition, producers will have more freedom here, and the two will be distinguished mainly by sugar, Cream being sweeter. The best, sweetened with PX, combine the toffee, leather and walnut of the dry wine with the dried fruit of the sweet; cheaper versions can be cloying. The terms Amontillado, Oloroso and Palo Cortado are reserved for dry wines: Oloroso dulce no longer exists.

Age-indicated Sherries. Four categories: VORS and VOS, at least thirty and twenty years average age, with each batch approved by a tasting panel; and twelve and fifteen years old, applying to a whole solera, so less precise. Only Amontillado, Palo Cortado, Oloroso and PX qualify.

To sum up: albariza and Palomino; classification, fortification to fifteen or seventeen per cent and sobretabla; the solera and its criaderas; flor and oxidative ageing; Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Palo Cortado and Oloroso; PX and Muscat; Pale Cream, Medium and Cream; VOS and VORS; and the pending reforms of the Jerez DO.

Port is made by adding grape spirit to fermenting juice to create a sweet, alcoholic wine. The technique has been used here since the eighteenth century, and similar wines are now made around the world. Port comes in red, white and rosé, but here we focus on red.
Two locations. The industry is split between the twin cities of Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia, on either side of the Douro's mouth, and the vineyards, which begin seventy kilometres upstream.

In the vineyard. There are three sub-regions: the Baixo Corgo, giving the lightest wines; the Cima Corgo, with the greatest number of top vineyards; and the Douro Superior, still sparsely planted but also renowned for top wine.

The climate is broadly warm continental, as the Serra do Marão shields the area from cool, rain-bearing Atlantic winds. But it varies: the Baixo Corgo in the west is coolest and wettest, and it gets progressively hotter and drier to the east. Growers face spring frosts and occasional downpours at flowering or harvest; summer days are very hot and growing-season rainfall very low. Viticulture is possible thanks to schist bedrock, which fractures vertically so roots can reach deep water built up by winter rains.

Topography. In the Baixo and Cima Corgo, vineyards are on very tall, very steep slopes above the Douro and its tributaries. Growers exploit this: it can be much cooler at the top than the bottom, and some north-facing sites are deliberately chosen to avoid full sun. But simply managing such slopes is a huge, costly challenge. Traditionally vines were planted on narrow terraces supported by stone walls, called socalcos: a few rows each, no mechanisation, expensive walls, but still widely used. Newer patamares are terraces without walls, wide enough for tractors. Where slopes are gentler, vinha ao alto plants vines up and down the slope, with cross-slope roads from which machinery is winched. Both systems are prone to erosion, and vinha ao alto is not viable on the steepest slopes.

Grape varieties. Most red Ports are complex blends of many varieties, thick-skinned and tannic, with black fruit and floral aromas. Five are preferred for premium Port: Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Touriga Nacional and Tinto Cão.

In the winery. Fermentation is stopped by fortification when alcohol reaches five to nine per cent, to keep sweetness; so it lasts only about twenty-four to thirty-six hours. Normal red wine extraction is not vigorous enough for the colour and tannin expected, so other techniques are used.

Foot treading is the traditional method and the benchmark: teams tread the grapes for three to four hours in shallow granite troughs called lagares; once fermentation starts, treading stops and the cap is punched down regularly. Very labour-intensive, it is now used only for some premium wines. Autovinifiers, one of the earliest automated methods and still widely used: the carbon dioxide from fermentation pushes juice up into a holding tank; at a set pressure, a valve releases and the wine floods back over the cap, and the cycle restarts, every fifteen to twenty minutes in active fermentation, giving far more skin contact than pumping over; as pre-fermentation extraction is limited, many now have mechanical paddles. Piston plungers and robotic lagares imitate treading: round, open steel vats where pistons push the cap down, or a rectangular tank the size of a lagar with a moving gantry of robotic feet that crush the grapes and then punch down. Many consider them as good as foot treading, and they are widely used for premium wines.

Fortification kills the yeast, giving a stable sweet wine of nineteen to twenty-two per cent. All Port is sweet, but some more than others, depending on house style and timing of fortification. The spirit, aguardente, can be no stronger than seventy-seven per cent; with low alcohol before fortification, a lot is needed: on average twenty per cent of a bottle of Port is spirit, compared with about three and a half per cent in Fino Sherry.

Maturation. Ports are usually taken downstream to Vila Nova de Gaia, whose cooler coastal climate suits slow maturation. Some, notably Tawnies, have always been kept up the Douro, where heat speeds ageing and colour loss; with air-conditioned warehouses, more wine is now aged in the vineyard area. Maturation uses old oak vessels, small and very large, and now also steel, never new oak. This gives two broad styles: ruby and tawny.

Ruby styles keep primary fruit: oxygen is limited by fairly short ageing in very large oak vessels or steel. This covers Ruby, Reserve Ruby, LBV and Vintage. All are deeply coloured with intense primary fruit at bottling. Ruby, Reserve Ruby and some LBVs are fined and filtered and don't improve in bottle; some LBVs and all Vintage Ports are unfiltered and can age for a long time, turning garnet with tertiary notes of cooked fruit, prune, leather and wet leaves.

True Tawnies undergo long oxidative ageing in barrels called pipes. Made like rubies, they differ only in maturation: they turn garnet then tawny, and only the very oldest become fully brown. Fruit becomes raisiny, with walnut, coffee, chocolate and caramel. They throw their deposit in wood, need little treatment and are ready on release. Nearly all Ports, even vintage styles, blend varieties and sites, and blending continues throughout maturation.
Types. Nearly all Port is red, and all the styles below are non-vintage, except LBV and Vintage, which come from a single year.

Inexpensive Ports. Ruby blends wines of one to three years, lacking the concentration and tannin of premium rubies. Basic Tawny shows browning but is no older than a ruby: its colour comes from lighter wines from the Baixo Corgo, some White Port, hot maturation in the Douro or heavy fining.
Special categories. Reserve, or Reserva, applies to Ruby and Tawny of higher quality, approved by an official tasting panel; a Reserve Tawny must spend at least six years in wood.

LBV, Late Bottled Vintage, is a single-vintage wine aged four to six years before bottling, mostly in large oak, making it more approachable than Vintage Port. Most are fined and filtered, like a high-quality Reserve Ruby, ready to drink. A few are unfiltered: closer to Vintage, they benefit from bottle age, throw a deposit and need decanting.

Tawny with an indication of age undergoes long oxidative ageing in pipes and may be labelled ten, twenty, thirty or forty years old, if it shows the character typical of that age: it is an average age, not that of the youngest component. The bottling year must be shown, as these wines lose freshness in bottle. They are the finest Tawnies, exceptionally complex and concentrated, often the flagship of specialist houses.

Vintage Port. Producers must register their intention in the second year after harvest and bottle by the third. Ageing is in large oak or steel, with no fining or filtering. On release these are the most concentrated, tannic Ports; some drink them young, but they can age for decades, throwing heavy sediment. For most houses Vintage is the flagship, made on average three times a decade, from the best wines of their best vineyards. Each house decides whether to declare; according to the new edition, some years, such as twenty eleven and twenty sixteen, are declared by the vast majority, while for others, such as twenty fifteen, there is less consensus.

Single Quinta Vintage Port comes from a single estate, or quinta, named on the label. Small producers with one quinta declare only in great years. Large houses with several quintas blend the best of all of them in top years, and in other years release their best wines as Single Quinta Vintage: less prestigious, but high quality, often aged in bottle by the house and released ready to drink.

To sum up: the Douro, its three sub-regions, schist and terraces; five main grapes; short fermentation, intense extraction and fortification to nineteen to twenty-two per cent; ruby and tawny; Reserve, LBV, ten- to forty-year-old Tawnies; and Vintage and Single Quinta Vintage Port.

Fortified wines are made all over the world, and classic styles such as Port and Sherry have been copied successfully in many regions. We can't cover them all, so we focus on fortified Muscats, made in many of the major wine countries.

Several grape varieties are called Muscat, but all have low to medium acidity and perfumed aromas of orange blossom, rose and grape. They thrive in warm and hot climates, but the best sites have some cooling, which preserves acidity and aroma. There are two broad styles: youthful and unaged, or fully developed after long ageing.

Youthful, unaged Muscats are medium gold, floral and aromatic. In vineyard and winery, the aim is the purest varietal character. They are sweet but rarely luscious. They are made in many regions; a notable example is Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, from the Southern Rhône. Grapes are picked ripe and healthy, without raisining or drying, which would add dried fruit notes masking the pure varietal character. After crushing, the juice may be separated from the skins, but skin contact is widely used for more aroma and richness, sometimes continuing through part or all of fermentation. Fermentation is cool and stopped by fortification with ninety-six per cent grape spirit, giving a sweet wine. To keep primary fruit, the wines are stored in inert vessels, protected from oxygen, until bottling.

Fully developed, aged Muscats range from amber to brown and can be sweet or luscious. They are made in many countries, and some of the most celebrated luscious examples come from Rutherglen in Australia. Style depends on harvest timing, when the wine is fortified, and the length and type of ageing. For a sweet wine, grapes are picked ripe and healthy; for a luscious style, some raisining on the vine may be allowed, but carefully: it adds complexity, but too much loses the Muscat aromas. Fermentation is nearly always on the skins. According to the new edition, for luscious styles the wine is drained, pressed and fortified when alcohol has reached just one or two per cent, leaving a great deal of sugar.

These wines then undergo oxidative ageing that can last decades. Old wood is essential, since new oak would clash with the grape aromas, and large vessels are widely used, sometimes in warm conditions. They turn amber, then brown, with pronounced oxidative aromas, yet even very old wines often keep their Muscat aromas; the oldest are often given an aromatic lift by blending in a little younger wine before bottling.

To sum up: Muscats with orange blossom, rose and grape; the youthful style, such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, with skin contact, cool fermentation, fortification and protection from oxygen; and the aged style, such as Rutherglen, sometimes raisined, fortified very early and aged for a long time in old wood.
